patrice-lumumba.s: Patrice Lumumba was a Congolese nationalist, leader of the Mouvement National Congolais, who became the first prime minister of the independent Congo in June 1960. Within weeks the army mutinied and Katanga seceded, and his appeal for Soviet aid set him against Belgium, the…

patrick-john.s: Patrick John was a Dominican trade unionist and politician of the Dominica Labour Party who became the island's first prime minister on independence in 1978. His government faced strikes and mass protests, and he was forced from office in 1979.

patrick-tonyn.s: Patrick Tonyn was a British army officer who was governor of the Province of East Florida from 1774 to 1785. During the American Revolutionary War he made the colony a refuge for loyalists and a base for raids into Georgia.

pau-claris.s: Pau Claris was a Catalan cleric, canon of La Seu d'Urgell, who was president of the Generalitat of Catalonia during the Reapers' War. As a royal army advanced on Barcelona, he proclaimed a Catalan Republic under French protection in January 1641, and days later placed…

paul-kagame.s: Paul Kagame is a Rwandan soldier and politician who commanded the Rwandan Patriotic Front forces that ended the genocide against the Tutsi in 1994. He was vice-president and defence minister before becoming president in 2000.

paul-the-deacon.s: Paul the Deacon was a Benedictine monk and historian from a noble Lombard family of Friuli, educated at the royal court of Pavia. After the Frankish conquest he spent some years at Charlemagne's court before returning to Monte Cassino.

pavel-tsitsianov.s: Pavel Tsitsianov was a Russian general of Georgian descent who commanded Russian forces in the Caucasus from 1802. He stormed Ganja in January 1804, killing Javad Khan, and forced several khanates to accept Russian protection.

payen-the-butler.s: Payen the Butler was a Crusader noble, butler of the kings of Jerusalem, who became lord of Oultrejordain, the lands east of the Jordan. In 1142 he built the great castle of Kerak on a ridge east of the Dead Sea, which became the centre of the lordship and controlled the…

paynda-khan-tanoli.s: Paynda Khan Tanoli was chief of the Tanoli tribe and ruler of Amb, in the Hazara region of today's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, in the early 19th century. He resisted the expanding Sikh Empire, fighting its governors of Hazara, and lost part of his lands to them.

peace-of-pressburg-1805.s: The Peace of Pressburg was signed on 26 December 1805 at Pressburg (Bratislava) between France and Austria after Napoleon's victory at Austerlitz. Austria ceded Venetia to Napoleon's Kingdom of Italy and Tyrol, Burgau and other lands to Bavaria and Württemberg, which became…

pearl-river.s: The Pearl River is the great river system of southern China, formed by the West, North and East rivers, which meet in a broad delta at Guangzhou before reaching the South China Sea. In ancient times its western branches linked the highlands of Guizhou with the lowlands of Nanyue.

pearl-river-mississippi-louisiana.s: The Pearl River flows about 790 kilometres through Mississippi and along the Louisiana border into Lake Borgne and the Gulf of Mexico. Its lower course separated the Florida Parishes, part of the short-lived Republic of West Florida in 1810, from the lands to the east that…

pedakomati-vema-reddi.s: Pedakomati Vema Reddi was a king of the Reddi dynasty of coastal Andhra, ruling from Kondavidu from about 1403 to 1420. A patron of letters and himself an author in Sanskrit, he kept the great Telugu poet Srinatha at his court.

pedda-soma-bhupal.s: Pedda Soma Bhupal was a local chief who founded the Gadwal samasthan around 1663 in the land between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers, in today's Telangana. He built the fort at Gadwal, which became the seat of a family that ruled as tributaries of the Nizams of Hyderabad…

pedrarias-davila.s: Pedrarias Dávila was a Spanish soldier and colonial governor who arrived in 1514 as governor of Castilla de Oro, on the Isthmus of Panama. His rule was marked by violent raids on Indigenous peoples and by rivalry with Vasco Núñez de Balboa, whom he had executed in 1519.

pedro-caetano-pereira.s: Pedro Caetano Pereira was a ruler of Makanga, an Afro-Portuguese warlord state north of the Zambezi near Tete in Mozambique. With his father Gonçalo Caetano Pereira he built the state in the mid-19th century as the Portuguese prazo system broke down, ruling from fortified…

pedro-de-mendoza.s: Pedro de Mendoza was a Spanish nobleman and conquistador to whom Charles V granted the Río de la Plata governorate in 1534. He led a large expedition that founded the first settlement of Buenos Aires in 1536, but hunger and attacks by local peoples forced most settlers away.

pedro-de-valdivia.s: Pedro de Valdivia was a Spanish conquistador who served under Francisco Pizarro in Peru and then led an expedition south, founding Santiago in February 1541. As the first royal governor of Chile he founded Concepción, Valdivia and other towns and pushed into Mapuche lands.

pelopidas.s: Pelopidas was a Theban general and statesman who led the exiles who freed Thebes from its Spartan garrison in 379 BCE. With Epaminondas he revived the Boeotian League, commanded the Sacred Band at Leuctra in 371 BCE and helped make Thebes the leading power in Greece.

peoples-national-movement.s: The People's National Movement is a political party of Trinidad and Tobago founded by the historian Eric Williams in 1956. It won the elections that year, led the colony to independence in 1962 and governed without a break until 1986.

peoples-revolutionary-government-grenada.s: The People's Revolutionary Government was the socialist government of Grenada formed after the New Jewel Movement under Maurice Bishop overthrew Eric Gairy on 13 March 1979. It built close ties with Cuba and began an international airport at Point Salines.

pepin-ii-of-aquitaine.s: Pepin II of Aquitaine was the son of Pepin I, king of Aquitaine, and a grandson of Louis the Pious. Passed over when his father died in 838, he fought a long war against his uncle Charles the Bald for Aquitaine and held much of it in the 840s.

pepin-of-italy.s: Pepin of Italy was a son of Charlemagne, born Carloman, who was crowned king of Italy in 781 to rule the conquered Lombard kingdom. He campaigned against the Avars and the Duchy of Benevento.

perdiccas-ii-of-macedon.s: Perdiccas II was king of Macedon from about 448 to about 413 BCE, who repeatedly changed sides between Athens and Sparta in the Peloponnesian War. In 432 BCE he persuaded the Chalcidian towns to revolt from the Delian League and to concentrate their people at Olynthus,…

pericles.s: Pericles was an Athenian statesman and general who dominated the democracy from the 450s until his death in 429 BCE. He used the tribute of the Delian League, whose treasury had been moved to Athens, to fund the building programme of the Acropolis, including the Parthenon.

perth-amboy.s: Perth Amboy is a port city in New Jersey at the mouth of the Raritan River on Raritan Bay. Scottish proprietors founded it in the 1680s as the capital of East Jersey, naming it after the Earl of Perth.

petar-dobrovic.s: Petar Dobrović was a Serbian painter from Pécs and one of the leading modernist painters of Yugoslavia. When the Treaty of Trianon returned the Baranya region to Hungary, he was proclaimed president of the short-lived Serbian-Hungarian Baranya-Baja Republic in August 1921.

petar-kresimir-iv.s: Petar Krešimir IV was king of Croatia from 1058 to 1074, of the Trpimirović dynasty. He brought the Byzantine towns and islands of Dalmatia under his rule and styled himself king of Croatia and Dalmatia.

peter-chester.s: Peter Chester was a British army officer who served as governor of the Province of West Florida from 1770 until its capture by Spanish forces in 1781. He governed from Pensacola alongside an elected assembly, with which he often quarrelled.

peter-fraser.s: Peter Fraser was a Scottish-born New Zealand Labour politician who was prime minister of New Zealand from 1940 to 1949. He led the country through the Second World War, built on the welfare state founded under Michael Joseph Savage, and helped draft the United Nations Charter…

peter-iii-of-russia.s: Peter III was emperor of Russia for six months in 1762, a grandson of Peter the Great raised in Holstein. In 1745 he married Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst, who took the name Catherine.

peter-kenilorea.s: Sir Peter Kenilorea was a Solomon Islands teacher and politician who became chief minister in 1976 and the first prime minister when the islands became independent from Britain on 7 July 1978. He served as prime minister again in the mid-1980s and later as speaker of the…

peter-tali-coleman.s: Peter Tali Coleman was an American Samoan politician who became the first person of Samoan descent to be appointed governor, in 1956, and the territory's first elected governor in 1977. He served further elected terms until 1993 and also held senior posts in the Trust…

peteris-stucka.s: Pēteris Stučka was a Latvian Bolshevik lawyer and writer who led the Soviet government of Latvia proclaimed in December 1918. His regime took Riga in January 1919 and ruled much of the country with harsh revolutionary measures, but it was driven out by Latvian, Baltic German…

petro-kalnyshevsky.s: Petro Kalnyshevsky was the last otaman of the Zaporozhian Sich, holding the office for most years from 1762 to 1775. When Catherine II's army destroyed the Sich in 1775 he was arrested and exiled to the Solovetsky Monastery in the White Sea, where he was held for decades and…

petro-shelest.s: Petro Shelest was first secretary of the Communist Party of Ukraine from 1963 to 1972. While loyal to Moscow, he defended Ukrainian economic interests and tolerated some promotion of Ukrainian language and culture.

phanariotes.s: The Phanariotes were members of wealthy Greek families of the Phanar, the Greek quarter of Constantinople around the Ecumenical Patriarchate. From the late 17th century they served the Ottoman state as dragomans, and from the 1710s the sultans appointed them princes of…

phaya-choeng.s: Phaya Choeng is the founder of the Tai Lue kingdom of Sipsong Panna in the upper Mekong valley of southern Yunnan. According to Tai Lue chronicles, he united the Tai principalities of the region in 1180 and founded his capital at Chiang Hung, modern Jinghong.

philaretos-brachamios.s: Philaretos Brachamios was an Armenian general in Byzantine service who, after the defeat at Manzikert in 1071, built an independent principality in Cilicia and northern Syria. At its height it included Antioch, Edessa, Melitene and Marash.

philip-francis-little.s: Philip Francis Little was a lawyer from Prince Edward Island who became the first premier of the Colony of Newfoundland when responsible government was introduced in 1855. Leader of the Liberal Party, which drew strong support from Irish Catholics, he served until 1858 and…

philip-i-of-taranto.s: Philip I of Taranto was an Angevin prince, son of Charles II of Naples, who received the Principality of Taranto in 1294. He also held the Angevin claims to the Kingdom of Albania and the Principality of Achaea and, through his marriage to Catherine of Valois, the title of…

philip-iii-of-france.s: Philip III, called the Bold, was king of France from 1270 to 1285, the son of Louis IX. He inherited the lands of the counts of Toulouse, and in 1274 he handed the Comtat Venaissin, which had passed to the French crown after the Albigensian Crusade, to Pope Gregory X.

philip-iii-of-spain.s: Philip III was king of Spain and, as Philip II, king of Portugal from 1598 to 1621, during the Iberian Union. He left government largely to his favourite, the Duke of Lerma, made peace with England in 1604 and agreed the Twelve Years' Truce with the Dutch in 1609.

philip-duke-of-parma.s: Philip, Duke of Parma, was a son of Philip V of Spain and Elisabeth Farnese who founded the Bourbon-Parma line. Under the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle of 1748 he received the duchies of Parma, Piacenza and Guastalla.

philip-of-hachberg-sausenberg.s: Philip of Hachberg-Sausenberg was margrave of Hachberg-Sausenberg in the Breisgau and count of Neuchâtel in the late 15th century. He served the dukes of Burgundy and then the French crown as a soldier and diplomat, holding high offices.

philip-of-milly.s: Philip of Milly was a Crusader noble of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, lord of Nablus, who exchanged it in 1161 for the lordship of Oultrejordain with its castles of Kerak and Montréal. He became Grand Master of the Knights Templar in 1169 and died in 1171.

philip-otto-of-salm.s: Philip Otto of Salm was a count of the Rhinegrave branch of the house of Salm in the Vosges, raised to the rank of prince of the Holy Roman Empire in 1623. The elevation turned his lands, centred on Badonviller and Senones, into the Principality of Salm.

philip-sigismund-of-brunswick-wolfenbutt.s: Philip Sigismund of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel was a Lutheran prince of the House of Welf who administered the prince-bishoprics of Verden from 1586 and Osnabrück from 1591 until his death in 1623. As administrator he consolidated the Reformation in Verden, where Lutheran rulers…

philip-the-handsome.s: Philip the Handsome was the son of Emperor Maximilian I and Mary of Burgundy and inherited the Burgundian Netherlands as a child in 1482, with his father as regent. His marriage to Joanna of Castile made him king of Castile in 1506, but he died that year.

philip-v-of-spain.s: Philip V was king of Spain from 1700 to 1746, the first of the Bourbon dynasty. A grandson of Louis XIV, he inherited the throne as Philip of Anjou under the will of Charles II, which caused the War of the Spanish Succession.

philip-vi-of-france.s: Philip VI was king of France from 1328 to 1350, the first of the House of Valois. His accession over the claim of Edward III of England led to the Hundred Years' War, in which he was defeated at Crécy in 1346.

philip-william-elector-palatine.s: Philip William was duke of Palatinate-Neuburg and of Jülich and Berg from 1653, and Elector Palatine from 1685 to 1690. When the Simmern line of the Palatinate died out in 1685 he inherited the electorate, bringing a Catholic dynasty to the Palatinate.

philippe-leclerc-de-hauteclocque.s: Philippe Leclerc de Hauteclocque was a French general who joined the Free French in 1940. From Chad he led raids into Italian Libya, taking Kufra in 1941 and the Fezzan in 1942–1943, then commanded the 2nd Armoured Division, which liberated Paris in August 1944 and Strasbourg…

philippe-pastour-de-costebelle.s: Philippe Pastour de Costebelle was a French officer and the last governor of Plaisance, the French colony on Newfoundland, from 1706. After the Treaty of Utrecht of 1713 handed Newfoundland to Britain, he moved the settlers to Île Royale (Cape Breton Island) and became its…

philippine-revolution.s: The Philippine Revolution was the armed struggle against Spanish rule launched by the Katipunan secret society in August 1896. After a truce in 1897 it revived in 1898 under Emilio Aguinaldo during the Spanish–American War, leading to the declaration of independence on 12 June…

philippine-american-war.s: The Philippine–American War was fought between the United States and the First Philippine Republic after Spain ceded the islands to the United States in 1898. Fighting broke out in February 1899, and Filipino forces turned to guerrilla warfare.

phocaeans.s: The Phocaeans were the Ionian Greeks of Phocaea on the Aegean coast of Anatolia, famed seafarers who explored the western Mediterranean. They founded Massalia (Marseille) around 600 BCE and Alalia on Corsica, and traded with Tartessos in southern Iberia.

phra-bang.s: The Phra Bang is a gilded standing Buddha image, the palladium of the Lao monarchy, after which the city of Luang Prabang is named. Tradition holds that Fa Ngum brought it from Cambodia in the 14th century together with Theravada Buddhism.

phuntsog-namgyal.s: Phuntsog Namgyal was the first Chogyal, or king, of Sikkim, consecrated at Yuksom in 1642 by three Tibetan Buddhist lamas. Founder of the Namgyal dynasty, he organised a Buddhist monarchy over the Bhutia and Lepcha peoples and set up the administration of the kingdom.

piero-soderini.s: Piero Soderini was a Florentine statesman elected gonfaloniere of justice for life in 1502, leading the republic restored after the expulsion of the Medici in 1494. With Niccolò Machiavelli as his secretary he created a citizen militia.

pierre-belain-desnambuc.s: Pierre Belain d'Esnambuc was a Norman sea captain who founded the first permanent French colony in the Caribbean. He landed on Saint Christopher in 1625 and, backed by Cardinal Richelieu's Compagnie de Saint-Christophe, shared the island with the English.

pierre-buyoya.s: Pierre Buyoya was a Tutsi army officer who twice seized power in Burundi, ruling from 1987 to 1993 and again from 1996 to 2003. In his first term he opened the way to multiparty elections, which he lost to Melchior Ndadaye in 1993.

pierre-dugua-de-mons.s: Pierre Dugua de Mons was a Huguenot merchant and nobleman from Saintonge who held the French royal monopoly of the fur trade in North America. In 1604 he led the expedition, with Samuel de Champlain, that wintered on Saint Croix Island, and in 1605 he founded Port-Royal, the…

pierre-laval.s: Pierre Laval was a French politician who served as prime minister in the 1930s and became the leading figure of collaboration in Vichy France. As head of government from 1942 to 1944 he worked closely with Nazi Germany, sending French workers to the Reich and assisting the…

pierre-mendes-france.s: Pierre Mendès France was a French Radical politician and prime minister from June 1954 to February 1955. After the defeat at Dien Bien Phu he negotiated the Geneva Accords that ended the First Indochina War, and he opened the path to Tunisian autonomy.

pierre-nkurunziza.s: Pierre Nkurunziza was a Hutu former rebel commander of the CNDD-FDD who became president of Burundi in 2005, after the civil war. His decision to seek a disputed third term in 2015 led to protests, a failed coup attempt and a wave of repression and emigration.

pierre-poivre.s: Pierre Poivre was a French horticulturist and administrator who served as intendant of the Isle de France (Mauritius) and Bourbon from 1767 to 1772. He smuggled clove and nutmeg plants out of the Dutch-controlled Moluccas to break the Dutch spice monopoly, and developed the…

pilaji-rao-gaekwad.s: Pilaji Rao Gaekwad was a Maratha commander who founded the power of the Gaekwad family in Gujarat. Serving under the Dabhade senapatis, he seized Songadh in 1721 and raided Mughal Gujarat from there until he was assassinated in 1732.

pillar-of-eliseg.s: The Pillar of Eliseg is a stone cross shaft near Llangollen in north-east Wales, raised in the 9th century by Cyngen ap Cadell, king of Powys, in honour of his great-grandfather Eliseg. Its now largely illegible Latin inscription traced the royal line of Powys back to…

pinnata-castra.s: Pinnata Castra, 'the winged camp', is a place in north-east Scotland listed in Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 CE among the towns of the Vacomagi. Its location is uncertain: it has been identified with the promontory fort at Burghead on the Moray coast and with the Roman…

pino-iii-ordelaffi.s: Pino III Ordelaffi was lord of Forlì in Romagna from 1466 until his death in 1480, one of the last rulers of the Ordelaffi family that had governed the city since the 13th century. He strengthened the fortress of Ravaldino.

pippin-of-herstal.s: Pippin of Herstal was mayor of the palace of Austrasia and, after his victory over Neustria at Tertry in 687, the real ruler of the whole Frankish kingdom under figurehead Merovingian kings. He fought the Frisians under Redbad and took Dorestad and Utrecht around 690.

pir-panjal-range.s: The Pir Panjal Range is a chain of the Lesser Himalaya that separates the Kashmir valley from the hills of Jammu and the Punjab plains. Its passes, above all the Pir Panjal Pass on the Mughal road, carried traffic into Kashmir for centuries, and small hill states such as…

piri-mehmed-pasha-ramadanid.s: Piri Mehmed Pasha was a 16th-century ruler of the Ramadanid family, the Turkmen dynasty that governed Adana in Cilicia as hereditary Ottoman governors after 1517. He is remembered chiefly as a builder: he completed the Great Mosque complex of Adana begun by his predecessor,…

pirmin.s: Saint Pirmin was a wandering bishop and monastic founder in the Frankish realm. In 724, with the support of Charles Martel, he founded the Benedictine abbey of Reichenau on Lake Constance, and in 727 Murbach in the Vosges, before founding Hornbach, where he died.

pithana.s: Pithana was a king of Kussara in central Anatolia in the 18th century BCE. According to the inscription of his son Anitta, he captured the trading city of Nesa (Kanesh) by night and treated its people well.

pitu-guli.s: Pitu Guli was an Aromanian revolutionary of the Internal Macedonian-Adrianople Revolutionary Organisation from Kruševo. In the Ilinden Uprising of August 1903 he led rebel bands that took the town and helped proclaim the Kruševo Republic.

pope-pius-ix.s: Pope Pius IX reigned from 1846 to 1878, the longest pontificate in history. Driven briefly from Rome by the revolution of 1848, he lost most of the Papal States to the Kingdom of Italy in 1860 and Rome itself in 1870, after which he called himself a prisoner in the Vatican.

placido-de-castro.s: Plácido de Castro was a Brazilian soldier and surveyor who led the rubber tappers of Acre in the Acrean Revolution against Bolivia in 1902–1903. His capture of Puerto Alonso prepared the Treaty of Petrópolis of 1903, by which Brazil acquired Acre.

plaek-phibunsongkhram.s: Plaek Phibunsongkhram was a Thai army officer, one of the leaders of the 1932 revolution that ended absolute monarchy, and prime minister from 1938 to 1944 and 1948 to 1957. He promoted a nationalist programme, renamed Siam as Thailand in 1939 and allied the country with Japan…

platt-amendment.s: The Platt Amendment was a 1901 rider to a United States army appropriations act that set the conditions for ending the American occupation of Cuba. Written into the Cuban constitution, it gave the United States the right to intervene in Cuba and to lease naval stations,…

pol-pot.s: Pol Pot was the leader of the Khmer Rouge and of Democratic Kampuchea from 1975 to 1979. His regime emptied the cities, abolished money and religion, and forced the population into rural labour camps, causing the deaths of some 1.5 to 2 million Cambodians by execution,…

polemon-ii-of-pontus.s: Polemon II was the last client king of Pontus, a grandson of Queen Pythodorida. The emperor Caligula gave him the kingdom in 38 CE, and Claudius added part of Cilicia.

polish-ukrainian-war.s: The Polish–Ukrainian War was fought from November 1918 to July 1919 over Eastern Galicia, after the collapse of Austria-Hungary. It began with fighting in Lviv between Polish residents and the forces of the West Ukrainian People's Republic.

pomare-iv.s: Pōmare IV was queen of Tahiti for fifty years, from 1827 to 1877. Her reign was dominated by rivalry between British Protestant missionaries and French Catholic priests, which led France to impose a protectorate in 1842 and to fight the Franco-Tahitian War of 1844–1847.

pomponius-mela.s: Pomponius Mela was a Roman geographer from southern Hispania, the earliest Latin author of a surviving geographical work. His De Chorographia, written around 43 CE, describes the coasts of the known world, with notes on peoples and places.

ponhea-yat.s: Ponhea Yat was a Khmer king traditionally regarded as the last ruler of Angkor. After the Siamese of Ayutthaya sacked Angkor around 1431, he moved the royal court south and settled it at Phnom Penh, at the confluence of the Mekong and Tonle Sap rivers.

pope-alexander-iii.s: Pope Alexander III reigned from 1159 to 1181. For nearly twenty years he resisted Emperor Frederick Barbarossa and a series of imperial antipopes, supporting the Lombard League, whose new city of Alessandria was named after him.

pope-clement-viii.s: Pope Clement VIII reigned from 1592 to 1605. He absolved Henry IV of France in 1595 and brought the Duchy of Ferrara under direct papal rule in 1598, refusing to recognise Cesare d'Este as heir.

pope-gregory-vii.s: Pope Gregory VII, born Hildebrand, reigned from 1073 to 1085 and gave his name to the Gregorian reform. His struggle with Emperor Henry IV over the investiture of bishops led to Henry's penance at Canossa in 1077.

pope-honorius-iii.s: Pope Honorius III reigned from 1216 to 1227. He confirmed the Dominican order in 1216 and the Franciscan rule in 1223, and promoted the Fifth Crusade.

pope-innocent-iv.s: Pope Innocent IV reigned from 1243 to 1254. At the First Council of Lyon in 1245 he declared Emperor Frederick II deposed, and he sent envoys to the Mongols.

pope-leo-ix.s: Pope Leo IX, born Bruno of Egisheim-Dagsburg, was bishop of Toul before reigning as pope from 1049 to 1054. He travelled widely to enforce church reform against simony and clerical marriage.

pope-pius-v.s: Pope Pius V, a Dominican and former inquisitor, reigned from 1566 to 1572 and enforced the decrees of the Council of Trent. In 1569 he raised Cosimo I de' Medici to Grand Duke of Tuscany, in 1570 he excommunicated Elizabeth I of England, and he organised the Holy League whose…

pope-sixtus-iv.s: Pope Sixtus IV reigned from 1471 to 1484. He built the Sistine Chapel and refounded the Vatican Library, but was notorious for advancing his nephews, among them Girolamo Riario, for whom he acquired Imola and Forlì.

pope-stephen-ii.s: Pope Stephen II reigned from 752 to 757. When the Lombards took Ravenna and threatened Rome, he crossed the Alps in 753–754, the first pope to do so, and anointed the Frankish king Pepin the Short.

porfirio-diaz.s: Porfirio Díaz was a Mexican general, hero of the war against the French intervention, who seized power in 1876 and ruled almost continuously until 1911. The period, called the Porfiriato, brought railways, mines and foreign investment but also great concentration of land and…

port-vila.s: Port Vila is a port town on the island of Efate and the capital of Vanuatu. In 1889 French and other settlers there declared the short-lived commune of Franceville, independent of both Britain and France.

porto-longone.s: Porto Longone, today Porto Azzurro, is a harbour town on the east coast of Elba. Spain built a large star-shaped fortress there in 1603 and added it to the State of the Presidi, its chain of coastal garrisons in Tuscany, giving the Spanish crown a base beside the Principality…

porto-torres.s: Porto Torres is a port town in north-western Sardinia, the Roman colony of Turris Libisonis. In the Middle Ages it gave its name to the Judicate of Torres (Logudoro), and its Romanesque basilica of San Gavino is the largest in Sardinia.

potatau-te-wherowhero.s: Pōtatau Te Wherowhero was a leading chief of the Waikato tribes and a noted warrior of the Musket Wars. In 1858 he was crowned at Ngāruawāhia as the first Māori King, chosen by the Kīngitanga movement to unite tribes and protect Māori land against sales to settlers.

prague-castle.s: Prague Castle is a vast castle complex above the Vltava in Prague, founded in the late 9th century by the Přemyslid duke Bořivoj. It has been the seat of Bohemian dukes and kings, of Holy Roman emperors, and of Czechoslovak and Czech presidents, and contains St Vitus Cathedral.

pratap-malla.s: Pratap Malla was king of Kantipur (Kathmandu) from 1641 to 1674, the most celebrated ruler of the Malla kingdoms of the Kathmandu valley. A poet who wrote in several languages, he enlarged the Hanuman Dhoka palace, built the Rani Pokhari pond and set up a famous inscription in…

pravahana-jaivali.s: Pravahana Jaivali was a king of Panchala who appears in the Chandogya and Brihadaranyaka Upanishads. In these texts he instructs the Brahmin Uddalaka Aruni and his son Shvetaketu in the doctrine of the five fires and the paths of the dead, one of the earliest statements of the…

pravarasena-ii.s: Pravarasena II was a 5th-century king of the main branch of the Vakataka dynasty in the Deccan, son of Rudrasena II and the Gupta princess Prabhavatigupta. He is credited with the Prakrit poem Setubandha, on Rama's bridge to Lanka, and founded a new capital at Pravarapura.

pravir-chandra-bhanj-deo.s: Pravir Chandra Bhanj Deo was the last ruling Maharaja of Bastar, installed as a child in 1936. After the state merged into India in 1948 he became a champion of the Adivasi peoples of Bastar in disputes over land and forests with the government.

prempeh-ii.s: Prempeh II was Asantehene from 1931 to 1970, succeeding his uncle Prempeh I. In 1935 the British restored the Asante Confederacy and recognised him as its head.

prince-frederick-of-noer.s: Prince Frederick of Noer, of the Augustenburg branch of the Danish royal house, was a leader of the German movement in Schleswig-Holstein. In March 1848 he joined the provisional government at Kiel and took command of its army, seizing the fortress of Rendsburg at the start of…

prince-george-of-greece-and-denmark.n: Prince George of Greece and Denmark
prince-george-of-greece-and-denmark.s: Prince George of Greece and Denmark was the second son of King George I of Greece. In December 1898 the great powers appointed him High Commissioner of the autonomous Cretan State, which he governed from Chania until 1906.

prince-of-transylvania.s: Prince of Transylvania was the title of the rulers of the Principality of Transylvania, first taken by John Sigismund Zápolya when he gave up the Hungarian royal title at the Treaty of Speyer in 1570. The princes were elected by the Transylvanian diet and ruled under Ottoman…

prince-rupert-of-the-rhine.s: Prince Rupert of the Rhine was a nephew of Charles I of England, a Royalist cavalry commander in the English Civil War and later an admiral. A leading backer of the fur-trading voyages to Hudson Bay, he became the first governor of the Hudson's Bay Company when it was…

princes-stone.s: The Prince's Stone is the base of an ancient Roman column that stood at Karnburg in Carinthia, where the princes of Carantania and later the dukes of Carinthia were installed. In the ceremony a free peasant seated on the stone questioned the new ruler in Slovene before handing…

princes-town-ghana.s: Princes Town, known locally as Pokesu, is a coastal village near Cape Three Points in western Ghana. In 1683 the Brandenburg African Company built the fort of Gross Friedrichsburg there, the headquarters of the Brandenburger Gold Coast, which traded in gold and enslaved people…

principality-of-lucca-and-piombino.s: The Principality of Lucca and Piombino was a Napoleonic state in Tuscany created in 1805 for Napoleon's sister Elisa Bonaparte and her husband Felice Baciocchi. It replaced the old Republic of Lucca and absorbed the Principality of Piombino.

prithvideva-ii.s: Prithvideva II was a king of the Kalachuri dynasty of Ratanpur in Chhattisgarh in the 12th century. He extended the kingdom and fought the Eastern Gangas of Kalinga, and numerous inscriptions and coins survive from his reign.

prithvipal-sen.s: Prithvipal Sen was the last king of Palpa, a hill kingdom in western Nepal ruled by the Sen dynasty. Palpa had stayed independent of Gorkha through marriage alliances, but in 1806 Prithvipal Sen was lured to Kathmandu and killed in the massacre that followed the murder of Rana…

privilegium-minus.s: The Privilegium Minus was a charter issued by Emperor Frederick Barbarossa in 1156 that raised the Margraviate of Austria to a duchy. It compensated Henry II Jasomirgott of the Babenberg family for giving up Bavaria, and granted the new duchy unusual rights, including…

prolaya-vema-reddi.s: Prolaya Vema Reddi was the founder of the Reddi kingdom in coastal Andhra. A former follower of the Kakatiyas, he joined the Musunuri Nayaks in the revolt against the Delhi Sultanate and around 1325 established his own rule, with his capital at Addanki.

provenzan-salvani.s: Provenzan Salvani was the leader of the Ghibelline government of Siena in the mid-13th century. He was among the commanders when Siena crushed Florence at the Battle of Montaperti in 1260, and he dominated the city afterwards.

przemko-of-scinawa.s: Przemko of Ścinawa was a Silesian Piast duke, a son of Henry III of Głogów, who received Ścinawa on the Oder as his share of his father's lands. He was one of the first rulers of the small Duchy of Ścinawa and was killed in 1289 at the Battle of Siewierz, fighting in the…

przemysl-ii.s: Przemysł II was duke of Greater Poland who gained Pomerelia in 1294 and was crowned King of Poland at Gniezno in 1295, the first royal coronation in Poland for over two centuries. He was murdered at Rogoźno in February 1296, probably by agents of Brandenburg, and his lands…

pshemakho-kotsev.s: Pshemakho Kotsev was a Kabardian politician who led the government of the Mountainous Republic of the Northern Caucasus in 1918–1919. He sought a federal democratic state of the mountain peoples, independent of Russia, but the republic was crushed between the Bolsheviks and…

purdil-khan.s: Purdil Khan was the eldest of the Kandahar Sardars, Barakzai brothers who took Kandahar after the Durrani Empire broke up in 1818. A half-brother of Dost Mohammad Khan of Kabul, he led the brothers' joint rule of the principality until his death in 1830, when Kohandil Khan…

pushpa-kamal-dahal.s: Pushpa Kamal Dahal, known as Prachanda, led the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) through its insurgency against the monarchy from 1996 to 2006. After the peace agreement the Maoists won the 2008 elections that abolished the monarchy, and he became the republic's first prime…

pyotr-masherov.s: Pyotr Masherov was a Soviet Belarusian leader, a partisan commander in the Second World War and Hero of the Soviet Union. As first secretary of the Communist Party of Byelorussia from 1965 to 1980 he oversaw rapid industrial growth and the commemoration of the war.

pyramid-texts.s: The Pyramid Texts are the oldest Egyptian religious writings, spells carved on the walls of the burial chambers of pyramids to help the king reach the afterlife. They first appear in the pyramid of Unas, last king of the Fifth Dynasty, and were used by later Old Kingdom kings…

pyrrhus-of-epirus.s: Pyrrhus was a king of the Molossians and of Epirus, sheltered as an infant by the Taulantian king Glaukias. Invited by Taras in 280 BCE, he defeated Rome at Heraclea and Asculum at such cost that a 'Pyrrhic victory' became proverbial.

pythian-games.s: The Pythian Games were the festival of Apollo at Delphi, one of the four Panhellenic games of ancient Greece. Reorganised by the Amphictyonic League in 582 BCE after the First Sacred War, they were held every four years and, unlike the Olympics, included contests in music and…

pshish.s: The Pshish is a river of the North-West Caucasus in Russia, a left tributary of the Kuban. It rises on the northern slopes of the Greater Caucasus and flows north through Krasnodar Krai and Adygea.

protagoras.s: Protagoras was a Greek philosopher from Abdera and the most famous of the sophists, the paid teachers of rhetoric and argument in 5th-century BCE Greece. He is known for the saying that 'man is the measure of all things'.

port-royal-acadia.s: Port-Royal was the capital of French Acadia, founded in 1605 by Pierre Dugua de Mons and Samuel de Champlain on the Annapolis Basin in present-day Nova Scotia. Destroyed by English raiders in 1613, it was re-established nearby and changed hands several times.

paxbolonacha.s: Paxbolonacha was the ruler of Acalan, the Chontal Maya state on the Candelaria river, when Hernán Cortés passed through on his march to Honduras in 1525. During that visit the captive Aztec ruler Cuauhtémoc was executed in Acalan's territory.

paxbolon-maldonado-papers.s: The Paxbolon-Maldonado Papers are a collection of colonial documents from Campeche, Mexico, that include a rare text in the Chontal Maya language written in the early 17th century for Pablo Paxbolon, a descendant of the rulers of Acalan. They trace the dynasty back to the 14th…

phormio.s: Phormio was an Athenian admiral of the 5th century BCE. Early in the Peloponnesian War he commanded a squadron based at Naupactus and in 429 BCE won two notable naval victories over larger Peloponnesian fleets in the Gulf of Corinth.

phalaris.s: Phalaris was tyrant of Acragas in Sicily from about 570 to 554 BCE. He extended the young city's power, but ancient writers remembered him for his cruelty, above all for the hollow bronze bull in which victims were said to be roasted alive.

philopoemen.s: Philopoemen was a general and statesman of Megalopolis who served eight times as strategos of the Achaean League. He reformed the league's army on the Macedonian model, defeated the Spartan tyrant Machanidas at Mantinea in 207 BCE and brought Sparta into the league in 192 BCE.

parliament-of-aland.s: The Parliament of Åland, the Lagting, is the legislature of the self-governing Åland Islands of Finland. It first met in Mariehamn in 1922 under the autonomy settlement confirmed by the League of Nations, with Julius Sundblom as its first speaker.

party-of-labour-of-albania.s: The Party of Labour of Albania was the ruling communist party of Albania. Founded in Tirana in November 1941 as the Albanian Communist Party, with Yugoslav help, it led the Partisan resistance and took power in 1944.

plateau-dalbion.s: The Plateau d'Albion is a high limestone plateau in Provence, south-eastern France, between Mont Ventoux and the Montagne de Lure. Ancient sources place the Celto-Ligurian Albici in this area, and their name may survive in that of the plateau.

potsdam-agreement.s: The Potsdam Agreement was signed on 1 August 1945 at the end of the Potsdam Conference between the United States, the Soviet Union and the United Kingdom. It set out the principles of the Allied occupation of Germany, including demilitarisation, denazification,…

portola-expedition.s: The Portolá expedition was a Spanish overland expedition led by Gaspar de Portolá in 1769–1770 to occupy Alta California, prompted by fears of Russian and British advances on the Pacific coast. Accompanied by the Franciscan Junípero Serra, it founded San Diego, and its scouts…

pago-pago.s: Pago Pago is the main town and harbour of American Samoa, on one of the finest natural harbours in the South Pacific, on the island of Tutuila. The United States acquired coaling rights there in 1878 and established a naval station in 1900, which administered the territory…

philadelphia.s: Philadelphia is the largest city of Pennsylvania, on the Delaware river in the eastern United States. William Penn founded it in 1682 as the capital of his Quaker colony, on land earlier settled by Lenape and Swedes.

padua.s: Padua (Padova) is a city in the Veneto, north-eastern Italy. As Patavium it was a leading city of the ancient Veneti and a wealthy Roman municipium, the home of the historian Livy.

pareatges-of-andorra.s: The Pareatges of Andorra were agreements signed in 1278 and 1288 by the Bishop of Urgell, Pere d'Urtx, and the Count of Foix, Roger-Bernard III, after years of conflict over Andorra. They established a joint and undivided lordship over the valleys, shared by the two co-princes.

pere-durtx.s: Pere d'Urtx was Bishop of Urgell in Catalonia in the second half of the 13th century. After long conflict with the counts of Foix over the lordship of Andorra, he signed the first Pareatge with Count Roger-Bernard III in 1278, establishing the joint sovereignty of the bishops…

penkovka-culture.s: The Penkovka culture is an early Slavic archaeological culture of the 6th and 7th centuries, found in the forest-steppe of Ukraine and Moldova, between the Dniester and the Dnieper and beyond. Its small settlements of sunken huts, hand-made pottery and metalwork are usually…

polyperchon.s: Polyperchon was a Macedonian general who served under Philip II and Alexander the Great. In 319 BCE the dying regent Antipater named him guardian of the kings in preference to his own son Cassander, setting off a civil war among Alexander's successors.

polonnaruwa.s: Polonnaruwa is a city in the North Central Province of Sri Lanka that served as the island's capital from the 11th to the 13th century. The Cholas ruled from it after taking Anuradhapura, and Vijayabahu I and Parakramabahu I kept it as the Sinhalese capital, adorning it with…

pensacola.s: Pensacola is a port city on Pensacola Bay in north-western Florida. A short-lived Spanish colony was planted there in 1559, and a lasting Spanish settlement was founded in 1698.

parliament-of-quillin.s: The Parliament of Quillín was a peace meeting held in January 1641 between the Spanish governor of Chile, the Marquis of Baides, and Mapuche leaders. It recognised the Biobío River as the frontier between Spanish Chile and the independent Mapuche lands and allowed missionaries…

pheidon-of-argos.s: Pheidon was a king of Argos, probably in the 7th century BCE, who made his city the leading power of the Peloponnese. Ancient writers credited him with introducing standard weights and measures, and later tradition wrongly said he struck the first Greek coins.

polykleitos.s: Polykleitos was a Greek sculptor of Argos, active in the second half of the 5th century BCE and famous for his bronze statues of athletes. His Doryphoros, or Spear-Bearer, illustrated his treatise the Canon on the ideal proportions of the human body, and he made the gold and…

petrarch.s: Petrarch, Francesco Petrarca, was an Italian poet and scholar born in Arezzo in 1304. His Italian love poems to Laura, collected in the Canzoniere, shaped European lyric poetry for centuries, and his search for classical manuscripts made him a founder of Renaissance humanism.

papiamento.s: Papiamento is a creole language spoken on Aruba, Bonaire and Curaçao in the southern Caribbean. Its vocabulary draws mainly on Portuguese and Spanish, with Dutch, English and African influences, and it developed among enslaved Africans and settlers from the 17th century.

peoples-electoral-movement-aruba.s: The People's Electoral Movement, in Papiamento Movimiento Electoral di Pueblo or MEP, is a political party in Aruba founded by Betico Croes in 1971. It led the campaign that won Aruba separate status within the Kingdom of the Netherlands in 1986, and it has since alternated in…

psamtik-i.s: Psamtik I was the founder of Egypt's Twenty-sixth, or Saite, Dynasty, reigning from 664 to 610 BCE. Beginning as an Assyrian vassal, he reunited Egypt, threw off Assyrian control and relied on Greek and Carian mercenaries, opening Egypt to Greek traders.

panini.s: Panini was an ancient Indian grammarian, probably active in the 5th or 4th century BCE in the north-west of the subcontinent, traditionally associated with Shalatula near Gandhara. His Ashtadhyayi, a treatise of nearly 4,000 rules, gives a complete and highly compressed…

paithan.s: Paithan is a town on the Godavari river in Maharashtra, western India. As ancient Pratishthana it was one of the main cities of the Deccan, named in early Buddhist texts and known to Greek and Roman traders as Paithana.

parthenon.s: The Parthenon is the temple of Athena Parthenos on the Acropolis of Athens, built between 447 and 432 BCE under Pericles by the architects Ictinus and Callicrates, with sculpture supervised by Phidias. It later served as a church, a Latin cathedral and a mosque.

peisistratus.s: Peisistratus was a tyrant of Athens who seized power three times between about 561 and 546 BCE and ruled until his death in 527 BCE. He kept the outward forms of Solon's constitution, promoted farming and public building, and expanded the Panathenaic festival.

pathankot.s: Pathankot is a city in the Punjab state of India, at the foot of the Himalayas where the roads to Jammu and Himachal Pradesh meet. The surrounding area was the land of the ancient Audumbaras, and the Pathania Rajputs, who later ruled Nurpur, took their name from the town.

pippinids.s: The Pippinids were a Frankish noble family of Austrasia, named after Pippin of Landen and Pippin of Herstal, who held the office of mayor of the palace in the 7th and 8th centuries. Through it they gained effective control of the Frankish kingdoms while Merovingian kings reigned.

protocol-of-korce.s: The Protocol of Korçë was an agreement signed on 10 December 1916 between the French military commander in the area and Albanian notables during the First World War. It created an autonomous Albanian province of Korçë under French protection, with its own administration,…

pa-sak-river.s: The Pa Sak is a river of central Thailand, about 513 km long, which rises in Loei province and flows south to join the Chao Phraya at Ayutthaya. Its confluence with the Lopburi and Chao Phraya rivers formed the island on which Ayutthaya was founded in 1351.

philip-davis.s: Philip Davis, known as Brave Davis, is a Bahamian lawyer and politician who became prime minister of the Bahamas in September 2021. Leader of the Progressive Liberal Party, he had served as deputy prime minister under Perry Christie from 2012 to 2017 before leading the party…

pribina.s: Pribina was a Slavic prince who ruled Nitra in the early 9th century until Mojmír I of Moravia expelled him around 833. He entered Frankish service, and around 839 Louis the German granted him lands in Lower Pannonia, where he built a fortified seat at Mosapurc, now Zalavár,…

palma.s: Palma is the capital of Mallorca and of the Balearic Islands, Spain, on a wide bay on the island's south-west coast. Founded as a Roman town after 123 BCE by Quintus Caecilius Metellus, it became Madina Mayurqa under Muslim rule and the capital of the Kingdom of Majorca after…

pollentia.s: Pollentia was a Roman town on the north-east coast of Mallorca, next to modern Alcúdia, founded by Quintus Caecilius Metellus after his conquest of the Balearics in 123 BCE. It became the island's most important Roman city, with a forum, temples and a small theatre, before…

pliva.s: The Pliva is a river in western Bosnia and Herzegovina that flows through the Pliva lakes and joins the Vrbas at Jajce in a waterfall over 20 metres high in the centre of the town. Its valley formed part of the defences of Jajce, the royal Bosnian fortress that became the seat…

prince-eugene-of-savoy.s: Prince Eugene of Savoy was a Paris-born general in Habsburg service and one of the greatest commanders of his age. He defeated the Ottomans at Zenta in 1697, shared victory with Marlborough at Blenheim in 1704 in the War of the Spanish Succession, and in the war of 1716 to…

palapye.s: Palapye is a town in central Botswana, between Gaborone and Francistown. Khama III moved the capital of the Bangwato there from Shoshong in 1889, and the hill town at Phalatswe, with its large stone church, became one of the biggest settlements in the region.

pamplona.s: Pamplona is the capital of Navarre in northern Spain, in a basin at the foot of the western Pyrenees. Founded by Pompey around 75 BCE, it became in the 9th century the seat of the Basque kingdom of Pamplona under Íñigo Arista, later called the Kingdom of Navarre, which was…

pheretime.s: Pheretime was a queen of Cyrene in the 6th century BCE, wife of Battus III and mother of Arcesilaus III. After her son was murdered at Barca, she asked the Persian satrap of Egypt, Aryandes, for help, and his army took the city around 515 BCE.

pavagadh.s: Pavagadh is a hill in Panchmahal district, Gujarat, India, crowned by the Kalika Mata temple, an important Hindu pilgrimage site. Its fortress was held by Chauhan Rajput rulers until Mahmud Begada of the Gujarat Sultanate captured it, with nearby Champaner, in 1484.

pratapsinh-gaekwad.s: Pratapsinh Gaekwad was the last ruling Maharaja of Baroda, succeeding his grandfather Sayajirao Gaekwad III in 1939. He acceded to India in 1947, and in 1949 Baroda was merged into Bombay State.

peloponnese.s: Morea was the name used from the Middle Ages to the 19th century for the Peloponnese, the large peninsula of southern Greece. It was divided after 1204 between the Frankish Principality of Achaea, Venetian ports and the Byzantine Despotate of the Morea, and conquered by the…

perseus-of-macedon.s: Perseus was the last king of the Antigonid dynasty of Macedonia, son of Philip V, reigning from 179 to 168 BCE. Rome went to war with him in the Third Macedonian War, and he was decisively defeated by Lucius Aemilius Paullus at Pydna in 168 BCE.

poienesti-lukashevka-culture.s: The Poienești-Lukashevka culture is an Iron Age archaeological culture of the late centuries BCE, named after sites in Romanian Moldavia and the Republic of Moldova. It is known mainly from cemeteries of cremation burials and settlements between the Carpathians and the Dniester.

probus-emperor.s: Marcus Aurelius Probus was Roman emperor from 276 to 282, a soldier from Sirmium in Pannonia. He drove Germanic invaders out of Gaul, secured the Rhine and Danube frontiers and settled large groups of barbarians, among them Bastarnae, inside the empire.

piet-retief.s: Piet Retief was a Voortrekker leader from the eastern Cape Colony who led a party of emigrants into Natal during the Great Trek. In February 1838, while negotiating a land grant, he and his companions were killed on the orders of the Zulu king Dingane at uMgungundlovu.

pagasetic-gulf.s: The Pagasetic Gulf, or Gulf of Volos, is a nearly enclosed inlet of the Aegean Sea in Thessaly, Greece, sheltered by the Pelion peninsula. The ancient cities of Pagasae and Demetrias stood on its shores, and the modern port of Volos lies at its head.

picardy.s: Picardy is a historical region of northern France, centred on the Somme valley, with Amiens as its main city and Beauvais and Saint-Quentin among its towns. A French province under the old regime, it was an administrative region from the 1960s until 2016, when it merged with…

pandua-malda.s: Pandua is a historic town in the Malda district of West Bengal, India, north of the old capital Gaur. In the 14th century the Ilyas Shahi sultans made it the capital of the Bengal Sultanate, and its monuments include the great Adina Mosque and the Eklakhi Mausoleum.

prilep.s: Prilep is a city in the Pelagonia plain of central North Macedonia. Above it stand the ruins of the Towers of Marko, the fortress of the 14th-century King Vukašin and his son Prince Marko, who ruled the Kingdom of Prilep after the break-up of the Serbian Empire until the…

pechenegs.s: The Pechenegs were a Turkic nomadic people who dominated the steppes north of the Black Sea from the late 9th century, after driving the Magyars westward. They raided and served as mercenaries for Byzantium, Kievan Rus' and Bulgaria, and killed Prince Sviatoslav of Kiev in 972.

prabhashankar-pattani.s: Sir Prabhashankar Pattani was an Indian administrator who served as diwan, or chief minister, of Bhavnagar State in Kathiawar, and as a member of the Council of India in London. He was regarded as one of the ablest administrators of the princely states and was a friend of…

pant-sachiv.s: The Sachiv, or Pant Sachiv, was one of the eight ministers of the Ashta Pradhan council created by Shivaji, responsible for royal correspondence and records. The office became hereditary in the family of Shankaraji Narayan, appointed by Rajaram in the 1690s, and the Pant…

pune.s: Pune, formerly Poona, is a city on the Deccan plateau in Maharashtra, western India. Shivaji spent his youth there, and in the 18th century it became the seat of the Peshwas, the Maratha chief ministers, with their palace of Shaniwar Wada.

peene.s: The Peene is a river in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, north-eastern Germany, about 100 km long. It flows east through Demmin and Anklam into the Szczecin Lagoon, and its name is also given to the Peenestrom channel separating the island of Usedom from the mainland.

piltene.s: Piltene, in German Pilten, is a small town on the Venta river in Kurzeme, western Latvia. Its castle was a residence of the bishops of Courland.

prabuty.s: Prabuty, in German Riesenburg, is a small town in the Pomeranian Voivodeship of northern Poland. In the Middle Ages its castle was the residence of the bishops of Pomesania, while their cathedral stood at nearby Marienwerder.

primorsk-kaliningrad-oblast.s: Primorsk, in German Fischhausen, is a small town on the Vistula Lagoon in the Kaliningrad Oblast of Russia. In the Middle Ages its castle was the residence of the bishops of Samland, whose cathedral stood in Königsberg.

panarukan.s: Panarukan is a coastal town in Situbondo Regency on the north coast of East Java, Indonesia. In the 16th century it was a port of the Hindu kingdom of Blambangan, and Sultan Trenggana of Demak died during a campaign against it in 1546.

puputan-bayu.s: Puputan Bayu was a rising of the people of Blambangan in eastern Java against the Dutch East India Company in 1771–1772. Led by Rempeg Jagapati from the fortified village of Bayu, the rebels inflicted heavy losses on Company forces before being crushed, and the war, with…

phonen.s: Phonen was a king of the Blemmyes in the 5th century, known from a letter in Greek that he sent to Abourni, king of the Nobadians, which was found at Qasr Ibrim in Lower Nubia. The letter deals with the conflict between the two peoples over the Nile valley and is one of the…

publius-cornelius-scipio-nasica-consul-1.s: Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica was a Roman politician, the son of Gnaeus Scipio Calvus. In 204 BCE he was chosen as the best man in Rome to receive the sacred stone of the Magna Mater.

phanagoria.s: Phanagoria was an ancient Greek city on the Taman peninsula, on the Asian side of the Cimmerian Bosporus, founded by settlers from Teos around 540 BCE. It became the second city of the Bosporan Kingdom and an important port for the grain trade.

pinnes.s: Pinnes was a Pannonian leader who took part with Bato the Breucian in the Great Illyrian Revolt against Rome from 6 CE. In 8 CE Bato the Breucian handed him over to the Romans in return for favourable terms, a betrayal for which Bato was then executed by his ally Bato the…

pennines.s: The Pennines are a range of hills and moors running north and south through northern England, from the Peak District to the Tyne Gap near the Scottish border, and often called the backbone of England. They divide the north-west from the north-east and have long shaped…

peoples-progressive-party-guyana.s: The People's Progressive Party is a political party of Guyana founded in 1950 by Cheddi Jagan, Janet Jagan and Forbes Burnham. It won the 1953 elections in British Guiana, but Britain suspended the constitution after 133 days, fearing a communist government.

peoples-progressive-party-the-gambia.s: The People's Progressive Party was a political party of The Gambia, founded in 1959 and led by Dawda Jawara. With strong support in the rural Protectorate, it won the elections of 1962, led the country to independence in 1965 and governed until the military coup of 1994.

pampanga.s: Pampanga is a province in central Luzon in the Philippines, north of Manila Bay, home of the Kapampangan people. Fertile and close to Manila, it supplied food and soldiers to the Spanish colony.

puebla-tlaxcala-valley.s: The Puebla-Tlaxcala Valley is a highland basin of central Mexico, east of the volcanoes Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl, shared by the modern states of Puebla and Tlaxcala. It was home to major centres such as Cholula, Cacaxtla, Tlaxcala and Huexotzinco.

pyrgi.s: Pyrgi was the chief port of the Etruscan city of Caere, on the Tyrrhenian coast at modern Santa Severa, north-west of Rome. Its sanctuary held temples of the goddess Uni, where in 1964 the Pyrgi Tablets were found: gold sheets of about 500 BCE recording in Etruscan and…

picts.s: The Picts were the people of northern and eastern Scotland in late antiquity and the early Middle Ages, first named by a Roman writer in 297. Descended from the Iron Age Caledonians and other tribes, they spoke a Brittonic language and left carved symbol stones.

pays-de-caux.s: The Pays de Caux is a chalk plateau region of Normandy, France, north of the Seine estuary between Le Havre and Dieppe, ending at the sea in white cliffs such as those of Étretat. It takes its name from the Caleti, the Gallic people who lived there before the Roman conquest.

puebla-state.s: Puebla is a state of central Mexico, east of Mexico City, with its capital at the city of Puebla. Its highlands, bordered by the volcanoes Popocatépetl and Pico de Orizaba, were home to major Mesoamerican centres such as Cholula and Cantona.

peter-canisius.s: Peter Canisius was a Dutch Jesuit priest, born at Nijmegen, who became one of the leading figures of the Catholic Counter-Reformation in the German-speaking lands. His catechisms were reprinted hundreds of times, and he founded or guided Jesuit colleges across central Europe.

puerto-cabello.s: Puerto Cabello is a port city on the Caribbean coast of Venezuela, in Carabobo state, with one of the best natural harbours in the country. In the 18th century it was the base of the Guipuzcoan Company and was strongly fortified.

pascoal-moreira-cabral.s: Pascoal Moreira Cabral was a bandeirante from São Paulo who led an expedition into the far west of Brazil in the early 18th century. In 1718 his party found gold on the Coxipó river, and in 1719 he founded the mining camp that became Cuiabá.

pero-do-campo-tourinho.s: Pero do Campo Tourinho was a Portuguese nobleman from Viana do Castelo who received the hereditary Captaincy of Porto Seguro from King John III in 1534. He arrived with settlers in 1535 and founded Porto Seguro and other villages.

pichincha-province.s: Pichincha is a province in the northern highlands of Ecuador, containing the capital, Quito, and named after the Pichincha volcano that rises above the city. Before the Inca conquest its northern part was home to the Caranqui and Cayambi, whose mound sites such as Cochasquí…

philip-the-arab.s: Philip the Arab was Roman emperor from 244 to 249, born in the province of Arabia in southern Syria. He made peace with the Sasanian king Shapur I after the death of Gordian III, fought the Carpi on the Danube, and in 248 celebrated the thousandth anniversary of Rome.

poem-of-almeria.s: The Poem of Almería is an incomplete Latin poem in hexameters, written in the mid-12th century and preserved with the Chronicle of Alfonso the Emperor. It celebrates the campaign of Alfonso VII of León and Castile and his allies against Almería in 1147, describing the…

petexbatun.s: Petexbatún is a region of the south-western Petén in Guatemala, around Lake Petexbatún and the river of that name, a tributary of the Pasión. In the Late Classic period it was dominated by a Maya kingdom ruled from Dos Pilas and later Aguateca, which conquered Ceibal in 735.

pastry-war.s: The Pastry War was the first French intervention in Mexico, in 1838–1839. France, pressing claims for damages to its nationals, including a French pastry cook in Mexico City, blockaded Mexican ports and took the fortress of San Juan de Ulúa at Veracruz.

penedes.s: The Penedès is a historic region of Catalonia between Barcelona and Tarragona, divided into the comarques of Alt Penedès, Baix Penedès and Garraf. In antiquity it was home to the Iberian Cessetani, and in the Middle Ages it was a frontier march of the county of Barcelona.

prithviraj-raso.s: The Prithviraj Raso is an epic poem in Brajbhasha attributed to Chand Bardai, said to have been the court poet of Prithviraj Chauhan. It tells, with much legend, of Prithviraj's life, his elopement with Samyukta and his wars against Muhammad of Ghor.

pithekoussai.s: Pithekoussai was an early Greek settlement on the island of Ischia in the Bay of Naples, founded in the first half of the 8th century BCE by colonists from Chalcis and Eretria in Euboea. It was the earliest lasting Greek foundation in the western Mediterranean and a trading…

popocatepetl.s: Popocatépetl is an active volcano in central Mexico, at about 5,400 metres the country's second-highest peak, on the borders of the states of Puebla, Morelos and Mexico. Its name means 'smoking mountain' in Nahuatl.

pattadakal.s: Pattadakal is a village on the Malaprabha river in Bagalkot district of Karnataka, India, with a group of 7th- and 8th-century temples built by the Chalukyas of Badami. Used for royal coronations, it combines northern Nagara and southern Dravida styles; the largest, the…

panduranga.s: Panduranga was the southernmost region of Champa, around modern Phan Rang and Phan Thiết in south-central Vietnam. After the Vietnamese conquest of Vijaya in 1471 it became the last centre of Cham kingship, surviving as a vassal of the Nguyễn lords and later of the Nguyễn…

phan-thiet.s: Phan Thiết is a coastal city in south-central Vietnam, formerly the capital of Bình Thuận province. It lay in the southern Cham region of Panduranga and passed to the Vietnamese in the 17th and 18th centuries.

paramardi.s: Paramardi was the last powerful king of the Chandela dynasty, ruling Bundelkhand from about 1165 to 1203. Prithviraj Chauhan defeated him and sacked Mahoba in 1182, and in 1203 Qutb al-Din Aibak captured his fortress of Kalinjar.

pachacuti.s: Pachacuti, born Cusi Yupanqui, was the ninth Sapa Inca, ruling from about 1438 to 1471. According to Inca tradition he saved Cusco from the Chanka, deposed his father Viracocha Inca and began the conquests that turned the kingdom of Cusco into the Inca Empire.

patan-gujarat.s: Patan is a city in northern Gujarat, India, known in medieval times as Anahilavada or Anahilapataka. Founded by tradition around 746 by Vanaraja of the Chavda dynasty, it was the capital of Gujarat under the Chaulukyas and Vaghelas until Alauddin Khalji's conquest at the end…

phnom-kulen.s: Phnom Kulen is a sandstone plateau in Siem Reap province, Cambodia, about 40 kilometres north-east of Angkor. In 802 Jayavarman II held a ceremony there proclaiming himself universal monarch (chakravartin) and Cambodia free of Javanese overlordship, an act traditionally taken…

parthenos-chersonesus.s: Parthenos, the Maiden, was the patron goddess of the Greek city of Chersonesus Taurica in the Crimea. Greek writers identified her with Artemis and with the virgin goddess of the Taurians, to whom, according to Herodotus, shipwrecked strangers were sacrificed.

palakus.s: Palacus was a king of the Scythians in the Crimea in the late 2nd century BCE, a son of Scilurus. Ruling from Scythian Neapolis near modern Simferopol, he pressed the Greek city of Chersonesus, which called in Mithridates VI of Pontus.

pithora-painting.s: Pithora painting is a ritual wall-painting tradition of the Rathwa, Bhil and Bhilala communities of eastern Gujarat and western Madhya Pradesh, India. Painted in bright colours on the inner walls of houses, often to fulfil a vow, the paintings show horses, riders, deities,…

piomingo.s: Piomingo, "Mountain Leader", was a Chickasaw leader of the late 18th century who headed the faction favouring alliance with the United States after the American Revolutionary War. He was among the Chickasaw signers of the Treaty of Hopewell in 1786, which set the nation's…

piilanihale.s: Piʻilanihale is a heiau, a Hawaiian temple, at Hāna on the east coast of Maui, regarded as the largest ancient temple platform in Polynesia. Built of basalt stones, its terraced wall rises about 15 metres.

palayakkarar.s: The Palayakkarar, known in English as Poligars and in Kannada as Palegars, were military chiefs of south India who held territories called palayams under the Vijayanagara Empire and its successor Nayaka states in return for military service and tribute. Many, such as the…

pushmataha.s: Pushmataha (c. 1764–1824) was a Choctaw chief, head of one of the three Choctaw districts. He rejected Tecumseh's call for a pan-Indian alliance in 1811, led Choctaw warriors on the American side against the Red Sticks in the Creek War and fought under Andrew Jackson at New…

preliminary-peace-convention.s: The Preliminary Peace Convention was the agreement signed in Rio de Janeiro on 27 August 1828 by the Empire of Brazil and the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata, under British mediation, that ended the Cisplatine War. Both sides gave up their claims to the disputed Banda…

peace-of-antalcidas.s: The Peace of Antalcidas, or King's Peace, was the settlement imposed by the Persian king Artaxerxes II in 387–386 BCE, negotiated by the Spartan Antalcidas, that ended the Corinthian War. It recognised Persian rule over the Greek cities of Asia Minor and Cyprus and declared…

pointe-a-pitre.s: Pointe-à-Pitre is the largest town and main commercial port of Guadeloupe, on the island of Grande-Terre at the southern end of the channel separating it from Basse-Terre. Developed from the 1760s, it grew into the economic centre of the colony, though the town of Basse-Terre…

penal-transportation.s: Penal transportation was the punishment of sending convicted criminals to a distant colony. Britain transported about 50,000 convicts to its American colonies before 1776 and about 162,000 to Australia between 1788 and 1868, mainly to New South Wales, Van Diemen's Land and…

prince-edward-island.s: Prince Edward Island is the smallest province of Canada, an island in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Known to the French as Île Saint-Jean, it passed to Britain in 1763, became a separate colony in 1769 and was renamed after Prince Edward, Duke of Kent, in 1799.

providence-rhode-island.s: Providence is the capital and largest city of Rhode Island, at the head of Narragansett Bay. Roger Williams founded it in 1636 after his banishment from Massachusetts, on land obtained from the Narragansett, as a refuge for freedom of conscience.

peoples-action-party.s: The People's Action Party is a political party in Singapore, founded in 1954 by Lee Kuan Yew and others, at first in alliance with left-wing trade unionists. It won the 1959 elections that brought self-government, led Singapore into Malaysia in 1963 and out again in 1965, and…

prohibition-in-the-united-states.s: Prohibition in the United States was the nationwide ban on the production, import and sale of alcoholic drinks from 1920 to 1933, under the Eighteenth Amendment to the Constitution. It encouraged bootlegging, smuggling and organised crime, with rum runners operating from the…

pitch-lake.s: Pitch Lake is the largest natural deposit of asphalt in the world, at La Brea in south-western Trinidad. Covering about 40 hectares, it was used by Walter Raleigh in 1595 to caulk his ships.

port-phillip-district.s: The Port Phillip District was an administrative district of the colony of New South Wales covering present-day Victoria, from 1836 to 1851. Centred on Melbourne, it was governed from 1839 by a superintendent, Charles La Trobe.

patrick-henry.s: Patrick Henry was a Virginian lawyer and orator who became a leading voice of resistance to British rule. He opposed the Stamp Act in 1765 and in 1775 urged Virginia to arm with the words 'Give me liberty, or give me death!'.

perth.s: Perth is the capital of Western Australia, on the Swan River near the Indian Ocean coast. It was founded in 1829 by Captain James Stirling as the capital of the Swan River Colony and grew slowly until the gold rushes of the 1890s.

perth-scotland.s: Perth is a city in central Scotland on the River Tay, near the royal centre of Scone. A royal burgh from the 12th century, it was often the seat of the Scottish court and Parliament in the Middle Ages, and James I was murdered there in 1437.

penateka.s: The Penateka, or Honey Eaters, were the southernmost division of the Comanche, living on the Edwards Plateau of central Texas. Closest to Spanish, Mexican and Texan settlement, they had the most contact with outsiders and suffered heavily from epidemics and from the Council…

palio-of-asti.s: The Palio of Asti is a bareback horse race held each September in Asti, Piedmont, first recorded in 1275, when the Astigiani ran it under the walls of Alba during a war. Riders represent the city's districts and nearby towns, and the race is preceded by a large historical…

pinamonte-bonacolsi.s: Pinamonte Bonacolsi was lord of Mantua from 1272 until his death in 1293. Having made himself captain of the people and removed rival families, he ended the commune's government and founded the rule of the Bonacolsi family.

paglia.s: The Paglia is a river of central Italy that rises on Monte Amiata in southern Tuscany and flows through Umbria past the foot of Orvieto's tufa cliff to join the Tiber. Its valley carried routes between Tuscany and Rome, including the Via Francigena pilgrim road.

pope-urban-iv.s: Pope Urban IV, born Jacques Pantaléon in Troyes, was pope from 1261 to 1264, a former archdeacon of Liège and patriarch of Jerusalem. He spent much of his reign at Orvieto and Viterbo, invited Charles of Anjou to take the Kingdom of Sicily from the Hohenstaufen, and in 1264…

perugino.s: Perugino, born Pietro Vannucci, was an Italian Renaissance painter of the Umbrian school who worked mainly in Perugia and Florence. Known for calm, balanced compositions and gentle figures, he painted the Delivery of the Keys in the Sistine Chapel and decorated the Collegio…

palazzo-dei-priori-perugia.s: The Palazzo dei Priori is the town hall of Perugia, begun in 1293 and enlarged into the 15th century, facing the Fontana Maggiore. It housed the priors who governed the commune and the guild of merchants, whose Collegio del Cambio was frescoed by Perugino.

palazzo-dei-priori-volterra.s: The Palazzo dei Priori is the town hall of Volterra in Tuscany, built from 1208 to 1257 and considered the oldest surviving town hall in Tuscany. Its stone façade, decorated with the coats of arms of Florentine governors, served as a model for the Palazzo Vecchio in Florence.

palazzo-gotico.s: The Palazzo Gotico is the medieval town hall of Piacenza, begun in 1281 as the seat of the commune's government. It combines a ground floor of marble arcades with an upper storey of brick decorated with windows and battlements, in the Lombard Gothic style.

prato-cathedral.s: Prato Cathedral, dedicated to Santo Stefano, grew from the parish church around which the town developed and was enlarged from the 12th to the 15th century. It holds the relic of the Holy Girdle of the Virgin, shown from an external pulpit by Donatello and Michelozzo, and…

pope-clement-iii.s: Pope Clement III, born Paolo Scolari in Rome, was pope from 1187 to 1191. A Roman himself, he made peace with the Roman Senate in 1188, recognising the commune in return for its acknowledgement of papal sovereignty, which allowed popes to return to the city.

pope-innocent-ii.s: Pope Innocent II, born Gregorio Papareschi, was pope from 1130 to 1143. His election was contested by the antipope Anacletus II, and with the support of Bernard of Clairvaux and the emperor Lothair III he prevailed after a long schism.

palazzo-dei-papi-viterbo.s: The Palazzo dei Papi in Viterbo was built from 1255 to 1266 as a residence for the popes, who often lived in the city in the 13th century. It was the site of the papal election of 1268–1271, the longest in history, during which the citizens locked the cardinals in and removed…

peoples-national-congress.s: The People's National Congress is a political party in Guyana founded in 1957 by Forbes Burnham after he split from the People's Progressive Party. Supported mainly by Afro-Guyanese, it led Guyana to independence in 1966 and ruled until 1992, from 1970 under a socialist…

periander.s: Periander was tyrant of Corinth from about 627 to 587 BCE, son and successor of Cypselus. Under him Corinth reached the height of its power, founding Potidaea and Apollonia, controlling Corcyra, and building the diolkos, a paved track for hauling ships across the Isthmus.

prut.s: The Prut is a river of Eastern Europe, about 950 kilometres long, rising in the Ukrainian Carpathians and flowing south-east to join the Danube near Reni. For much of its course it forms the border between Romania and Moldova.

petronilla-countess-of-bigorre.s: Petronilla was countess of Bigorre from 1194 until her death in 1251. She married five times, among others Gaston VI of Béarn, Nuño Sánchez and Guy de Montfort, son of Simon de Montfort, leader of the Albigensian Crusade.

petronilla-of-aragon.s: Petronilla was queen of Aragon from 1137 to 1164, the daughter and heiress of Ramiro II. Betrothed as an infant in 1137 to Ramon Berenguer IV, Count of Barcelona, who then governed Aragon, she married him in 1150.

provins.s: Provins is a medieval town south-east of Paris, in the Seine-et-Marne department of France, once one of the main towns of the counts of Champagne. It hosted two of the annual Champagne fairs, which made it one of the largest towns in France in the 13th century.

philip-louis-ii-count-of-hanau-munzenber.n: Philip Louis II, Count of Hanau-Münzenberg
philip-louis-ii-count-of-hanau-munzenber.s: Philip Louis II (1576–1612) was Count of Hanau-Münzenberg from 1580. A Calvinist, in 1597 he invited Reformed refugees from the Netherlands and Wallonia to found the New Town of Hanau beside the old town, bringing gold-working, jewellery and textile trades that shaped the…

pope-pius-iv.s: Pius IV (1499–1565), born Giovanni Angelo Medici in Milan, was pope from 1559 to 1565. He reconvened the Council of Trent in 1562 and confirmed its decrees in 1564, completing the main programme of the Catholic Reformation.

philip-de-montmorency-count-of-horn.n: Philip de Montmorency, Count of Horn
philip-de-montmorency-count-of-horn.s: Philip de Montmorency (1524–1568), Count of Horne, was a nobleman of the Habsburg Netherlands, admiral of Flanders and a knight of the Golden Fleece. With Egmont and William of Orange he led the noble opposition to Philip II's religious policy.

philip-i-count-of-katzenelnbogen.s: Philip the Elder (1402–1479) was the last Count of Katzenelnbogen, ruling one of the richest counties of the Rhineland through its tolls at Rheinfels and Burg Katz. He outlived his son, so on his death the county passed to his daughter Anna's husband, Landgrave Henry III of…

paderborn.s: Paderborn is a city in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, at the springs of the Pader. Charlemagne held assemblies there from 777 and met Pope Leo III there in 799, and it became the seat of a bishopric, later a prince-bishopric that lasted until 1802.

peugeot.s: Peugeot is a French car maker founded by an industrial family from the Montbéliard area, Lutherans like most of the region's people. The family turned a mill into a steel foundry in 1810, making saws, tools, coffee mills and springs, then bicycles and, from 1889, motor vehicles.

pedro-ansurez.s: Pedro Ansúrez (c. 1037–1118) was a Leonese count and one of the leading magnates of Alfonso VI of León and Castile. As lord of Valladolid he developed the town, building a bridge over the Pisuerga and founding churches including Santa María la Antigua, and he is regarded as…

pope-sylvester-ii.s: Pope Sylvester II, born Gerbert of Aurillac, was a French scholar who became the first French pope, reigning from 999 to 1003. As a young monk he studied in Catalonia, at Vic and probably Ripoll, where he learned mathematics and astronomy drawn from Arabic sources, and he…

pallars.s: Pallars is a historic region of the Catalan Pyrenees around the valley of the Noguera Pallaresa river. Once a district of the Frankish county of Toulouse, it became a hereditary county under Ramon I around 872 and was divided in 1011 into Pallars Jussà and Pallars Sobirà.

percheron.s: The Percheron is a breed of heavy draught horse from the Perche region of north-western France, usually grey or black. Developed from local horses, probably with some Arab blood, it became famous in the 19th century for pulling coaches, guns and farm machinery, and was…

province-of-hanover.s: The Province of Hanover was a province of Prussia created after Prussia annexed the Kingdom of Hanover in 1866, with its capital at Hanover. It covered most of present-day Lower Saxony and in 1922 absorbed the former Waldeck district of Pyrmont.

piedmont.s: Piedmont is a region of north-western Italy, enclosed on three sides by the Alps and Apennines, with Turin as its capital. From the 11th century the house of Savoy gained lands there, and Piedmont became the core of its state after the capital moved to Turin in 1563.

pietism.s: Pietism was a movement of renewal within German Lutheranism in the late 17th and 18th centuries, stressing personal faith, Bible study in small groups and practical charity. It was launched by Philipp Jakob Spener and developed at the University of Halle by August Hermann…

prince-carl-of-solms-braunfels.s: Prince Carl of Solms-Braunfels was a German nobleman and officer who served as the first commissioner-general of the Adelsverein, a society that organised German emigration to Texas. In 1845 he led the first settlers inland from the Gulf Coast and founded the town of New…

prattigau.s: The Prättigau is an Alpine valley of the Landquart river in the canton of Graubünden, eastern Switzerland. Held by the counts of Toggenburg and later largely by the Habsburgs, its communities joined the League of the Ten Jurisdictions in 1436.

pope-benedict-ix.s: Benedict IX, born Theophylactus of Tusculum, was pope three times between 1032 and 1048, the only man to hold the office on more than one occasion. A nephew of Benedict VIII and John XIX, he was made pope young by his family, the counts of Tusculum.

pope-benedict-viii.s: Benedict VIII, born Theophylactus of Tusculum, was pope from 1012 to 1024, the first of three popes from the family of the counts of Tusculum. He crowned Henry II emperor in 1014, encouraged Pisa and Genoa against Muslim raiders in Sardinia, and held a reforming synod at Pavia…

peronne.s: Péronne is a town on the Somme in Picardy, northern France. Its castle was where Count Herbert II of Vermandois held King Charles the Simple prisoner until his death in 929, and where Louis XI was forced to agree the Treaty of Péronne with Charles the Bold in 1468.

philip-i-count-of-flanders.s: Philip of Alsace was Count of Flanders from 1168 to 1191, one of the most powerful princes of his age. He promoted Flemish towns and trade, held Vermandois through his wife Elisabeth, and acted as guardian of the young Philip II of France, but lost much of Vermandois to him by…

prince-maximilian-of-wied-neuwied.s: Prince Maximilian of Wied-Neuwied was a German naturalist and explorer. He led an expedition to south-eastern Brazil in 1815–1817 and, with the Swiss artist Karl Bodmer, travelled up the Missouri River in 1832–1834, recording the Plains peoples such as the Mandan.

pembroke-pembrokeshire.s: Pembroke is a town in Pembrokeshire, south-west Wales, on a ridge above the Pembroke River. It grew around the castle founded by the Normans in 1093, which became the centre of the earldom and county palatine of Pembroke.

pembroke-castle.s: Pembroke Castle is a medieval castle in Pembroke, south-west Wales, founded by Arnulf de Montgomery in 1093. William Marshal rebuilt it in stone from about 1200, adding its great round keep.

pope-clement-vi.s: Clement VI, born Pierre Roger, was pope from 1342 to 1352, ruling from Avignon. He bought Avignon from Queen Joanna I of Naples, enlarged the papal palace, and organised the naval league that captured Smyrna from the Aydinids in 1344.
