pipil.s: The Pipil are a Nahua people of western and central El Salvador, descended from migrants from central Mexico who arrived between about the 10th and 12th centuries. They founded lordships such as Cuzcatlan, resisted the Spanish conquest from 1524, and speak Nawat, a language…

peter-von-scholten.s: Peter von Scholten was a Danish official who served as governor-general of the Danish West Indies from 1827 to 1848. He improved conditions for the enslaved and promoted gradual reform, and on 3 July 1848, faced with a slave revolt on St Croix, he declared the immediate…

pitambara-peeth.s: Pitambara Peeth is a Hindu temple complex in the town of Datia, Madhya Pradesh, India, dedicated to the goddess Bagalamukhi in her form as Pitambara, the goddess in yellow, and also to Dhumavati. It was founded in the 20th century by an ascetic known as Swamiji and stands…

portmahomack.s: Portmahomack is a village on the Tarbat peninsula in Easter Ross, Scotland. Excavations from 1994 to 2007 revealed a Pictish monastery of the 6th to 9th centuries beneath and around its church, with workshops for vellum, metalwork and glass and fragments of fine carved stones.

penycloddiau.s: Penycloddiau is an Iron Age hillfort in the Clwydian Range of north-east Wales, one of the largest in the country, enclosing about 21 hectares within its ramparts. Excavations since 2012 have found traces of round houses and a Bronze Age burial cairn reused in the Iron Age.

promona.s: Promona was a hill fortress near modern Drniš in Dalmatia, Croatia, held by the Delmatae in the 1st century BCE. During his Illyrian campaign of 35–33 BCE, Octavian besieged and captured it, one of a series of strongholds he took to subdue the peoples behind the Adriatic coast.

publius-cornelius-scipio-nasica-corculum.s: Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Corculum was a Roman statesman and general, consul in 162 and 155 BCE. In his second consulship he defeated the Delmatae and destroyed their stronghold of Delminium, earning a triumph.

pleistos.s: The Pleistos is a small river in Phocis, central Greece, flowing through a deep gorge below the sanctuary of Delphi and across the olive plain to the Gulf of Corinth near Kirrha. The sanctuary stands on the slopes of Mount Parnassus above its valley, and the gorge forms part…

pythia.s: The Pythia was the priestess of Apollo at Delphi who spoke the god's oracles. Seated on a tripod in the inner part of the temple, she answered questions from cities and individuals, and her words were then put into form by priests.

pembrokeshire.s: Pembrokeshire is a county in the south-west corner of Wales, with its administrative centre at Haverfordwest and the cathedral city of St Davids. Its southern part, settled by English and Flemish colonists under the Normans, became known as 'Little England beyond Wales'.

paris-peace-accords.s: The Paris Peace Accords were signed on 27 January 1973 by the United States, North Vietnam, South Vietnam and the Viet Cong's Provisional Revolutionary Government, after years of negotiation. They provided for a ceasefire, the withdrawal of the remaining US forces and the…

pulaar.s: Pulaar is the variety of the Fula language spoken in the Senegal River valley, the old region of Futa Toro, and in Senegal, Mauritania, the Gambia and Guinea-Bissau. It belongs to the Atlantic branch of the Niger-Congo family.

panagia-parigoritissa.s: The Panagia Parigoritissa is a Byzantine church in Arta, western Greece, built in the late 13th century by the ruler of Epirus Nikephoros I Komnenos Doukas and his wife Anna. Its unusual tall, box-like exterior hides a domed interior with columns and mosaics.

padang-roco-inscription.s: The Padang Roco inscription is an inscription of 1286 carved on the base of a statue of Amoghapasa found at Padang Roco in Dharmasraya, West Sumatra. It records that King Kertanegara of Singhasari sent the statue from Java as a gift to the Malayu king Tribhuwanaraja Mauli…

pamalayu-expedition.s: The Pamalayu expedition was a military and diplomatic expedition sent in 1275 by King Kertanegara of Singhasari in Java to the Malayu kingdom of Sumatra, centred at Dharmasraya. It aimed to bring the Strait of Malacca region under Javanese influence, perhaps as a defence…

pristina.s: Pristina is the capital and largest city of Kosovo. In the Middle Ages it was a market town near the mining centres of Novo Brdo and Trepča and a residence of Serbian rulers, including Vuk Branković in the late 14th century, and the Battle of Kosovo of 1389 was fought nearby.

peoples-rally-for-progress.s: The People's Rally for Progress is the ruling party of Djibouti, founded in 1979 by President Hassan Gouled Aptidon. It was the only legal party from 1981 until a new constitution of 1992 allowed a limited number of parties.

penthievre.s: Penthièvre is a historic region of northern Brittany, France, around Lamballe and the bay of Saint-Brieuc. It became a county held by a branch of the ducal house of Brittany in the 11th century, and the claim of Joan of Penthièvre to the duchy led to the Breton War of…

pyotr-krasnov.s: Pyotr Krasnov was a Russian general and writer who led the anti-Bolshevik Don Cossacks in 1918–1919 as ataman of the Almighty Don Host. With German support he raised a sizeable Don army and besieged Tsaritsyn, but resigned in February 1919 after Germany's defeat.

pasion-river.s: The Pasión River is a river of the Petén lowlands of northern Guatemala and a tributary of the Usumacinta. In the Classic Maya period it was a major trade route between the highlands and the lowlands, with cities such as Cancuén, Ceibal and Altar de Sacrificios along its banks.

pripyat-river.s: The Pripyat is a river of Eastern Europe, about 760 kilometres long, flowing east from north-western Ukraine through southern Belarus to join the Dnieper north of Kyiv. Its basin forms the Pripyat Marshes, one of the largest wetlands in Europe, which shaped settlement and…

pelagonia.s: Pelagonia is a plain and historical region in the south of North Macedonia, around Bitola and Prilep, extending into north-western Greece. In antiquity it was the land of the Pelagones, and in the Roman settlement of 167 BCE it formed one of the four republics into which…

pactus-alamannorum.s: The Pactus Alamannorum is the earliest surviving law code of the Alemanni, compiled in Latin in the early 7th century, probably under the Frankish king Chlothar II. It survives only in fragments and consists mainly of lists of compensation payments for injuries and offences.

pshavs.s: The Pshavs are a Georgian highland people of Pshavi, in the upper valleys of the Aragvi and Iori rivers in north-eastern Georgia. Their communities kept local shrines and customs and supplied fighters to the dukes of Aragvi and the Georgian kings.

passau.s: Passau is a city in Lower Bavaria, Germany, where the Inn and the Ilz meet the Danube near the Austrian border. Its bishopric, organised by Saint Boniface in 739, became one of the largest dioceses of the Holy Roman Empire, reaching far down the Danube, and from 1217 its…

premyslid-dynasty.s: The Přemyslid dynasty ruled Bohemia from the late 9th century until 1306, first as dukes and from 1198 as hereditary kings. Named after the legendary ploughman Přemysl, husband of Princess Libuše, it produced Saint Wenceslas, Ottokar II, who briefly ruled Austria, and…

piast-dynasty.s: The Piast dynasty was the first historical ruling house of Poland, from Mieszko I, baptised in 966, to the death of Casimir III the Great in 1370. After 1138 the realm fragmented into duchies held by rival Piast branches in Silesia, Masovia, Kuyavia and elsewhere.

philip-i-duke-of-burgundy.s: Philip of Rouvres was Duke of Burgundy from 1349 and the last of its Capetian dukes. Succeeding his grandfather Odo IV as a small child, he also inherited the counties of Artois and Burgundy and married Margaret of Flanders.

pena-amaya.s: Peña Amaya is a flat-topped mountain in the north of the province of Burgos, Spain, the site of an ancient hill fort of the Cantabri. It remained an important stronghold in Roman and Visigothic times and was captured by the Visigothic king Leovigild in 574.

pelagius-of-asturias.s: Pelagius was a Visigothic nobleman who founded the Kingdom of Asturias, ruling from about 718 until 737. He led a revolt against Muslim rule in the mountains of northern Spain and defeated a Muslim force at the Battle of Covadonga, traditionally dated 722, which later…

peter-of-cantabria.s: Peter of Cantabria was a duke of Cantabria in the early 8th century, known only from the Asturian chronicles of the late 9th century, which claim he descended from the Visigothic kings Leovigild and Reccared. His son Alfonso married Ermesinda, daughter of Pelagius, and became…

primoz-trubar.s: Primož Trubar was a Slovene Protestant reformer and the founder of the Slovene literary language. In 1550, in exile in Germany, he published the first two printed books in Slovene, a catechism and a primer, and he later led the Protestant church of Carniola.

pope-innocent-x.s: Innocent X, born Giovanni Battista Pamphili, was pope from 1644 to 1655. He prosecuted the Barberini nephews of his predecessor, protested against the Peace of Westphalia and condemned five propositions of Jansenism, and his portrait was painted by Diego Velázquez.

pope-urban-viii.s: Urban VIII, born Maffeo Barberini, was pope from 1623 to 1644. A patron of Bernini and of Baroque art, he enriched his nephews on a large scale and presided over the trial of Galileo in 1633.

polish-czechoslovak-war.s: The Polish–Czechoslovak War, also called the Seven-Day War, was a brief conflict in late January 1919 over Cieszyn Silesia. Czechoslovak troops advanced against Polish forces to gain control of the region's coalfields and its railway, before the Allied powers imposed a ceasefire.

pope-paul-ii.s: Paul II, born Pietro Barbo, was pope from 1464 to 1471. A Venetian and nephew of Pope Eugene IV, he built the Palazzo Venezia in Rome, abolished the college of abbreviators and imprisoned humanists of the Roman Academy, among them Platina.

palazzo-schifanoia.s: The Palazzo Schifanoia is a palace in Ferrara built for the Este family from 1385 as a place of leisure. Its Hall of the Months, painted around 1470 for Duke Borso d'Este by Francesco del Cossa, Ercole de' Roberti and others, combines scenes of court life, astrological figures…

pomerelia.s: Pomerelia, or Gdańsk Pomerania, is a historical region of northern Poland west of the lower Vistula, centred on Gdańsk. Ruled by native dukes until 1294, it passed to Poland and was seized by the Teutonic Order in 1308.

palazzo-te.s: The Palazzo Te is a villa on the edge of Mantua, built between 1524 and 1534 for Federico II Gonzaga to designs by Giulio Romano. Conceived as a pleasure palace, it is a landmark of Mannerist architecture.

philip-of-swabia.s: Philip of Swabia (1177–1208) was a son of Frederick Barbarossa and King of the Romans from 1198. After the death of his brother Henry VI, the Staufen party elected him king while the Welfs elected Otto IV, starting a long civil war.

palazzo-della-pilotta.s: The Palazzo della Pilotta is a large palace complex in Parma, begun by the Farnese dukes around 1583 and never completed. It houses the Teatro Farnese, the National Gallery of Parma, the Palatine Library and the archaeological museum.

podolian-voivodeship.s: The Podolian Voivodeship was a province of the Kingdom of Poland and later the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, formed from western Podolia in 1434 with its seat at Kamianets-Podilskyi. A frontier land exposed to Tatar and Ottoman raids, it was held by the Ottomans from 1672 to…

peace-of-bautzen.s: The Peace of Bautzen was signed on 30 January 1018 between Emperor Henry II and Duke Bolesław I the Brave of Poland, ending fifteen years of intermittent war. Poland kept Lusatia and Milsko, and later that year German knights joined Bolesław's expedition to Kiev.

poznan.s: Poznań is a city in west-central Poland on the Warta river, the historical capital of Greater Poland. One of the main strongholds of the early Piast state, it became the seat of Poland's first bishopric in 968, and its cathedral holds the tombs of early rulers.

pomeranians-slavic-tribe.s: The Pomeranians were a West Slavic people who lived along the Baltic coast between the Oder and the Vistula in the early Middle Ages. Their tribes were united under local dukes such as Wartislaw I and converted to Christianity by Otto of Bamberg in the 1120s.

pomerania-stettin.s: Pomerania-Stettin was a partition of the Duchy of Pomerania, created in 1295 for Otto I and ruled by a line of the Griffin dukes from Stettin (Szczecin). It covered the lands along the lower Oder and was several times reunited with Pomerania-Wolgast and divided again.

pomerania-wolgast.s: Pomerania-Wolgast was a partition of the Duchy of Pomerania, created in 1295 for Bogislaw IV and ruled by Griffin dukes from Wolgast. It covered the coastal lands north of the Peene, with Hanseatic towns such as Stralsund and Greifswald, and was itself divided several times.

philip-julius-duke-of-pomerania-wolgast.s: Philip Julius (1584–1625) was Duke of Pomerania-Wolgast from 1592, at first under the guardianship of his uncle. He travelled widely in Europe as a young man and later quarrelled with his estates and with the town of Stralsund.

przemyslaw-of-raciborz.s: Przemysław (c. 1258–1306) was a Piast duke of Racibórz in Upper Silesia, the first ruler of the separate duchy created when the sons of Władysław of Opole divided their father's lands in 1281. He was succeeded by his son Leszek, the last duke of the line, while his daughter…

peace-of-cateau-cambresis.s: The Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis consisted of treaties signed in April 1559 between France and England and between France and Spain, ending more than sixty years of Italian Wars. France renounced its Italian claims but kept Calais and the bishoprics of Metz, Toul and Verdun,…

poor-conrad.s: Poor Conrad (Armer Konrad) was a peasant and townsmen's revolt in the Duchy of Württemberg in 1514, provoked by Duke Ulrich's new taxes on food and his heavy debts. The duke ended it partly by agreeing to the Treaty of Tübingen with the estates, which guaranteed their rights,…

peter-von-biron.s: Peter von Biron was the last Duke of Courland and Semigallia, ruling from 1769 to 1795. The son of Ernst Johann von Biron, he quarrelled constantly with the Courland nobility.

plymouth-sound.s: Plymouth Sound is a deep bay on the English Channel at the mouths of the rivers Tamar and Plym, between Devon and Cornwall. It shelters the port of Plymouth and the naval base at Devonport.

pytheas.s: Pytheas was a Greek navigator and geographer from Massalia, modern Marseille, who made a voyage to north-western Europe around 325 BCE. His work On the Ocean is lost but was quoted by later writers.

pieter-both.s: Pieter Both was the first Governor-General of the Dutch East Indies, appointed by the Dutch East India Company in 1609 and serving from 1610 to 1614. He set up company posts and treaties in the Moluccas and on Java.

penghu.s: Penghu, also called the Pescadores, is an archipelago of about 90 small islands in the Taiwan Strait. The Dutch occupied it from 1622 until a Ming fleet forced them to withdraw to Taiwan in 1624.

peace-of-munster.s: The Peace of Münster was the treaty signed in Münster on 30 January 1648 between Spain and the Dutch Republic, one of the settlements of the Peace of Westphalia. It ended the Eighty Years' War, with Spain recognising the independence of the United Provinces.

pharae-achaea.s: Pharae was an ancient Greek city in western Achaea in the Peloponnese, inland from Patrae, and one of the twelve cities of the original Achaean League. In 280 BCE it joined Dyme, Patrae and Tritaea in reviving the league, which grew into a major power in Hellenistic Greece.

patirruppattu.s: The Patirruppattu is an anthology of classical Tamil poetry, one of the Eight Anthologies of Sangam literature. It originally contained ten sets of ten poems, each praising a Chera king; the first and last sets are lost.

pugalur.s: Pugalur is a town in Karur district of Tamil Nadu, India. In rock shelters on the nearby hill of Arunattarmalai are Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions of about the 2nd century CE recording Jain beds carved for monks.

puhar.s: Puhar, also called Kaveripattinam, was the main port of the early Chola kings at the mouth of the Kaveri River in Tamil Nadu, India. Sangam poems such as the Pattinappalai and the epic Silappatikaram describe it as a busy harbour where foreign merchants traded.

peribsen.s: Peribsen was a king of the Second Dynasty of Egypt, around 2700 BCE. Unusually, he placed the animal of the god Seth rather than the falcon of Horus above his royal name, which may reflect religious or political division in the country.

plovdiv.s: Plovdiv is the second-largest city of Bulgaria, on the Maritsa river in the Upper Thracian Plain. Inhabited since prehistoric times, it was the Thracian Eumolpias, Philip II of Macedon's Philippopolis and the Roman capital of Thrace, with a well-preserved Roman theatre.

philip-carteret.s: Philip Carteret was the first governor of the English Province of New Jersey and then of East Jersey, a Jersey-born cousin of the proprietor Sir George Carteret. Arriving in 1665, he governed from Elizabethtown, quarrelled with settlers over quitrents, and clashed with…

paolo-matthiae.s: Paolo Matthiae is an Italian archaeologist who directed the excavations of the University of Rome La Sapienza at Tell Mardikh in Syria from 1964. His team identified the site as ancient Ebla in 1968 and in 1974–1975 found the royal archive of Palace G, some 17,000 cuneiform…

puig-des-molins.s: Puig des Molins is an ancient necropolis on a hill in the city of Ibiza, used from the Phoenician period in the 7th century BCE through Punic and Roman times. It contains thousands of tombs, including many rock-cut chambers, and has yielded terracotta figures, amulets and…

puuc.s: Puuc is a range of low hills and the surrounding region in the western Yucatán Peninsula of Mexico, and the name of the Maya architectural style that flourished there between about 700 and 1000 CE. Puuc buildings have plain lower walls and upper facades of finely cut stone…

padi.s: Padi was king of the Philistine city of Ekron around 700 BCE and a loyal vassal of Assyria. During the revolt against Sennacherib, Ekron's nobles and people deposed him and handed him over in chains to Hezekiah of Judah.

parmenides.s: Parmenides of Elea was a Greek philosopher of the early 5th century BCE from the colony of Elea in southern Italy. In a poem, On Nature, he argued that what is cannot come into being, change or pass away, and that the senses deceive.

porta-rosa.s: The Porta Rosa is a stone gateway of the 4th century BCE at the site of Elea, Roman Velia, in Campania, southern Italy. Spanning a road between the two quarters of the city, it uses a true round arch of fitted wedge-shaped stones, among the earliest known in Greek architecture.

pineios-elis.s: The Pineios is a river of Elis in the north-western Peloponnese of Greece, flowing west from the Erymanthos mountains to the Ionian Sea. The ancient city of Elis stood on its banks, and its fertile lowlands formed the core of Elean territory.

pineios-thessaly.s: The Pineios, ancient Peneus, is the main river of Thessaly in Greece, about 200 kilometres long. Rising in the Pindus mountains, it crosses the Thessalian plain past Trikala and Larissa and reaches the Aegean through the Vale of Tempe between Mount Olympus and Mount Ossa.

pyrrho.s: Pyrrho of Elis was a Greek philosopher regarded as the founder of scepticism. He travelled with Alexander the Great's army as far as India, where he reportedly met ascetic sages.

pyramid-of-the-niches.s: The Pyramid of the Niches is the best-known building of El Tajín, the pre-Columbian city in Veracruz, Mexico. It is a stepped platform of six tiers, its sides lined with 365 deep square niches thought to relate to the solar year, crowned by a temple and approached by a steep…

portendick.s: Portendick was a trading anchorage on the Atlantic coast of Mauritania, north of the Senegal River. From the 17th to the 19th century Dutch, English and French merchants traded there for gum arabic, the chief export of the Moorish emirates of the coast.

polykleitos-the-younger.s: Polykleitos the Younger was a Greek architect and sculptor of the 4th century BCE, probably a member of the family of the famous sculptor Polykleitos of Argos. The traveller Pausanias attributes to him the theatre and the round building, the tholos, at the sanctuary of…

peace-of-phoenice.s: The Peace of Phoenice was the treaty that ended the First Macedonian War between Rome and Philip V of Macedon in 205 BCE. It was negotiated at Phoenice in Epirus with the mediation of the Epirotes.

phoenice.s: Phoenice was an ancient Greek city in Chaonia, in north-western Epirus, near modern Finiq in southern Albania. It was the chief town of the Chaonians and a frequent meeting place of the Epirote League.

pennsylvania.s: Pennsylvania is a state in the north-eastern United States. It was founded in 1681 when Charles II granted the territory to William Penn, who made it a refuge for Quakers and other religious groups.

pide.s: PIDE was the political police of Portugal's Estado Novo. Founded in 1933 as the PVDE, it was renamed PIDE in 1945 and DGS in 1969.

pahar-singh-of-faridkot.s: Pahar Singh was the ruler of the Sikh state of Faridkot in the Punjab from 1827 to 1849. During the First Anglo-Sikh War of 1845–1846 he sided with the British East India Company against the Sikh Empire of Lahore, and he was rewarded with additional land and recognition.

paysandu.s: Paysandú is a city in western Uruguay on the east bank of the Uruguay river, opposite Colón in Argentina. It grew from an 18th-century mission outpost into a river port and meat-processing centre.

purificacion-uruguay.s: Purificación was the settlement founded by José Gervasio Artigas in 1815 on a plateau above the Uruguay river at Hervidero, north of Paysandú. It served as his headquarters and the seat of the Federal League's government, where he directed the war against Buenos Aires and the…

panglong-conference.s: The Panglong Conference was a meeting held at Panglong in the Shan States in February 1947, at which Aung San, representing the interim Burmese government, reached agreement with Shan, Kachin and Chin leaders. The Panglong Agreement of 12 February 1947 accepted their joining a…

pact-of-union-1921.s: The Pact of Union was an agreement signed at San José, Costa Rica, in January 1921, on the centenary of Central American independence, to recreate a federal union of the isthmus. Guatemala, El Salvador and Honduras ratified it and formed the Federation of Central America, with…

pliska.s: Pliska was the first capital of the First Bulgarian Empire, in north-eastern Bulgaria near Shumen, founded in the late 7th century after the Bulgars crossed the Danube. Its fortified enclosure contained palaces and, after the conversion to Christianity in 864, the Great…

preslav.s: Preslav was the capital of the First Bulgarian Empire from 893 to 972, near modern Veliki Preslav in north-eastern Bulgaria. Under Tsar Simeon I it became a centre of Slavonic literature, where the Preslav Literary School developed the Cyrillic alphabet, and it was famed for…

puerta-del-conde.s: The Puerta del Conde is a fortified gate in the colonial walls of Santo Domingo, named after the Count of Peñalva, who defended the city against an English attack in 1655. On the night of 27 February 1844 Dominican patriots gathered there to proclaim independence from Haiti…

plan-of-casa-mata.s: The Plan of Casa Mata was a declaration issued on 1 February 1823 by army officers who had been sent to put down Antonio López de Santa Anna's revolt at Veracruz. It called for the election of a new congress and gave power to the provincial deputations.

plan-of-iguala.s: The Plan of Iguala was the programme for Mexican independence proclaimed on 24 February 1821 at Iguala by Agustín de Iturbide and agreed with the insurgent Vicente Guerrero. It promised three guarantees: independence under a constitutional monarchy, the Catholic religion, and…

parantaka-i.s: Parantaka I was a king of the Chola dynasty who ruled from 907 to 955. He conquered the Pandya kingdom around 920, taking the title Maduraikonda, captor of Madurai, and campaigned against Sri Lanka.

palanan.s: Palanan is a remote municipality on the Pacific coast of Isabela province in north-eastern Luzon, Philippines, cut off from the interior by the Sierra Madre mountains. Emilio Aguinaldo, president of the First Philippine Republic, hid there during the Philippine–American War…

petrobras.s: Petrobras, Petróleo Brasileiro S.A., is Brazil's state-controlled oil company, created in 1953 by Getúlio Vargas after a nationalist campaign under the slogan The oil is ours. It held a monopoly over oil exploration and refining until 1997 and became one of the largest…

pasto.s: Pasto is a city in the Andes of south-western Colombia, capital of the Nariño Department, founded by the Spanish in the 1530s. During the wars of independence its people were strongly royalist, and it was there that Antonio Nariño was captured in 1814 during his southern…

pope-martin-v.s: Martin V, born Oddone Colonna, was pope from 1417 to 1431. His election at the Council of Constance ended the Western Schism, during which rival popes had competed for nearly 40 years.

protestant-union.s: The Protestant Union was a defensive alliance of Protestant German princes and cities formed at Auhausen in 1608 under the Calvinist Elector Palatine Frederick IV. It was a response to Bavaria's seizure of Donauwörth, and the Catholic League was founded against it in 1609.

paul-fagius.s: Paul Fagius was a German Protestant reformer and Hebrew scholar. As pastor at Isny he set up a Hebrew printing press with Elijah Levita around 1540, and he later worked with Martin Bucer in Strasbourg.

pegnitz.s: The Pegnitz is a river in Franconia, Bavaria, which flows from Franconian Switzerland through Nuremberg, dividing its old town, and joins the Rednitz at Fürth to form the Regnitz. Its water powered the mills and workshops of medieval Nuremberg, and the city grew on both its…

peter-parler.s: Peter Parler was a German architect and sculptor, son of Heinrich Parler, who became Emperor Charles IV's master builder in Prague from 1356. He continued St. Vitus Cathedral with innovative net vaulting, built the Charles Bridge and its Old Town tower, and carved portrait…

protective-division-of-quito.s: The Protective Division of Quito was the army raised by the Free Province of Guayaquil after its declaration of independence in October 1820 to free the Ecuadorian highlands from Spanish rule. After early successes it was defeated at Huachi in November 1820, and the liberation…

prussian-coup-of-1932.s: The Prussian coup of 20 July 1932, the Preußenschlag, was the removal of the Social Democratic-led government of the Free State of Prussia by Chancellor Franz von Papen, using an emergency decree of President Hindenburg. Papen took control as Reich commissioner for Prussia,…

pyotr-wrangel.s: Pyotr Wrangel was a Russian general and a leading commander of the White movement in the Russian Civil War. In April 1920 he succeeded Anton Denikin as commander of the White forces in southern Russia, held Crimea and advanced into southern Ukraine.

pierre-paul-de-la-grandiere.s: Pierre-Paul de La Grandière was a French admiral and governor of Cochinchina from 1863 to 1868. He organised the administration of the three eastern provinces ceded by the Treaty of Saigon in 1862, brought Cambodia under French protection in 1863, and in 1867 seized the three…

papeete.s: Papeete is the capital of French Polynesia, on the north-west coast of Tahiti. It grew around a harbour used by whalers and traders in the early 19th century and became the seat of the Pōmare monarchy and then of the French administration after the protectorate of 1842.

paul-gauguin.s: Paul Gauguin was a French Post-Impressionist painter, sculptor and printmaker. Leaving Europe in 1891, he spent most of his remaining years in Tahiti and the Marquesas Islands, where he painted the works, bold in colour and simplified in form, that shaped European images of…

parris-island.s: Parris Island is an island near Beaufort in South Carolina, United States. It was the site of the French Huguenot outpost of Charlesfort, built in 1562, and of the Spanish town of Santa Elena, capital of Spanish Florida for much of the period from 1566 to 1587.

puducherry-union-territory.s: Puducherry is a union territory of India formed from the four former French settlements of Pondicherry, Karaikal, Mahé and Yanam, which lie hundreds of kilometres apart. They were transferred to India de facto in 1954 and legally in 1962, and became a union territory in 1963.

paul-doumer.s: Paul Doumer was a French politician who served as governor-general of French Indochina from 1897 to 1902 and as president of France from 1931 until his assassination in 1932. In Indochina he centralised administration under the governor-general, set up a general budget…

philibert-tsiranana.s: Philibert Tsiranana was the first president of Madagascar, from 1959 to 1972. A teacher from the north-west, he founded the Social Democratic Party in 1956, became head of government of the autonomous Malagasy Republic in 1958 and led the island to independence on 26 June…

pouvanaa-a-oopa.s: Pouvanaa a Oopa was a Tahitian nationalist politician and First World War veteran who led the movement for Polynesian rights after 1945. He sat in the French National Assembly from 1949 and headed the territorial government, but campaigned for a 'no' vote in the 1958…

paknam-incident.s: The Paknam incident was a naval clash on 13 July 1893, when two French gunboats forced their way past the Siamese forts at Paknam, at the mouth of the Chao Phraya River, and anchored before Bangkok. France then blockaded the coast and issued an ultimatum, and by the treaty of…

philippe-petain.s: Philippe Pétain was a French general and marshal, celebrated as the defender of Verdun in 1916. In June 1940, as prime minister, he sought an armistice with Germany, and on 10 July parliament gave him full powers; as head of the French State at Vichy he pursued collaboration…

popular-front-france.s: The Popular Front was an alliance of the French Socialist, Radical and Communist parties, formed against fascism, which won the elections of 1936. Under Léon Blum, the first socialist prime minister, its government introduced the 40-hour week, two weeks' paid holiday and…

poppo-of-frisia.s: Poppo, also called Bubo, was a king of the Frisians in the early 8th century, probably the successor of Redbad. A pagan, he resisted Frankish expansion and Christian missions until Charles Martel invaded Frisia in 734 and defeated and killed him at the Battle of the Boarn.

priscillian.s: Priscillian was a Christian ascetic teacher in Hispania and bishop of Ávila in the late 4th century. His movement, which stressed strict asceticism and the reading of apocryphal texts, was accused of heresy and sorcery.

postumus.s: Postumus was a Roman general who founded the breakaway Gallic Empire. A commander on the Rhine, he was proclaimed emperor by his troops in 260, after Valerian's capture by the Persians, and killed Gallienus' son Saloninus at Cologne.

potala-palace.s: The Potala Palace in Lhasa, Tibet, was the winter residence of the Dalai Lamas and the seat of the Tibetan government. The Fifth Dalai Lama began it in 1645 on the Red Hill, on the site of an earlier palace attributed to Songtsen Gampo, and the central Red Palace was completed…

pradyumna-shah.s: Pradyumna Shah was the last king of independent Garhwal in the Himalayas before the Gorkha conquest. After a Gorkha invasion in the early 1790s he agreed to pay tribute to Nepal, and when the Gorkhas invaded again in 1803 he fled his capital at Srinagar.

phintias-of-acragas.s: Phintias was tyrant of Acragas, modern Agrigento, in Sicily in the early 3rd century BCE. In the disorder after the death of Agathocles of Syracuse he extended his power over neighbouring cities, and around 282 BCE he destroyed Gela and moved its people to a new city named…

peter-ii-of-cyprus.s: Peter II was king of Cyprus from 1369, after the murder of his father Peter I. At his coronation as king of Jerusalem in Famagusta in 1372, a quarrel over precedence between Genoese and Venetian merchants led to riots in which Genoese were killed.

paul-von-lettow-vorbeck.s: Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck was a German general who commanded the defence of German East Africa in the First World War. With a small force of German and African askari troops he won the Battle of Tanga in 1914 and then waged a long guerrilla campaign through Tanganyika,…

phoenix-islands.s: The Phoenix Islands are a group of eight atolls and coral islands in the central Pacific, part of Kiribati. Britain added them to the Gilbert and Ellice Islands colony in 1937, and Canton and Enderbury were jointly administered with the United States from 1939.

palar-river.s: The Palar is a river of southern India that rises in Karnataka, crosses a corner of Andhra Pradesh and flows east through northern Tamil Nadu, past Vellore and near Kanchipuram, to the Bay of Bengal south of Chennai. Its valley, with Kanchipuram and many temple towns, was the…

pondicherry.s: Pondicherry, officially Puducherry, is a coastal city in south-eastern India, south of Chennai. Founded as a French trading post by François Martin in 1674, it became the capital of French India and, under Dupleix in the 1740s, the base of France's bid for power in southern…

pyongyang.s: Pyongyang is the capital and largest city of North Korea, on the Taedong river. One of the oldest cities in Korea, it lay near the centre of late Gojoseon and of the Chinese commandery of Lelang, became the capital of Goguryeo in 427 and was later the Western Capital of Goryeo.

piura.s: Piura is a city in north-western Peru, near the Pacific coast. Founded by Francisco Pizarro in 1532 as San Miguel, it was the first Spanish city in Peru, set up before his march to meet the Inca ruler Atahualpa at Cajamarca.

parana-river.s: The Paraná is the second-longest river of South America, flowing about 4,880 kilometres from south-central Brazil along the borders of Paraguay and through Argentina to join the Uruguay river and form the Río de la Plata. With its tributary the Paraguay it was the main route…

parana-entre-rios.s: Paraná is a city in eastern Argentina, the capital of Entre Ríos Province, on the east bank of the Paraná river opposite Santa Fe. From 1853 to 1861 it was the capital of the Argentine Confederation under Justo José de Urquiza, while the State of Buenos Aires remained separate.

pskov.s: Pskov is one of Russia's oldest cities, on the Velikaya river near the Estonian border, first recorded in the chronicles under 903. A trading town of the Novgorod lands, it became a self-governing republic with its own assembly by the fourteenth century and was a frontier…

province-of-posen.s: The Province of Posen was a province of the Kingdom of Prussia from 1848 to 1920, formed when the Grand Duchy of Posen lost its special status after the Polish rising of 1848. With its capital at Posen (Poznań) and a Polish majority, it was a focus of conflict between…

prince-ferdinando-duke-of-genoa.s: Ferdinando, Duke of Genoa, was a prince of the House of Savoy, the second son of King Charles Albert of Sardinia, who commanded troops in the First Italian War of Independence in 1848–1849. In July 1848 the Sicilian parliament, having deposed the Bourbons, elected him King of…

peace-of-szatmar.s: The Peace of Szatmár was concluded in April 1711 between the Habsburg monarchy and the Hungarian insurgents of Francis II Rákóczi, ending the war of independence he had led since 1703. The rebels received an amnesty and the Habsburgs promised to respect the constitution and…

policarpo-bonilla.s: Policarpo Bonilla was a Honduran lawyer and Liberal politician who founded the Liberal Party of Honduras in 1891 and was president from 1894 to 1899, after taking power with Nicaraguan help. His government adopted a liberal constitution in 1894, and with the presidents of…

pohansko.s: Pohansko is the site of a large ninth-century Great Moravian stronghold near Břeclav in South Moravia, Czech Republic. Excavations have revealed a fortified area with a magnate's court, a stone church surrounded by burials and extensive craft workshops, making it one of the…

pedro-cieza-de-leon.s: Pedro Cieza de León was a Spanish soldier and chronicler who spent some seventeen years in South America from 1535. His Chronicle of Peru, the first part of which was published in 1553, describes the geography, peoples and history of the Andes and the Inca Empire, drawing on…

purang.s: Purang, or Burang, is a district in the far west of the Tibet Autonomous Region of China, near the borders of Nepal and India, close to Lake Manasarovar and Mount Kailash. In the 10th and 11th centuries it formed with Guge the kingdom founded by the descendants of Kyide…

pathein.s: Pathein, formerly Bassein, is a port city in the Irrawaddy Delta of southern Myanmar and capital of the Ayeyarwady Region. It was a provincial centre and port of the Mon kingdom of Hanthawaddy, trading across the Bay of Bengal, and later of the Burmese kingdoms.

pandit-seu.s: Pandit Seu was an Indian painter from Guler in the hills of present-day Himachal Pradesh, active in the early 18th century. He headed a family workshop of painters, and his sons Manaku and Nainsukh, together with their own sons, transformed Pahari painting and created the…

penn-museum.s: The Penn Museum, formally the University of Pennsylvania Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology, is a museum and research institution in Philadelphia founded in 1887. It has sponsored excavations across the world, including at Ur with the British Museum, at Hasanlu in Iran and…

pharisees.s: The Pharisees were a Jewish religious and political party of the Second Temple period, first attested under the Hasmoneans in the 2nd century BCE. They upheld an oral tradition of interpretation alongside the written Torah and believed in the resurrection of the dead.

piyusti.s: Piyusti was a king of Hatti in central Anatolia in the 18th century BCE, ruling from Hattusa. He is known from the inscription of Anitta of Kussara, which records that Anitta defeated him, took Hattusa by night, destroyed it and sowed it with weeds, cursing any king who…

pixodarus.s: Pixodarus was the youngest son of Hecatomnus and satrap of Caria from about 340 to 335 BCE, after ousting his sister Ada. He negotiated a marriage alliance with Philip II of Macedon, which the young Alexander tried to divert to himself.

pasok.s: PASOK, the Panhellenic Socialist Movement, is a Greek centre-left party founded in 1974 by Andreas Papandreou after the fall of the military junta. It governed Greece in 1981–1989, 1993–2004 and from 2009, alternating in power with New Democracy and expanding the welfare state.

peter-ochs.s: Peter Ochs was a Basel politician and historian who drafted the constitution of the Helvetic Republic, imposed under French influence in 1798. Closely tied to the French Directory, he sat in the republic's executive Directory until he was forced out in 1799.

philipp-albert-stapfer.s: Philipp Albert Stapfer was a Swiss theologian and statesman who served as minister of arts and sciences of the Helvetic Republic from 1798. He planned a national system of public schools, a national university and a national library, and supported the educator Johann Heinrich…

procopius.s: Procopius of Caesarea was a Byzantine historian of the 6th century and secretary to the general Belisarius. His 'History of the Wars' describes Justinian's campaigns against Persia, the Vandals and the Ostrogoths and is the main source for many peoples on the empire's frontiers.

publius-valerius-laevinus.s: Publius Valerius Laevinus was a Roman consul in 280 BCE who commanded the first Roman army to face Pyrrhus of Epirus in Italy. At the Battle of Heraclea in Lucania he was defeated by Pyrrhus, whose war elephants panicked the Roman cavalry, although the victors' own losses were…

peace-of-okahandja.s: The Peace of Okahandja was the settlement of 1870, negotiated with the help of German missionaries, that ended a decade of war between the Herero under Maharero and the Oorlam Afrikaners under Jan Jonker Afrikaner in central Namibia. It confirmed Herero independence and was…

passover.s: Passover is a major Jewish festival commemorating the Exodus of the Israelites from Egypt, celebrated in spring from the 15th day of the month of Nisan. In the Second Temple period it was a pilgrimage festival, when crowds came to Jerusalem to sacrifice the Passover lamb at…

publius-sulpicius-quirinius.s: Publius Sulpicius Quirinius was a Roman senator, consul in 12 BCE, who as governor of Syria carried out a census of Judaea in 6 CE, when it became a Roman province after the deposition of Archelaus. The census provoked the revolt of Judas of Galilee and is mentioned in the…

pula.s: Pula is a city at the southern tip of the Istrian peninsula in Croatia. As the Roman colony of Pietas Iulia it gained monuments such as its well-preserved amphitheatre of the 1st century CE.

pierre-daubusson.s: Pierre d'Aubusson was Grand Master of the Knights Hospitaller from 1476 to 1503. He strengthened the walls of Rhodes and led its defence against the Ottoman siege of 1480, in which the attackers were driven off.

palace-of-the-grand-master-rhodes.n: Palace of the Grand Master of the Knights of Rhodes
palace-of-the-grand-master-rhodes.s: The Palace of the Grand Master is a medieval fortress-palace in the old town of Rhodes, Greece, built by the Knights Hospitaller in the 14th century on the site of an earlier citadel. Badly damaged by an explosion in 1856, it was rebuilt by the Italian authorities in the 1930s.

pashtuns.s: The Pashtuns are an Iranian-speaking people of southern and eastern Afghanistan and north-western Pakistan, speaking Pashto and organised in many tribes and clans. Their customary code, Pashtunwali, stresses honour, hospitality and the tribal council, or jirga.

peter-magyar.s: Péter Magyar is a Hungarian lawyer and politician who broke with the governing Fidesz party in 2024 and became leader of the opposition Tisza party. He quickly built it into the main challenger to Viktor Orbán, winning second place in the European Parliament election of June…

priscus.s: Priscus of Panium was an Eastern Roman diplomat and historian of the 5th century. In 449 he accompanied an embassy to the court of Attila and wrote a vivid account of the Huns, describing their wooden palaces, banquets and the mixed peoples of the court.

petun.s: The Petun, or Tionontati, were an Iroquoian people living south of Georgian Bay in what is now Ontario, Canada, neighbours and close allies of the Wendat. The French named them after the tobacco they grew.

prasutagus.s: Prasutagus was king of the Iceni of East Anglia, who ruled as a client of Rome after the conquest of 43. On his death around 60 he left half his kingdom to the emperor Nero and half to his daughters, hoping to protect his family.

panchganga-river.s: The Panchganga is a river of southern Maharashtra, India, formed by the meeting of five streams near Kolhapur. It flows east past Kolhapur and Ichalkaranji and joins the Krishna near Kurundwad.

province-of-castellon.s: The Province of Castellón is the northernmost province of the Valencian Community in eastern Spain, with its capital at Castellón de la Plana. It stretches from the Mediterranean coast to the mountains of El Maestrat.

princess-bety.s: Bety was a princess of the Betsimisaraka of eastern Madagascar, the daughter of Ratsimilaho, founder of the Betsimisaraka confederation. She married a French soldier, Jean-Onésime Filet, known as La Bigorne, and in 1750 ceded Île Sainte-Marie to the French East India Company.

peoria.s: The Peoria were one of the main peoples of the Illinois Confederation, living along the Illinois river, where the city of Peoria bears their name. A Peoria man killed the Odawa leader Pontiac in 1769, bringing reprisals on the Illinois.

pontiac.s: Pontiac was an Odawa war leader who in 1763 led a broad alliance of Great Lakes peoples against British rule after the Seven Years' War, a conflict known as Pontiac's War. His forces besieged Detroit and captured several British forts.

pope-callixtus-ii.s: Callixtus II, born Guy of Burgundy, was pope from 1119 to 1124. A former archbishop of Vienne and kinsman of several royal houses, he ended the Investiture Controversy by agreeing the Concordat of Worms with Emperor Henry V in 1122.

pope-cornelius.s: Cornelius was bishop of Rome from 251 until his death in exile at Centumcellae in 253, and is venerated as a saint and martyr. His election was opposed by Novatian, who led a rigorist schism over the readmission of Christians who had lapsed during the Decian persecution.

passion-of-jesus.s: The Passion of Jesus is the Christian term for the suffering of Jesus in the last hours of his life, from his arrest in the garden of Gethsemane through his trial before Pontius Pilate to his crucifixion outside Jerusalem around 30 to 33 CE. It is told in all four Gospels and…

prum-urbar.s: The Prüm Urbar is a register of the estates, tenants and dues of Prüm Abbey in the Eifel, drawn up in 893. It lists the abbey's manors and the rents and labour services owed by its peasants, making it one of the most important sources on the manorial economy of the Carolingian…

plan-of-saint-gall.s: The Plan of Saint Gall is a drawing of an ideal Benedictine monastery made around 820 at Reichenau Abbey and sent to Abbot Gozbert of Saint Gall. Drawn on five sewn sheets of parchment, it shows a church, cloister and some forty other buildings, including workshops, gardens…

prince-maximilian-of-baden.s: Prince Maximilian of Baden was a German liberal aristocrat who served as the last chancellor of the German Empire in October and November 1918. He sought an armistice with the Allies and on 9 November 1918 announced the abdication of Wilhelm II on his own authority before…

prince-aimone-duke-of-aosta.s: Prince Aimone, Duke of Aosta, was a member of the Italian royal house of Savoy and an admiral. In May 1941 he was designated King of Croatia as Tomislav II under the agreements between Italy and the Independent State of Croatia, but he never went to Croatia and abdicated in 1943.

prakrit.s: Prakrit is the name for the vernacular Middle Indo-Aryan languages of ancient India, related to Sanskrit but simpler in sound and grammar. Ashoka's edicts and many early royal inscriptions are in Prakrit, and Pali and the languages of Jain scripture are forms of it.

philippine-commission.s: The Philippine Commission was a body appointed by the President of the United States to govern the Philippines. The second commission, under William Howard Taft, took over civil government from the army in 1901 and acted as the legislature, later as the upper house beside the…

philippine-organic-act-1902.s: The Philippine Organic Act of 1902 was the first basic law for the civil government of the Philippines under the United States. It confirmed the Philippine Commission, extended a bill of rights to Filipinos, and provided for an elected Philippine Assembly once peace and a…

panionium.s: The Panionium was the common sanctuary of the Ionian League, dedicated to Poseidon Helikonios, on the northern slopes of Mount Mycale in western Anatolia. Delegates of the twelve Ionian cities met there to discuss shared affairs and to celebrate the Panionia festival.

poundmaker.s: Poundmaker was a Plains Cree chief who accepted Treaty 6 with Canada in 1876 and settled on a reserve near Battleford. During the North-West Rebellion of 1885 his band's warriors repulsed a Canadian attack at Cut Knife Hill, but he restrained them from pursuing the retreating…

pervez-musharraf.s: Pervez Musharraf was a Pakistani army general who seized power in a coup in October 1999 and ruled until 2008, as chief executive and from 2001 as president. He made Pakistan an ally of the United States after the attacks of 11 September 2001 and survived several assassination…

paris-peace-treaties-1947.s: The Paris Peace Treaties were signed on 10 February 1947 between the Allied powers and the former Axis allies Italy, Romania, Hungary, Bulgaria and Finland. They set new borders, reparations and limits on armed forces.

palaikastro.s: Palaikastro is a village in eastern Crete and the site of a large Minoan town excavated since 1902. Finds include the ivory and gold Palaikastro Kouros and the Hymn to Diktaean Zeus, inscribed in the Roman period at the sanctuary of Diktaean Zeus there.

ptolemy-son-of-mennaeus.s: Ptolemy son of Mennaeus was the ruler of the Ituraeans in the 1st century BCE, with his capital at Chalcis in the Beqaa valley. He extended his power towards Damascus and the coast during the decline of the Seleucid Empire, and Pompey confirmed him in power in 63 BCE in return…

pnar-people.s: The Pnar people, also called Synteng or Jaintia, are a community of the Jaintia Hills in Meghalaya, north-east India, closely related to the Khasi and speaking a Khasic language. Their society is matrilineal, with property and clan membership passing through women.

patwon-ki-haveli.s: Patwon Ki Haveli is a group of five adjoining merchant mansions in Jaisalmer, Rajasthan, begun in 1805 by the wealthy trader Guman Chand Patwa for his sons. Built of yellow sandstone, the houses are known for their intricately carved facades, balconies and painted interiors.

peoples-national-party.s: The People's National Party is one of Jamaica's two main political parties, founded in 1938 by Norman Manley amid labour unrest. Social democratic in outlook, it governed under Manley in the years before independence and has alternated in power with the Jamaica Labour Party…

panchmahal-district.s: Panchmahal is a district of eastern Gujarat, India, with its headquarters at Godhra. Its hilly, forested country is home to many Bhil and other Adivasi communities.

padmadurg.s: Padmadurg is a sea fort on a rocky islet off Murud on the Konkan coast of Maharashtra, India. It was built by the Marathas in the 1670s and 1680s under Shivaji and his son Sambhaji as a base against the nearby Siddi fortress of Janjira, which they failed to capture.

pancasila.s: Pancasila is the official philosophy of the Indonesian state, set out by Sukarno in a speech of 1 June 1945. Its five principles are belief in one God, just and civilised humanity, the unity of Indonesia, democracy guided by deliberation and consensus, and social justice for…

paide.s: Paide, known in German as Weissenstein, is a town in central Estonia and the centre of Järva County. It grew around a castle built by the Livonian Order in 1265, whose octagonal tower, the Vallitorn, has been rebuilt.

palghar-district.s: Palghar is a district of Maharashtra, India, on the coast and hills north of Mumbai, created in 2014 from the northern part of Thane district. It has a large Adivasi population, especially Warli and Koli communities, and includes the town of Jawhar, former capital of the…

purgatorio.s: Purgatorio is the second part of Dante Alighieri's Divine Comedy, written in the early 14th century. It describes Dante's climb, guided by Virgil, up the mountain of Purgatory, where souls are cleansed of their sins before entering Paradise.

pulakeshin-i.s: Pulakeshin I was the founder of the Chalukya dynasty of Badami in Karnataka, India. In 543 he fortified Vatapi, modern Badami, and performed the horse sacrifice to proclaim his sovereignty, freeing his family from the overlordship of the Kadambas.

pucangan-inscription.s: The Pucangan inscription is a stone inscription of 1041 issued by Airlangga, king of Kahuripan in East Java, in Sanskrit and Old Javanese. It recounts the destruction of the court of his predecessor Dharmawangsa in 1016 and Airlangga's rise to restore the kingdom.

pakhal-lake.s: Pakhal Lake is a large artificial lake in the Warangal region of Telangana, India, created in 1213 during the reign of the Kakatiya king Ganapatideva. Like the nearby Ramappa lake, it was built by damming streams to irrigate the surrounding farmland, part of an extensive…

prataparudra-kakatiya.s: Prataparudra was the last ruler of the Kakatiya dynasty, reigning from Warangal from 1289 to 1323 as the grandson and successor of Rudramadevi. He faced repeated invasions by the Delhi Sultanate, paying tribute after Malik Kafur's siege of 1310.

prola-ii.s: Prola II was a chief of the Kakatiya dynasty in the Telangana region in the first half of the 12th century, ruling as a feudatory of the Western Chalukya Empire. As Chalukya power weakened he expanded his territory and is credited with defeating and capturing the Chalukya king…

pashupata-shaivism.s: Pashupata Shaivism is the oldest named Shaiva sect of Hinduism, traditionally founded by the teacher Lakulisha in the early centuries CE. Its ascetics worshipped Shiva as Pashupati, lord of creatures, and practised unconventional behaviour to court contempt and destroy pride.

punjab-states-agency.s: The Punjab States Agency was a political agency of British India, created in 1921 to manage relations between the British government and the princely states of the Punjab, among them Patiala, Bahawalpur, Nabha and Kapurthala and many smaller states. A British agent supervised…

psaumis-of-camarina.s: Psaumis was a citizen of Camarina, a Greek city on the south coast of Sicily, who won an Olympic victory with a chariot, probably in 452 BCE. The poet Pindar celebrated him in his fourth Olympian ode, and a fifth ode in his honour is also preserved under Pindar's name.

pushyavarman.s: Pushyavarman was the founder of the Varman dynasty of Kamarupa in Assam in the mid-4th century, known from the genealogies in the copper plates of his descendants. His reign was roughly contemporary with the Gupta emperor Samudragupta, whose Allahabad inscription lists…

petrozavodsk.s: Petrozavodsk is a city on the western shore of Lake Onega and the capital of the Republic of Karelia in Russia. It grew from an ironworks founded in 1703 on the orders of Peter the Great to make cannon.

parihaspora.s: Parihaspora was a city founded in the 8th century by Lalitaditya Muktapida, king of Kashmir, on a plateau near modern Srinagar. It served as his capital and was filled with temples, monasteries and a great stupa.

panembahan-girilaya.s: Panembahan Girilaya was ruler of Cirebon on the north coast of Java in the mid-17th century. He was held at the court of Mataram under Amangkurat I and died there in 1662.

pangeran-martawijaya.s: Pangeran Martawijaya was the elder son of Panembahan Girilaya of Cirebon and the first ruler of the Kasepuhan Sultanate. After he and his brother were freed from Mataram in 1677, Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa of Banten divided Cirebon among them, making him Sultan Sepuh, the senior…

pihhuniya.s: Pihhuniya was a Kaska leader of the late 14th century BCE, known from the annals of the Hittite king Mursili II. The annals say that, unlike other Kaska chiefs, he ruled 'in the manner of a king' and raided Hittite lands as far as the Upper Land.

panglao-island.s: Panglao is a small island off the south-western tip of Bohol in the central Philippines, joined to it by bridges. Before Spanish rule it was a trading community of the Bohol coast.

pedro-monteclaro.s: Pedro Monteclaro was a Filipino writer and local official from Miagao, Iloilo, on the island of Panay. In 1907 he published the Maragtas, a legendary history of Panay that he said was drawn from older writings and oral tradition.

poiessa.s: Poiessa was one of the four ancient cities of the island of Keos in the Cyclades, on its west coast. It was the smallest of the Keian tetrapolis, with Ioulis, Karthaia and Koressia.

popol-vuh.s: The Popol Vuh, 'Council Book', is the sacred narrative of the K'iche' Maya of Guatemala. Written in K'iche' in the Latin alphabet by anonymous nobles in the 1550s, it recounts the creation of the world, the exploits of the Hero Twins Hunahpu and Xbalanque, and the history of…

peroz-i.s: Peroz I was a Sasanian king of Persia who reigned from 459 to 484. He took the throne from his brother Hormizd III with Hephthalite help, drove the Kidarites from Bactria around 467 and endured a severe famine.

palermo.s: Palermo is the capital of Sicily, on a bay of the island's north-western coast. Founded by the Phoenicians and known to Greeks and Romans as Panormus, it was taken by the Aghlabids in 831 and became the capital of the Emirate of Sicily and then of the Norman kingdom, whose…

patrice-de-macmahon.s: Patrice de MacMahon was a French marshal of Irish descent and president of France from 1873 to 1879. He won the Battle of Magenta in 1859, was captured with Napoleon III at Sedan in 1870 and crushed the Paris Commune in 1871.

patagonia.s: Patagonia is the southern end of South America, shared by Argentina and Chile, stretching from the Colorado river and the southern Andes to Tierra del Fuego. It combines mountains, steppe plateaus and a fjord coast, and was long the land of Tehuelche, Mapuche and other peoples.

pindus.s: The Pindus is the main mountain range of mainland Greece, running southwards from the Albanian border between Epirus and Thessaly. Its highest peak, Smolikas, rises to 2,637 metres.

perthshire.s: Perthshire is a historic county of central Scotland, stretching from the Highlands of Atholl and Breadalbane to the lowland valley of the Tay. It contains Scone, where Scottish kings were inaugurated, and the early church centre of Dunkeld, and in the Pictish period it lay at…

pradyota.s: Chanda Pradyota, also called Mahasena, was king of Avanti, ruling from Ujjain in the time of the Buddha. Buddhist and Jain texts remember him as powerful and violent: he is said to have threatened Rajagriha, capital of Magadha, and to have fought Udayana of Vatsa, who eloped…

pradyota-dynasty.s: The Pradyota dynasty ruled the kingdom of Avanti, centred on Ujjain in western India, in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE. Puranic tradition says it came to power when the minister Pulika killed the last king of an older line and installed his son Pradyota.

pura-kehen.s: Pura Kehen is a Hindu temple in Bangli, Bali, and the state temple of the former Kingdom of Bangli. Built in terraces on a hillside, it is among the oldest temples on the island, with inscriptions that go back to the early Balinese kingdoms.

prusias-i-of-bithynia.s: Prusias I was king of Bithynia from about 228 to 182 BCE. He expanded the kingdom at the expense of its neighbours, fought Byzantium in 220 BCE over its tolls on Black Sea shipping and warred with Pergamon.

porto.s: Porto is Portugal's second city, on the north bank of the Douro near its mouth. Known as Portus Cale in late antiquity, it gave its name to the County of Portugal after Christian forces took it in 868, and it grew into a trading port famous for the fortified wine named after it.

pays-de-retz.s: The Pays de Retz is a historic district south of the Loire estuary in western France, between Nantes and the Atlantic coast, now in the department of Loire-Atlantique. It was ceded to the Breton king Erispoe by the Treaty of Angers in 851 and remained part of Brittany thereafter.

perdiccas.s: Perdiccas was a Macedonian general of Alexander the Great who became regent of the empire after Alexander's death in 323 BCE. In 322 BCE he conquered Cappadocia, executing its ruler Ariarathes, to install Eumenes there.

perdiccas-i-of-macedon.s: Perdiccas I is named by Herodotus as the founder of the Argead royal house of Macedon in the 7th century BCE. Herodotus tells how he and his brothers, exiles from Argos, came to Macedonia and won the kingship; later writers added earlier kings such as Caranus.

pisiri.s: Pisiri was the last king of Carchemish, the leading Neo-Hittite kingdom on the Euphrates. Long a tributary of Assyria, he was accused of plotting with Mita (Midas) of Phrygia, and in 717 BCE Sargon II deposed him, deported him with his family and made Carchemish an Assyrian…

periyar-river.s: The Periyar is the longest river of Kerala, in south-western India, flowing about 244 kilometres from the Western Ghats to the Arabian Sea. A great flood in 1341 is said to have silted up the old port of Muziris near its mouth and opened a new harbour at Kochi, which then grew…

phasis-town.s: Phasis was an ancient Greek colony on the eastern Black Sea coast, founded by settlers from Miletus in the 6th century BCE near the mouth of the Phasis river (Rioni), close to modern Poti in Georgia. It was the main port of Colchis, linking the Greek world with the river route…

ptolemaeus-of-commagene.s: Ptolemaeus was the founder of the kingdom of Commagene in south-eastern Anatolia. A Seleucid governor of the region, he broke away from the weakening Seleucid Empire around 163 BCE and ruled as an independent king until about 130 BCE.

paul-i-subic-of-bribir.s: Paul I Šubić of Bribir was a Croatian nobleman who became ban of Croatia in the 1270s and the most powerful magnate of the kingdom. Ruling much of Croatia, Dalmatia and Bosnia almost independently, he styled himself lord of Bosnia and backed the Angevin Charles Robert for the…

pacta-conventa-croatia.s: The Pacta conventa is a document that claims to record an agreement of about 1102 between King Coloman of Hungary and twelve Croatian noble families, guaranteeing their lands and freedoms in return for accepting him as king. It survives only in a 14th-century copy, and most…

petar-snacic.s: Petar Snačić was the last native king of Croatia, chosen by Croatian nobles in 1093 in opposition to the Hungarian claim to the throne. He ruled from Knin and resisted the forces of Coloman of Hungary, falling at the Battle of Gvozd Mountain in 1097.

pacaritambo.s: Pacaritambo is a village in Paruro province, Peru, south of Cusco, associated with the Inca origin myth. Spanish chroniclers recorded that the ancestors of the Incas, Manco Capac and his siblings, emerged from the three windows of the cave of Tambo Toco there before travelling…

pindar.s: Pindar was a Greek lyric poet from Thebes, the most admired composer of choral odes in antiquity. His victory odes for winners at the Olympic, Pythian, Isthmian and Nemean games, written for rulers and aristocrats across the Greek world from Sicily to Cyrene and Rhodes,…

peoples-party-dalmatia.s: The People's Party was a political party in the Austrian Kingdom of Dalmatia, founded in the 1860s, that sought Dalmatia's union with Croatia-Slavonia and the use of Croatian in public life. Opposed by the Italian-speaking Autonomist Party, it won control of the Dalmatian diet…

pujavaliya.s: The Pujavaliya is a classic of Sinhala prose written in the 13th century by the monk Mayurapada Buddhaputra during the Dambadeniya period. Organised around the offerings made to the Buddha, it recounts the Buddha's life and includes a chronicle of the kings of Sri Lanka, and…

pura-luhur-uluwatu.s: Pura Luhur Uluwatu is a Hindu sea temple on a clifftop at the south-western tip of Bali, Indonesia, one of the island's principal directional temples. It is associated with the 16th-century priest Dang Hyang Nirartha, who is said to have attained spiritual liberation there.

palace-of-westminster.s: The Palace of Westminster in London is the meeting place of the Parliament of the United Kingdom, and before it of the Parliaments of England and Great Britain. A royal palace from the 11th century, it was rebuilt in Gothic Revival style by Charles Barry and Augustus Pugin…

pest-hungary.s: Pest is the eastern part of Budapest, on the flat left bank of the Danube opposite Buda. A trading town since the Middle Ages, it grew rapidly in the 18th and 19th centuries into Hungary's commercial and cultural centre, home of the National Museum and the Academy of Sciences,…

pharnavaz-i-of-iberia.s: Pharnavaz I was the first king of Iberia, or Kartli, in eastern Georgia, according to the medieval Georgian chronicles, which place him around 300 BCE. They credit him with uniting the country after the fall of the Achaemenid Empire, organising it into provinces under…

parshvanatha.s: Parshvanatha is the 23rd tirthankara of Jainism and the earliest Jain teacher widely regarded as a historical figure, traditionally placed about 250 years before Mahavira. Jain tradition says he was a prince of Varanasi, son of King Ashvasena, who renounced the world and…

paul-holle.s: Paul Holle was a French colonial officer from Saint-Louis in Senegal who commanded the fort at Médine on the upper Senegal River. In 1857, with a small garrison and the people of King Juka Sambala, he held the fort for three months against the army of El Hadj Umar Tall until…

pharasmanes-of-khwarazm.s: Pharasmanes was a king of Khwarazm (Chorasmia) in the late 4th century BCE, known from the historian Arrian. In the winter of 329–328 BCE he came to Alexander the Great at Bactra with 1,500 horsemen, offered an alliance and proposed a joint campaign towards the Black Sea;…

prasenajit.s: Prasenajit, known in Pali as Pasenadi, was king of Kosala in northern India in the time of the Buddha, ruling from Shravasti. Buddhist texts portray him as a lay follower and frequent questioner of the Buddha, and he was linked by marriage to Bimbisara of Magadha.

patan-durbar-square.s: Patan Durbar Square is the old royal square of Lalitpur (Patan) in the Kathmandu Valley, Nepal, in front of the palace of the Malla kings of Lalitpur. Most of its temples and palace courtyards date from the 17th and 18th centuries, among them the stone Krishna Mandir, and the…

paulinus-of-york.s: Paulinus was a Roman missionary sent to England in 601 to join Augustine's mission, and the first bishop of York. He went to Northumbria with Æthelburh of Kent on her marriage to King Edwin, whom he baptised at York in 627, and preached in Deira, Bernicia and Lindsey, where he…

poltsamaa.s: Põltsamaa, German Oberpahlen, is a town in central Estonia on the Põltsamaa river. Its castle, built by the Livonian Order in the 13th century, was the residence of Duke Magnus of Holstein as Ivan IV's vassal king of Livonia from 1570.

portlaoise.s: Portlaoise is the county town of County Laois in the Irish midlands. It grew from a fort built in the 1540s to subdue the O'Mores and was named Maryborough after Mary I when the plantation of Queen's County began in 1556.

palermo-stone.s: The Palermo Stone is the largest fragment of an ancient Egyptian royal annal carved on a basalt slab in the 5th Dynasty, around the 25th century BCE. Kept in Palermo since 1877, it lists early kings year by year with events such as festivals, Nile flood heights and…

pactolus.s: The Pactolus is a small river in western Turkey that flows from Mount Tmolus past the ruins of Sardis into the Gediz, the ancient Hermus. In antiquity it carried grains of electrum, a natural alloy of gold and silver, which enriched the Lydian kings and supplied the first coins.

pamheiba.s: Pamheiba, known as Garib Niwaz, was king of Manipur from 1709 to 1748. He made Hindu Vaishnavism the court religion, reportedly ordering the burning of older Meitei scriptures, and led repeated campaigns into Burma, raiding deep into the Irrawaddy valley.

polis-chrysochous.s: Polis Chrysochous is a small town on Chrysochous Bay in north-west Cyprus. It stands on the site of the ancient city-kingdom of Marion, which grew rich from nearby copper mines and was destroyed by Ptolemy I in 312 BCE, and of its successor Arsinoe, founded by Ptolemy II.

pura-meru.s: Pura Meru is a Hindu temple in Cakranegara on Lombok, Indonesia, built in 1720 under the Balinese rulers of the island. It is the largest temple on Lombok, with courtyards holding tiered meru shrines of eleven, nine and seven roofs dedicated to Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma.

pura-taman-ayun.s: Pura Taman Ayun is a royal Hindu temple at Mengwi in southern Bali, Indonesia, built as the state temple of the Mengwi kingdom. Surrounded by a broad moat, with tiered meru shrines, it expressed the rulers' authority over irrigation and fertility.

penda-of-mercia.s: Penda was the pagan king of Mercia who made it the strongest kingdom of the English Midlands in the mid-7th century. Allied with Welsh rulers, he killed Edwin of Northumbria at Hatfield Chase in 633 and Oswald at Maserfield in 642, and he defeated East Anglia and drove the…

papora-people.s: The Papora are an indigenous plains people of the coastal plain around present-day Taichung in west-central Taiwan. In the 17th century they belonged to the Middag alliance known from Dutch records, and after the Qing took Taiwan they lost much land to Chinese settlers.

pazeh-people.s: The Pazeh are an indigenous plains people of the Taichung basin in west-central Taiwan. Part of the 17th-century Middag alliance, they later lost much of their land to Chinese settlers, and many migrated to the Puli basin in the 19th century.

podgorica-assembly.s: The Podgorica Assembly was a gathering of elected representatives that met in Podgorica in November 1918, at the end of the First World War. On 26 November it deposed King Nicholas I and the Petrović-Njegoš dynasty of Montenegro and voted for unconditional union with Serbia,…

province-of-albacete.s: The Province of Albacete is a province of Castilla–La Mancha in south-eastern Spain, with its capital at the city of Albacete. It was created in Javier de Burgos's territorial division of 1833 from parts of the old Kingdom of Murcia and La Mancha.

pungo-andongo.s: Pungo Andongo is a massif of giant black rock formations in Malanje Province, Angola, which served as a royal stronghold of the kingdom of Ndongo. After the Portuguese stormed the fortress in 1671 and ended Ndongo's last independent kingship, they built a presidio there that…

patraos.s: Patraos was a king of Paeonia from about 335 to 315 BCE, during the reign of Alexander the Great, whose overlordship he accepted. He issued silver tetradrachms showing a Paeonian horseman spearing a fallen enemy, a design that underlines the kingdom's cavalry tradition.

palaepaphos.s: Palaepaphos, Old Paphos, was an ancient city in south-west Cyprus, at modern Kouklia. Inhabited from the Late Bronze Age, it was the capital of the kingdom of Paphos and home to one of the most famous sanctuaries of Aphrodite, who was said to have risen from the sea nearby.

pergamon-altar.s: The Pergamon Altar is a monumental altar built on the acropolis of Pergamon in the reign of Eumenes II in the first half of the 2nd century BCE. Its frieze, about 113 m long, shows the battle of the gods and giants, a symbol of Attalid victories over the Galatians.

philetaerus.s: Philetaerus was the founder of the Attalid dynasty of Pergamon. An officer of Lysimachus, he guarded a treasure of 9,000 talents in the citadel of Pergamon, and in 282 BCE he went over to Seleucus I, keeping the fortress and the money.

papak.s: Papak, or Pabag, was a local ruler in Persis in south-western Iran in the early 3rd century CE and father of Ardashir I, the founder of the Sasanian Empire. According to tradition he was a priest at the temple of Anahita in Istakhr who seized power in the city around 205,…

pulvar-river.s: The Pulvar is a river in Fars Province, south-western Iran, which flows past Pasargadae and Persepolis to join the Kor River on the plain of Marvdasht. Its valley was the heartland of ancient Persis, and the Achaemenid and later Sasanian centres of Pasargadae, Persepolis and…

phrygians.s: The Phrygians were an Indo-European people who settled in central and western Anatolia after the collapse of the Hittite Empire around 1200 BCE, probably migrating from the Balkans. They built a kingdom centred on Gordion that flourished in the 8th century BCE under Midas,…

panticapaeum.s: Panticapaeum was an ancient Greek city on the site of modern Kerch in Crimea, founded by colonists from Miletus around 600 BCE. It became the capital of the Bosporan Kingdom, which controlled the Cimmerian Bosporus and exported grain to Athens.

pharnaces-i-of-pontus.s: Pharnaces I was king of Pontus from about 185 to about 160 BCE. He captured the Greek city of Sinope in 183 BCE and made it his capital, and fought a war against Eumenes II of Pergamon and other Anatolian rulers that ended with the peace of 179 BCE, in which he gave up most of…

prince-marko.s: Prince Marko, Marko Mrnjavčević, was the son of King Vukašin and ruled a realm around Prilep in Macedonia after his father's death at the Battle of the Maritsa in 1371. He became an Ottoman vassal and was killed fighting for the Ottomans against Mircea the Elder of Wallachia…

poseidon.s: Poseidon was the Greek god of the sea, earthquakes and horses, brother of Zeus. He was one of the most important gods of the Mycenaean world, receiving many offerings in the Linear B tablets of Pylos.

papeiha.s: Papeiha was a Polynesian Christian teacher from Raiatea who worked for the London Missionary Society. Landed at Aitutaki in 1821, he went to Rarotonga in 1823 and is credited with converting the island to Christianity before European missionaries arrived to stay.

perfeddwlad.s: The Perfeddwlad, the "Middle Country", was the name for the four cantrefi of north-east Wales between the River Conwy and the River Dee: Rhos, Rhufoniog, Dyffryn Clwyd and Tegeingl. Lying between Gwynedd and England, it was repeatedly fought over by Welsh princes and English…

ploiesti.s: Ploiești is a city in southern Romania, north of Bucharest, at the centre of the Prahova oil region. From the late 19th century it became the hub of the Romanian oil industry, with refineries that made it one of Europe's main sources of petroleum.

pope-boniface-viii.s: Pope Boniface VIII, born Benedetto Caetani, was pope from 1294 to 1303. He proclaimed the first Jubilee in 1300, issued the bull Unam sanctam in 1302 asserting papal supremacy, and in 1297 granted Sardinia and Corsica to James II of Aragon.

peoples-radical-party.s: The People's Radical Party was a Serbian political party founded in 1881 by Nikola Pašić and others, with a strong base among the peasantry. After the May Coup of 1903 it dominated the parliamentary governments of the Kingdom of Serbia, and it remained a leading party in the…

pemayangtse-monastery.s: Pemayangtse Monastery is a Buddhist monastery of the Nyingma school near Pelling in western Sikkim, India, founded in the late 17th or early 18th century. It was one of the leading monasteries of the kingdom of Sikkim, whose monks were traditionally drawn from Bhutia families…

pozega-croatia.s: Požega is a town in the Slavonia region of eastern Croatia, in a fertile valley ringed by hills. A county seat of the medieval Kingdom of Hungary, it was taken by the Ottomans in 1537 and returned to Habsburg rule in 1688, after which it again became the seat of Požega County.

philocyprus.s: Philocyprus was king of Soloi in Cyprus in the early 6th century BCE. Plutarch relates that, on the advice of the Athenian lawgiver Solon, who visited him, he moved his city to a better site in the plain and named it Soloi in Solon's honour.

palace-of-vouni.s: The Palace of Vouni stands on a hilltop above the north-west coast of Cyprus, near ancient Soloi. Built around 500 BCE, perhaps by a pro-Persian ruler of Marion to watch over Soloi after the revolt against Persia, it was later rebuilt in Greek style and was destroyed by fire…

pevensey-castle.s: Pevensey Castle is a medieval castle in East Sussex, England, built inside the walls of the Roman fort of Anderitum. The fort was erected in the late 3rd century as one of the Saxon Shore defences, and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records its storming by Ælle and the South Saxons…

pomare-i.s: Pōmare I, born Tū, was a Tahitian chief who founded the Pōmare dynasty and the Kingdom of Tahiti. Using muskets obtained from visiting ships and the help of Bounty mutineers, he extended his power over Tahiti and Moorea from about 1788.

pomare-v.s: Pōmare V was the last king of Tahiti, reigning from 1877 to 1880. The son of Queen Pōmare IV, he succeeded under the French protectorate and in 1880 ceded Tahiti and its dependencies to France in return for a pension.

pumiyaton.s: Pumiyaton was the last Phoenician king of Kition in Cyprus, reigning from about 362 to 312 BCE. He bought the city-kingdom of Tamassos and its copper mines from its king Pasicyprus.

pedieos.s: The Pedieos is the longest river of Cyprus, rising in the Troodos mountains and flowing north-east through Nicosia across the Mesaoria plain towards Famagusta Bay. Ancient settlements in its valley included Tamassos, Idalion and Ledra.

pandukabhaya.s: Pandukabhaya was, according to the Sri Lankan chronicles, the king who founded Anuradhapura as his capital around 437 BCE. The Mahavamsa tells of his long struggle with his uncles for the throne and credits him with planning the city, its reservoirs and its quarters for…

panduvasudeva.s: Panduvasudeva was, according to the Mahavamsa, the second king of Sri Lanka, a nephew of Prince Vijaya who came from India to succeed him. He is said to have ruled from Upatissa Gama and married the Shakya princess Bhaddakaccana, and his grandson Pandukabhaya founded…

puttalam.s: Puttalam is a town on the north-west coast of Sri Lanka, on the Puttalam Lagoon. The nearby coast is one of the places linked by tradition with the landing of Prince Vijaya, and the area has long been known for its salt pans and coconut plantations.

prince-vijaya.s: Prince Vijaya is the legendary first king of Sri Lanka, said in the Pali chronicles to have been exiled from northern India and to have landed on the island with 700 followers on the day of the Buddha's death, traditionally 543 BCE. He married the Yakkha woman Kuveni, founded…

peterborough-abbey.s: Peterborough Abbey was a Benedictine monastery in eastern England, founded around 655 as Medeshamstede in the time of Peada of the Middle Angles. Destroyed by Danes in the 9th century and refounded in the 10th, it continued the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle until 1154.

peada.s: Peada was a son of Penda of Mercia, made ruler of the Middle Angles around 653. To marry Alhflæd, daughter of Oswiu of Northumbria, he accepted baptism and brought four priests to preach among his people.

portici.s: Portici is a town on the Bay of Naples at the foot of Vesuvius, in Campania, southern Italy. The Bourbon king Charles built a royal palace there from 1738, close to the newly discovered ruins of Herculaneum.

polybius.s: Polybius was a Greek historian from Megalopolis in Arcadia, taken to Rome as a hostage in 167 BCE, where he became a friend of Scipio Aemilianus and witnessed the destruction of Carthage in 146 BCE. His Histories, in 40 books, explain how Rome came to dominate the…

pierre-bataillon.s: Pierre Bataillon was a French Marist missionary who led the Catholic mission to Wallis Island from 1837. Within a few years the island's whole population had converted, and he became vicar apostolic of Central Oceania, as bishop, in 1843.

polynesians.s: The Polynesians are the peoples of the islands within the Polynesian triangle of the central and southern Pacific, from Hawaii to New Zealand and Easter Island. Descended from Austronesian seafarers of the Lapita culture, they reached Tonga and Samoa around 900–800 BCE and…
