prayagraj.s: Prayagraj, called Allahabad from the time of Akbar until 2018, is a city in Uttar Pradesh, India, at the confluence of the Ganges and Yamuna, a sacred bathing place for Hindus. It hosts the Kumbh Mela, one of the largest religious gatherings in the world.

pilliya.s: Pilliya was a king of Kizzuwatna in south-eastern Anatolia in the 15th century BCE. He concluded a treaty with the Hittite king Zidanta II, and a tablet found at Alalakh records another treaty between him and Idrimi of Mukish, settling the return of fugitives.

puduhepa.s: Puduhepa was a Hittite queen of the 13th century BCE, wife of Hattusili III and the daughter of a priest of Lawazantiya in Kizzuwatna. She was one of the most powerful queens of the ancient Near East: she shared in government, judged cases, reorganised the state cults along…

praxiteles.s: Praxiteles was an Athenian sculptor of the 4th century BCE, one of the most admired artists of ancient Greece. His Aphrodite of Knidos, the first large-scale female nude in Greek sculpture, made the city a destination for visitors.

philitas-of-cos.s: Philitas of Cos was a Greek poet and scholar of the early Hellenistic age, born on Kos around 340 BCE. He was tutor to the future Ptolemy II Philadelphus and is regarded as the first poet-scholar of the Hellenistic period, writing elegies and a glossary of rare words.

poro.s: The Poro is a secret society for men among peoples of Sierra Leone, Liberia, Guinea and Côte d'Ivoire, including the Mende, Temne, Kpelle and Vai. It initiates boys into adulthood through training in bush camps and has long held religious, political and judicial authority,…

polotsk.s: Polotsk is one of the oldest cities of Belarus, on the Western Dvina River, first mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under 862. In the 10th century it was ruled by the Scandinavian Rogvolod, and it later became the seat of an independent principality under Vseslav and his…

parikshit.s: Parikshit was a Kuru king of the late Vedic period, praised in a hymn of the Atharvaveda for the peace and prosperity of his realm. With his son Janamejaya he is credited by modern historians with making the Kuru state the dominant power of northern India.

purus.s: The Purus were one of the leading tribes of the Rigveda, living in the Punjab in the early Vedic period and rivals of the Bharatas, whom they opposed in the Battle of the Ten Kings. They later merged with the Bharatas to form the Kurus.

parahu.s: Parahu was a ruler of the Land of Punt shown in the reliefs of Queen Hatshepsut's temple at Deir el-Bahari, which record an Egyptian expedition to Punt around 1470 BCE. He is depicted with a dagger and a beard, greeting the Egyptian envoys, together with his wife Ati, who is…

pha-that-luang.s: Pha That Luang is a large gold-covered Buddhist stupa in Vientiane, Laos, built by King Setthathirath around 1566 on the site of an older shrine. It was damaged in the Siamese sack of Vientiane in 1828 and restored in the 20th century.

phetsarath-ratanavongsa.s: Prince Phetsarath Ratanavongsa was a Lao nationalist leader and viceroy of the Kingdom of Luang Prabang. After the Japanese surrender in 1945 he declared the unification and independence of Laos and led the Lao Issara movement, going into exile in Thailand when the French…

phra-prang-sam-yot.s: Phra Prang Sam Yot is a temple in Lopburi, Thailand, with three linked towers in the Khmer style. Built around the late 12th or early 13th century, probably as a Hindu shrine, it was later converted to Buddhist use.

plav.s: Plav is a town in north-eastern Montenegro, beside Lake Plav at the foot of the Prokletije mountains. Together with nearby Gusinje it was assigned to Montenegro by the Congress of Berlin in 1878, but Albanian forces of the League of Prizren resisted the handover.

prizren.s: Prizren is a city in southern Kosovo, at the foot of the Šar Mountains. It was an important town of medieval Serbia and later an Ottoman trading centre with mosques, a stone bridge and the Serbian Orthodox church of Our Lady of Ljeviš.

paris-peace-conference-1919-1920.s: The Paris Peace Conference was the meeting of the victorious Allied powers after the First World War, opened in January 1919 and dominated by Britain, France, the United States and Italy. It drew up the Treaty of Versailles with Germany and the treaties of Saint-Germain,…

pashupatinath-temple.s: The Pashupatinath Temple is a Hindu temple of Shiva as Pashupati, 'lord of animals', on the Bagmati river in Kathmandu, Nepal. Already a major shrine in the Licchavi period, it is the most sacred Hindu site in Nepal and draws pilgrims from across South Asia; the present…

pachacamac.s: Pachacamac is an archaeological site in the Lurín valley south of Lima, Peru, one of the largest and longest-lived religious centres of the ancient Andes. Occupied from about 200 CE, it grew around the cult of the creator god Pachacamac, whose oracle drew pilgrims from far…

pentathlus.s: Pentathlus was a Greek leader from Cnidus who, according to Diodorus and Pausanias, led settlers from Cnidus and Rhodes to found a colony near Lilybaeum in western Sicily around 580 BCE. The attempt failed in fighting with the Elymians of Segesta and the Phoenicians,…

peoples-seimas.s: The People's Seimas was the parliament of Lithuania elected on 14–15 July 1940 under Soviet occupation, in a vote with a single list of Communist-approved candidates. On 21 July it proclaimed Lithuania a Soviet socialist republic and asked to join the Soviet Union, which…

persephone.s: Persephone was a Greek goddess, daughter of Zeus and Demeter, carried off by Hades to be queen of the underworld. Her yearly return to her mother was linked to the growth of crops, and she was worshipped with Demeter in the Eleusinian Mysteries.

parliament-of-mechelen.s: The Parliament of Mechelen was the supreme court established by Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, at Mechelen in 1473 for his Low Countries lands. Abolished after his death in 1477, it was restored in 1504 as the Great Council of Mechelen, which served as the highest court…

pinerolo.s: Pinerolo is a town in Piedmont, Italy, south-west of Turin at the entrance to the valleys leading to the French Alps. From the 1290s it was the seat of the Savoy-Achaea branch that ruled Piedmont.

plauen.s: Plauen is a city in the Vogtland region of south-western Saxony, Germany, on the White Elster. From the 13th century it was the seat of a branch of the advocates (Vögte) of Weida, and it later passed to Saxony.

paolo-malatesta.s: Paolo Malatesta, called il Bello, was a son of Malatesta da Verucchio, lord of Rimini, and served as captain of the people in Florence in 1282. His love affair with his sister-in-law Francesca da Polenta ended when his brother Giovanni, called Gianciotto, killed them both…

paradiso-dante.s: Paradiso is the third and final part of Dante Alighieri's Divine Comedy, completed shortly before his death in 1321. Guided by Beatrice, Dante ascends through the heavenly spheres to the vision of God.

pleissenland.s: The Pleissenland was an imperial territory in what is now eastern Thuringia and western Saxony, around Altenburg, Zwickau and Chemnitz, named after the Pleisse river. Organised by the Hohenstaufen emperors in the 12th century as a royal domain, it was administered by imperial…

pisidia.s: Pisidia was a mountainous region of south-western Anatolia, north of Pamphylia in the Taurus mountains. Its warlike people long resisted Persian and Hellenistic rulers, and the Romans founded colonies there such as Pisidian Antioch, visited by the apostle Paul.

pax-julia.s: Pax Julia was a Roman town in southern Lusitania, on the site of modern Beja in Portugal's Alentejo region. Founded as a colony in the time of Julius Caesar or Augustus, it became the seat of one of the province's judicial districts (conventus).

patara.s: Patara was a port city of ancient Lycia, near the mouth of the Xanthos river in south-western Turkey. It had a famous oracle of Apollo and was a meeting place of the Lycian League, whose council chamber (bouleuterion) has been restored.

pinara.s: Pinara was a city of ancient Lycia on the western side of the Xanthos valley in south-western Turkey, and one of the six largest members of the Lycian League. It lies below a sheer cliff honeycombed with hundreds of rock-cut tombs, and its ruins include a theatre, an odeon and…

plutarch.s: Plutarch was a Greek writer and philosopher from Chaeronea in Boeotia, who also served as a priest at Delphi. His Parallel Lives pair biographies of famous Greeks and Romans, and his Moralia gather essays on ethics, religion and customs.

puntland.s: Puntland is an autonomous state in north-eastern Somalia, declared in 1998 by clan leaders after the collapse of the central government. Its capital is Garowe, and it includes Cape Guardafui and the ports of Bosaso and Eyl.

pasni.s: Pasni is a fishing port on the Makran coast of Balochistan, Pakistan, on the Arabian Sea. In the 19th and early 20th centuries it was one of the harbours through which Makran traded, and it lay in Makran State until that state joined Pakistan in 1948 and was merged into…

pusiga.s: Pusiga is a town in the Upper East Region of Ghana, near the borders with Togo and Burkina Faso. Mole-Dagbani tradition names it as the home of Na Gbewaa, the ancestor of the ruling houses of Mamprugu, Dagbon, Nanumba and the Mossi kingdoms, and his shrine there is still…

percy-cox.s: Sir Percy Cox was a British army officer and colonial administrator who spent most of his career in the Persian Gulf and Mesopotamia. As civil commissioner and then High Commissioner in Iraq from 1920 to 1923, he helped install Faisal I as king and set up the mandate government.

plague-of-athens.s: The Plague of Athens was an epidemic that struck Athens in 430 BCE, the second year of the Peloponnesian War, and returned in the winter of 427–426 BCE. The population, crowded inside the city walls by Pericles' strategy of avoiding battle on land, suffered terribly, and…

peasants-revolt.s: The Peasants' Revolt of 1381 was the largest popular rising in medieval England. Triggered by the third poll tax in four years, and fed by resentment of serfdom and of the laws holding down wages after the Black Death, rebels from Essex and Kent marched on London in June 1381,…

partition-of-india.s: The Partition of India was the division of British India into two independent dominions, India and Pakistan, on 14–15 August 1947. The boundary, drawn by a commission under Cyril Radcliffe and published only after independence, split the provinces of Punjab and Bengal along…

palestine-liberation-organization.s: The Palestine Liberation Organization is the umbrella organisation founded in 1964 to represent the Palestinian people and their claim to statehood. Dominated from 1969 by Yasser Arafat and Fatah, it fought Israel from Jordan and then Lebanon, was recognised by the Arab states…

peel-commission.s: The Peel Commission was a British royal commission led by Lord Peel, appointed in 1936 to investigate the causes of the Arab revolt in Mandatory Palestine. Its report of July 1937 concluded that the mandate was unworkable and proposed, for the first time, partition into a…

puro-mangkunegaran.s: The Puro Mangkunegaran is the palace of the Mangkunegara princes in Surakarta (Solo), Central Java, Indonesia, begun after the house was founded in 1757. Built in Javanese style around one of the largest open pavilions (pendopo) in Java, it houses collections of gamelan, dance…

portoviejo.s: Portoviejo is the capital of Manabí province on the coast of Ecuador. It was founded by the Spanish in 1535 in the lands of the Manteño people, making it one of the oldest Spanish towns in the country.

piyale-pasha.s: Piyale Pasha was an Ottoman admiral (Kapudan Pasha) under Suleiman the Magnificent and Selim II, of Croatian or Hungarian origin. He defeated a Spanish-led fleet at Djerba in 1560, commanded the fleet at the unsuccessful siege of Malta in 1565, and took Chios from the Genoese…

pforzheim.s: Pforzheim is a city at the northern edge of the Black Forest in Baden-Württemberg, Germany. It was a residence of the margraves of Baden in the Middle Ages, and from 1767 it developed a major jewellery and watchmaking industry, earning the name 'Gold City'.

philippine-welser.s: Philippine Welser was the daughter of a merchant of the wealthy Welser family of Augsburg. In 1557 she secretly married Archduke Ferdinand II of Austria, a marriage later accepted on condition that their children could not inherit Habsburg lands.

paraetonium.s: Paraetonium was an ancient port on the Mediterranean coast west of Alexandria, on the site of modern Marsa Matruh in Egypt. Alexander the Great passed through it on his way to the oracle of Siwa in 331 BCE, and Mark Antony stayed there after his defeat at Actium in 31 BCE.

puritans.s: The Puritans were English Protestants of the late sixteenth and seventeenth centuries who sought to purify the Church of England of practices they considered Catholic, stressing preaching, strict morality and congregational discipline. Pressure under Charles I drove some…

protis.s: Protis was the leader of the Greek settlers from Phocaea who, according to tradition, founded Massalia (Marseille) around 600 BCE. In the legend told by the Roman historian Justin, he arrived as Nannus, king of the local Segobrigii, held a feast at which his daughter Gyptis…

plered.s: Plered was the capital of the Mataram Sultanate in Java under Amangkurat I, who moved his court there from nearby Kerta in the 1640s. Lying south-east of present-day Yogyakarta, it had a walled palace and an artificial lake.

pandavas.s: The Pandavas are the five brothers Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula and Sahadeva, heroes of the Indian epic Mahabharata. Sons of King Pandu's wives Kunti and Madri, they lose their kingdom to their cousins the Kauravas, spend years in exile, including a final year in…

pratap-chandra-bhanj-deo.s: Pratap Chandra Bhanj Deo was the last ruling Maharaja of Mayurbhanj, a princely state in Odisha, from 1928 to 1949. In 1947 he introduced an elected government with a responsible ministry, and Mayurbhanj held out longer than the other Orissa states, but it merged into the…

phraaspa.s: Phraaspa was a royal city of Media Atropatene in north-western Iran. In 36 BCE Mark Antony besieged it during his campaign against Parthia, but after the Parthians and Medes destroyed his siege train he had to abandon the siege and retreat to Armenia with heavy losses.

phylakopi.s: Phylakopi is a Bronze Age town site on the north coast of Melos in the Cyclades, Greece. Occupied from about 2300 to 1100 BCE, it grew rich on the island's obsidian and on sea trade, and its remains show successive Cycladic, Minoan and Mycenaean influence, including frescoes…

pieria.s: Pieria is a region of Central Macedonia in northern Greece, lying between Mount Olympus and the western shore of the Thermaic Gulf, with Katerini as its main town. In antiquity it was the home of the Pierians and was associated with the Muses, and it was absorbed into the…

pointe-noire.s: Pointe-Noire is the second city and main seaport of the Republic of the Congo, on the Atlantic coast. It grew from the 1920s as the ocean terminus of the Congo-Ocean railway from Brazzaville, built at a heavy cost in lives of conscripted African workers and opened in 1934.

piyamaradu.s: Piyamaradu was a western Anatolian warlord of the 13th century BCE, known from Hittite texts such as the Tawagalawa letter and the Manapa-Tarhunta letter. Of uncertain origin, possibly a member of the royal house of Arzawa, he raided Hittite vassal lands from bases such as…

pampa-grande.s: Pampa Grande is an archaeological site in the Lambayeque valley on the north coast of Peru, the largest centre of the late Moche period around 600 to 700 CE. Built after the older Moche centres to the south declined amid climatic crises, it covered several square kilometres…

palaung.s: The Palaung, who call themselves Ta'ang, are a Mon-Khmer-speaking people of the northern Shan hills of Myanmar and neighbouring parts of China. Traditionally Theravada Buddhists and famous as tea growers, they lived under the rule of Shan princes such as those of Momeik and…

pao-people.s: The Pa'O are a Karen-speaking people of the southern Shan State of Myanmar, living mainly around Taunggyi and the hills near Inle Lake, and are one of the country's larger ethnic minorities. Traditionally Buddhist farmers known for growing thanaphet leaves for cheroots, they…

plymouth-montserrat.s: Plymouth is the abandoned capital of Montserrat, a British territory in the Caribbean. The island's main town and port since colonial times, it was buried under ash and pyroclastic flows by the eruptions of the Soufrière Hills volcano, which began in 1995 and destroyed the…

princess-milica-of-serbia.s: Milica was the wife of Prince Lazar of Serbia and, after his death at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389, regent for their son Stefan Lazarević. She negotiated vassalage with the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I, gave her daughter Olivera in marriage to him and kept the principality intact.

portus-itius.s: Portus Itius was the harbour in the land of the Morini, in northern Gaul, from which Julius Caesar sailed for his second invasion of Britain in 54 BCE. Caesar describes it as the most convenient crossing point, about 30 Roman miles from Britain.

port-st-johns.s: Port St Johns is a town on the Wild Coast of the Eastern Cape in South Africa, at the mouth of the Mzimvubu River. Its sheltered estuary interested British officials as a harbour, and Britain obtained it from the Mpondo in 1878, isolating Pondoland from the sea before its…

pelias.s: In Greek mythology, Pelias was the king of Iolkos in Thessaly who seized the throne from his half-brother Aeson. Warned by an oracle to beware a man wearing one sandal, he sent Aeson's son Jason to fetch the Golden Fleece.

purnaiah.s: Purnaiah was a minister of Mysore who served Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan as head of finance. After Tipu's death in 1799 the British made him diwan to the boy king Krishnaraja Wodeyar III, and he ran the restored state until 1811, rebuilding its finances and administration under…

pittacus.s: Pittacus was a statesman of Mytilene on Lesbos, counted among the Seven Sages of Greece. He helped overthrow the tyrant Melanchrus and won fame by killing the Athenian commander Phrynon in single combat at Sigeion.

pausanias-geographer.s: Pausanias was a Greek traveller and geographer of the 2nd century CE, probably from Asia Minor. His Description of Greece, in ten books, records the cities, monuments, works of art and local traditions of mainland Greece in the Roman period.

pausanias-general.s: Pausanias was a Spartan general and regent for the young king Pleistarchus. He commanded the Greek army that defeated the Persians at Plataea in 479 BCE and in 478 BCE took Byzantium.

petra.s: Petra is an ancient city in southern Jordan, set in sandstone mountains near the Wadi Araba. It was the capital of the Nabataeans, who grew rich from the caravan trade in incense and spices and carved tombs and temples into its rose-coloured cliffs.

pawaya.s: Pawaya is a village and archaeological site near Gwalior in Madhya Pradesh, India, identified with ancient Padmavati, capital of a Naga dynasty in the 3rd and 4th centuries. Excavations have found Naga coins, a brick temple platform and fine Gupta-period sculpture.

parihar.s: The Parihars are a Rajput clan of northern and central India who claim descent from the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty, which ruled much of northern India from the 8th to the 11th century. Parihar families held small states in Bundelkhand and Baghelkhand, among them Nagod and…

pandacan.s: Pandacan is a district of the City of Manila in the Philippines, on the south bank of the Pasig River. Originally a riverside settlement within the lands of the pre-colonial polity of Namayan, it developed as a separate town under Spanish rule and was incorporated into Manila…

puranas.s: The Puranas are a large genre of Sanskrit texts of the Hindu tradition, composed and revised from around the 3rd to the 16th century CE. The eighteen major Puranas cover cosmology, myths of the gods, pilgrimage, ritual and the genealogies of ancient kings.

pua-district.s: Pua is a district in the upper Nan valley of Nan Province in northern Thailand. The Nan chronicles place the first seat of the Nan kingdom there in the late 13th century, before the capital moved south and was established at the present city of Nan in the 14th century.

piluoge.s: Piluoge was king of Nanzhao from 728 to 748, ruler of Mengshe, the southernmost of the six principalities, or zhao, around Erhai Lake in Yunnan. With Tang support he subdued the other principalities and united the region by 738, when the Tang court named him Prince of Yunnan.

psylli.s: The Psylli were an ancient Libyan people living on the shores of the Gulf of Sirte in present-day Libya. Herodotus tells that they perished when they marched against the south wind, and that the Nasamones took over their lands.

pietermaritzburg.s: Pietermaritzburg is the capital of KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, founded by Voortrekkers in 1838 and named after the Boer leaders Piet Retief and Gerrit Maritz. It was the seat of the Natalia Republic and then of the British Colony of Natal and Natal Province.

pregolya.s: The Pregolya is a river in Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast, formed by the junction of the Instruch and the Angrapa and flowing about 123 km west to the Vistula Lagoon. Kaliningrad, formerly Königsberg, stands on its banks, and it was the main waterway of historic Prussia.

portara.s: The Portara is a massive marble doorway on the islet of Palatia at the harbour of Naxos town, Greece, the only standing part of an unfinished temple begun around 530 BCE under the tyrant Lygdamis. The temple, probably dedicated to Apollo, was abandoned after Lygdamis fell.

pretoria.s: Pretoria is the administrative capital of South Africa, in Gauteng province. Founded in 1855 by Marthinus Wessel Pretorius and named after his father Andries Pretorius, it became the capital of the South African Republic in 1860 and later of the Transvaal Colony.

parthenope-city.s: Parthenope was a Greek settlement founded by colonists from Cumae on the Bay of Naples, probably in the 7th century BCE, and named after a Siren whose tomb was shown there. When Neapolis, the 'new city', was founded nearby around 470 BCE, the older town became known as…

philocles-king-of-sidon.s: Philocles was king of Sidon in Phoenicia and a leading commander of Ptolemy I and Ptolemy II of Egypt in the early 3rd century BCE. As commander of the Ptolemaic fleet he supervised the League of the Islanders in the Cyclades, and inscriptions from Delos and other islands…

peter-claver.s: Peter Claver was a Spanish Jesuit priest who spent nearly forty years in Cartagena de Indias ministering to enslaved Africans arriving on slave ships. He met the ships, brought food and medicine, nursed the sick and baptised many thousands.

popayan.s: Popayán is a city in south-western Colombia, capital of the Cauca department, founded by Sebastián de Belalcázar in 1537. In the colonial era it was a wealthy seat of landowners and mine owners whose gold mines in the Pacific lowlands were worked by enslaved Africans, and it…

patroon.s: A patroon was a landholder in New Netherland granted a large estate, a patroonship, by the Dutch West India Company under its Charter of Freedoms and Exemptions of 1629, in return for settling fifty adults there within four years. Patroons held manorial rights over their…

phayao.s: Phayao is a town in northern Thailand on the shore of Kwan Phayao lake, capital of Phayao province. According to northern Thai chronicles it was founded in the 11th century, and it was the seat of an independent Tai principality whose ruler Ngam Mueang allied with Mangrai of…

pierre-pigneau-de-behaine.s: Pierre Pigneau de Behaine was a French Catholic missionary and titular bishop of Adran who supported Nguyen Anh in his war against the Tay Son. In 1787 he negotiated the Treaty of Versailles promising French military aid, and when the French government failed to honour it he…

pemba-mozambique.s: Pemba, called Porto Amélia under Portuguese rule, is a port city on Pemba Bay, one of the largest natural harbours of Africa, and the capital of Cabo Delgado province in northern Mozambique. It was founded in 1904 by the Niassa Company, which moved its headquarters there from…

pyatigorsk.s: Pyatigorsk is a spa town in Stavropol Krai, Russia, in the Caucasian Mineral Waters area at the foot of Mount Beshtau, whose five peaks give the town its name. Founded as a Russian fort and resort in the early 19th century, it is associated with the poet Mikhail Lermontov, who…

peterhof-novgorod.s: The Peterhof was the Hanseatic League's trading post, or Kontor, in Novgorod, named after its church of St Peter. Founded in the late 12th century by German merchants who took over from traders of Gotland, it was one of the League's four principal Kontore, exchanging Western…

pompeii.s: Pompeii was an ancient town in Campania, southern Italy, near the Bay of Naples, buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE. An Oscan town later dominated by Samnites, it became a Roman colony in 80 BCE.

panuco-river.s: The Pánuco River is a river of eastern Mexico that drains part of the central highlands and reaches the Gulf of Mexico at Tampico. Its lower valley was the land of the Huastec people and came under Spanish rule in the early 1520s.

pribislav-of-mecklenburg.s: Pribislav was the last prince of the Obotrites and the first Lord of Mecklenburg. The son of Niklot, who was killed fighting Henry the Lion in 1160, he accepted Christianity and Saxon overlordship in 1167 and received most of his father's lands back as a fief.

potsdam-declaration.s: The Potsdam Declaration was the statement issued on 26 July 1945 by the United States, Britain and China setting out the terms for Japan's surrender in the Second World War. It demanded the unconditional surrender of the armed forces, disarmament, occupation and the removal of…

panagyurishte-treasure.s: The Panagyurishte Treasure is a Thracian hoard of nine gold vessels found in 1949 near Panagyurishte in central Bulgaria. Weighing over 6 kilograms, it includes a phiale, an amphora-rhyton and several animal-headed rhyta decorated with scenes from Greek myth, and dates from…

polemon-i-of-pontus.s: Polemon I was a Roman client king of Pontus and later of the Bosporan Kingdom in the late 1st century BCE. The son of the orator Zeno of Laodicea, he was made king of part of Pontus by Mark Antony in 37 BCE, kept his throne under Augustus and married Queen Pythodorida.

pereshchepina-treasure.s: The Pereshchepina Treasure is a hoard of more than 800 gold and silver objects found in 1912 at Malaya Pereshchepina near Poltava in Ukraine. It contains Byzantine and Sasanian vessels, jewellery, weapons and rings, some bearing monograms read as the name of Kubrat.

pallava-script.s: The Pallava script is a Brahmic script that developed in southern India under the Pallava dynasty from around the 4th century CE. Carried across the Bay of Bengal by traders and priests, it was used for the earliest inscriptions of Southeast Asia, such as the yupa posts of…

pyramid-of-djoser.s: The Pyramid of Djoser, or Step Pyramid, is a six-stepped stone pyramid at Saqqara in Egypt, built for the Third Dynasty king Djoser in the 27th century BCE. Attributed to his official Imhotep, it began as a mastaba tomb and was enlarged in stages, and it is regarded as the…

pahang-river.s: The Pahang River is the longest river in Peninsular Malaysia, flowing about 460 km from the Titiwangsa Mountains east to the South China Sea near Pekan. Its valley has been the heartland of Pahang since early times, linking the gold and forest products of the interior to the…

pekan.s: Pekan is the royal town of the Malaysian state of Pahang, near the mouth of the Pahang River on the east coast of the Malay Peninsula. It was the seat of the first sultans of Pahang from around 1470 and later of the Bendahara rulers and the modern sultans, whose palace stands…

prince-kitashirakawa-yoshihisa.s: Prince Kitashirakawa Yoshihisa was a member of the Japanese imperial family who, as abbot of the Rinnōji temple at Ueno, fled Edo in 1868 and became nominal head of the Ōuetsu Reppan Dōmei, the northern alliance resisting the new imperial government. Pardoned after its defeat,…

passion-of-saints-perpetua-and-felicity.n: Passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicity
passion-of-saints-perpetua-and-felicity.s: The Passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicity is a Latin account of the martyrdom of a group of Christians in the amphitheatre at Carthage in 203. It includes a prison diary attributed to Vibia Perpetua, a young noblewoman, making it one of the earliest surviving texts written…

pratap-singha.s: Pratap Singha, or Susenghphaa, was king of the Ahom kingdom of Assam from 1603 to 1641. He created the offices of the Borbarua and the Borphukan, reorganised the paik labour system through his official Momai Tamuli Borbarua, and fought a long war with the Mughal Empire over…

purandar-singha.s: Purandar Singha was the last king of the Ahom kingdom of Assam. Installed by a court faction in 1818, he was driven out a year later by Burmese forces who restored Chandrakanta Singha.

purnananda-burhagohain.s: Purnananda Burhagohain was chief minister (Burhagohain) of the Ahom kingdom of Assam from 1784 to 1817 and its effective ruler for much of that time. He suppressed the last Moamoria resistance, restored much of the state after the rebellion and installed the kings Kamaleswar…

priarius.s: Priarius was king of the Alemannic Lentienses. In early 378, learning that much of the Western Roman army had been sent east, his people crossed the frozen Rhine into Alsace, but they were defeated by Gratian's generals Nannienus and Mallobaudes at Argentovaria.

peace-of-naupactus.s: The Peace of Naupactus, concluded in 217 BCE, ended the Social War between the Hellenic alliance led by Philip V of Macedon and the Aetolian League. The settlement left each side holding what it had, and Philip turned his attention west towards Italy and Rome.

persaeus.s: Persaeus of Citium was a Stoic philosopher, a pupil and housemate of Zeno of Citium. Sent by Zeno to the court of Antigonus II Gonatas at Pella, he became a royal adviser and was later placed in command of the Macedonian garrison of Acrocorinth, where he died, or according to…

phaenomena.s: The Phaenomena is a didactic poem by Aratus of Soli, written around 275 BCE at the court of Antigonus II Gonatas. In about 1,150 hexameter lines it describes the constellations, the movements of the heavens and weather signs, putting into verse the astronomy of Eudoxus of Cnidus.

panic-of-1890.s: The Panic of 1890, also called the Baring crisis, was a financial crisis set off when the London bank Baring Brothers, heavily exposed to Argentine bonds, came close to collapse. The Bank of England organised a rescue that prevented a wider panic in London.

pope-francis.s: Pope Francis, born Jorge Mario Bergoglio in Buenos Aires, was a Jesuit who served as Archbishop of Buenos Aires from 1998 and was elected pope on 13 March 2013. He was the first pope from the Americas and the first Jesuit pope, and his pontificate stressed care for the poor,…

pactos-de-mayo.s: The Pactos de Mayo were a set of agreements signed by Argentina and Chile on 28 May 1902. They submitted the two countries' border disputes to arbitration by the British crown, limited their naval armaments, and so ended a costly naval arms race that had threatened war in the…

peronism.s: Peronism, or Justicialism, is the Argentine political movement formed around Juan Perón in the 1940s, resting on organised labour, economic nationalism, state-led industry and social welfare. Banned after Perón's fall in 1955, it remained the country's largest political force,…

panathenaea.s: The Panathenaea was the chief festival of Athens, held each summer in honour of Athena Polias, with a grander version, the Great Panathenaia, every four years from 566 BCE. Its procession, carrying a new robe to the goddess on the Acropolis, is thought to be shown on the…

phidias.s: Phidias was an Athenian sculptor, regarded in antiquity as the greatest of the Greeks, who supervised the sculpture of the Parthenon under Pericles. His colossal gold and ivory statues of Athena Parthenos in the Parthenon and of Zeus at Olympia, one of the Seven Wonders of the…

piraeus.s: Piraeus is the port city of Athens, about ten kilometres south-west of the centre. Fortified on the initiative of Themistocles in the 490s and 480s BCE and laid out on a grid plan by Hippodamus, it was the base of the Athenian navy and the city's grain trade, and from about…

propylaea.s: The Propylaea is the monumental gateway to the Acropolis of Athens, built between 437 and 432 BCE to designs by the architect Mnesicles as part of the building programme of Pericles. Combining Doric and Ionic columns, it was left unfinished when the Peloponnesian War began,…

protogeometric-style.s: The Protogeometric style is the style of Greek pottery of about 1050–900 BCE, after the collapse of Mycenaean civilisation, decorated with concentric circles and semicircles drawn with compasses and multiple brushes. Athens, whose Kerameikos cemetery has yielded the finest…

phetracha.s: Phetracha was king of Ayutthaya from 1688 to 1703 and founder of the Ban Phlu Luang dynasty. Commander of the royal elephant corps under King Narai, he seized power as Narai lay dying in 1688, executed the minister Constantine Phaulkon and forced the French garrison to leave…

phra-khlang.s: The Phra Khlang was the Siamese minister of the treasury, whose department under the Ayutthaya and early Bangkok kings also managed royal trade, the ports and relations with foreign merchants and states. Holders of the office, such as Kosa Pan, were among the most powerful…

prasat-thong.s: Prasat Thong was king of Ayutthaya from 1629 to 1656 and founder of the Prasat Thong dynasty. A senior official, he seized the throne after a series of palace coups, drove out the Japanese community whose soldiers had supported his rivals, and built the temple of Wat…

pungnap-toseong.s: Pungnap Toseong is a large earthen-walled site on the south bank of the Han River in Songpa, south-eastern Seoul, built around the third century CE. Its walls, about 3.5 kilometres around, enclosed a royal centre, and many historians identify it as the northern fortress of…

paranda.s: Paranda is a town in Dharashiv (Osmanabad) district of Maharashtra, India, known for its large fort. The fort is traditionally attributed to Mahmud Gawan in the fifteenth century and was one of the strongholds of the Bahmani Sultanate.

philippe-de-rullecourt.s: Philippe de Rullecourt was a French adventurer and soldier who styled himself baron. On 6 January 1781, during the American War of Independence, he landed a small force in Jersey and took Saint Helier by surprise, forcing the lieutenant-governor to sign a surrender.

pierre-de-breze.s: Pierre de Brézé was a French nobleman, soldier and leading adviser of Charles VII, grand seneschal of Normandy. A supporter of Margaret of Anjou in the Wars of the Roses, he agreed with her in 1461 to help the Lancastrians in return for the Channel Islands, and his forces took…

pratapgad.s: Pratapgad is a hill fort in the Satara district of Maharashtra, western India, built in 1656 on the orders of Shivaji to guard the passes of the Western Ghats. Below its walls in November 1659 Shivaji killed the Bijapur general Afzal Khan, and his forces then defeated the…

ptoion.s: The Ptoion was a sanctuary of Apollo Ptoios on Mount Ptoon in Boeotia, near the city of Acraephia. It housed an oracle consulted from the archaic period onwards, and excavations there have recovered an exceptional series of marble kouroi dedicated in the sixth century BCE.

pagondas.s: Pagondas was a Theban commander and Boeotarch who led the Boeotian army to victory over Athens at the Battle of Delium in 424 BCE. He persuaded his reluctant fellow commanders to fight, drew up the Thebans 25 ranks deep and sent cavalry round a hill to surprise the Athenian…

phoebidas.s: Phoebidas was a Spartan commander who in 382 BCE, while leading troops north against Olynthus, seized the Cadmea, the citadel of Thebes, with the help of a pro-Spartan Theban faction. Sparta fined him but kept the garrison, an act widely condemned in Greece.

pharnaces-ii-of-pontus.s: Pharnaces II was a son of Mithridates VI of Pontus. In 63 BCE he led the revolt that drove his father to suicide and was rewarded by Pompey with the Bosporan Kingdom.

philo-of-byblos.s: Philo of Byblos was a Greek-language writer of the Roman period, born in Byblos. His Phoenician History, which he claimed to translate from the ancient Phoenician author Sanchuniathon, survives only in excerpts quoted by Eusebius of Caesarea.

pescennius-niger.s: Pescennius Niger was governor of Syria who was proclaimed emperor by his troops in 193 CE, in the civil war after the murder of Pertinax. Supported by the eastern provinces and by Byzantium, he was defeated by Septimius Severus at Cyzicus, Nicaea and finally Issus in 194 and…

philo-of-byzantium.s: Philo of Byzantium was a Greek engineer and writer on mechanics who worked in Alexandria and Rhodes. His Mechanical Collection, of which parts survive, covered levers, harbours, artillery, pneumatics and the attack and defence of fortified cities.

phocion.s: Phocion was an Athenian statesman and general, elected general forty-five times, known for his austere honesty. He helped relieve Byzantium against Philip II of Macedon in 340 BCE but generally urged accommodation with Macedon.

pliny-the-younger.s: Pliny the Younger was a Roman lawyer, senator and author, nephew and adopted son of Pliny the Elder. His published letters describe Roman public and private life, including the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 CE.

pyxis-of-al-mughira.s: The Pyxis of al-Mughira is a carved ivory box made in 968 at Madinat al-Zahra for al-Mughira, a younger son of the caliph Abd al-Rahman III. Its densely carved medallions show courtly scenes, musicians, hunters and animals, and an Arabic inscription records its date and owner.

pedanius-dioscorides.s: Pedanius Dioscorides was a Greek physician from Anazarbus in Cilicia who served with the Roman army. His De materia medica, describing some six hundred plants and their medicinal uses, was the standard pharmacological reference for more than fifteen centuries in Europe and the…

parti-quebecois.s: The Parti Québécois is a political party in Quebec that seeks sovereignty for the province, founded in 1968 by René Lévesque. It first won power in 1976, made French the official language of Quebec with the Charter of the French Language in 1977, and held referendums on…

pierre-trudeau.s: Pierre Trudeau was a Liberal prime minister of Canada from 1968 to 1979 and from 1980 to 1984. He made English and French official languages, invoked the War Measures Act in the October Crisis of 1970 and campaigned against Quebec sovereignty in the 1980 referendum.

prophezei.s: The Prophezei was a school of biblical study founded in Zürich in 1525 by Huldrych Zwingli in place of the old chapter school of the Grossmünster. Clergy and students met daily to read scripture in Hebrew, Greek and Latin and to expound it in German.

publius-canidius-crassus.s: Publius Canidius Crassus was a Roman general and partisan of Mark Antony, suffect consul in 40 BCE. In 36 BCE he campaigned in the Caucasus against the Iberians and Albanians, forcing them into alliance before Antony's Parthian expedition.

penalba-de-villastar.s: Peñalba de Villastar is a sandstone cliff near Villastar in the province of Teruel, Spain, bearing Celtiberian and Latin inscriptions carved around the first century BCE and first century CE. Among them are dedications to the Celtic god Lugus, also worshipped elsewhere in Europe.

pactyes.s: Pactyes was a Lydian whom Cyrus the Great put in charge of the treasury of Lydia after its conquest around 546 BCE. He rebelled against the Persians and besieged Sardis, then fled as a Persian army approached, seeking refuge in Cyme, Mytilene and finally Chios.

papua-new-guinea.s: Papua New Guinea is a country occupying the eastern half of the island of New Guinea and nearby islands in the south-western Pacific, with its capital at Port Moresby. Divided between British, later Australian, Papua and German New Guinea, it was administered by Australia from…

patrick-white.s: Patrick White was an Australian novelist and playwright, author of The Tree of Man, Voss and Riders in the Chariot. His novels explore the Australian landscape, isolation and spiritual search in a dense, demanding style.

paul-keating.s: Paul Keating was Treasurer of Australia from 1983 to 1991 and Labor prime minister from 1991 to 1996. As treasurer he oversaw the floating of the dollar, financial deregulation and tariff cuts, and in 1986 warned that Australia risked becoming a banana republic.

peace-of-cambrai.s: The Peace of Cambrai, called the Ladies' Peace, was signed on 3 August 1529 between Francis I of France and Emperor Charles V, negotiated by Louise of Savoy and Margaret of Austria. Francis gave up his claims in Italy and his suzerainty over Flanders and Artois and paid a…

philippa-of-hainaut.s: Philippa of Hainaut was queen of England as the wife of Edward III, whom she married in 1328. A daughter of William I, Count of Hainaut, she bore him many children, among them Edward the Black Prince and John of Gaunt.

province-of-hohenzollern.s: The Province of Hohenzollern, officially the Hohenzollern Lands, was a Prussian territory in southern Germany formed in 1850 from the principalities of Hohenzollern-Hechingen and Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen, whose princes had ceded them to King Frederick William IV. An exclave…

peire-vidal.s: Peire Vidal was a troubadour from Toulouse and one of the most admired Occitan poets of the late twelfth century. He travelled widely, serving patrons in Provence, Spain, Italy and Hungary, and was known for boastful, playful and inventive verse.

pierre-de-castelnau.s: Pierre de Castelnau was a Cistercian monk and papal legate sent by Pope Innocent III to combat Catharism in Languedoc. After excommunicating Raymond VI of Toulouse, he was murdered near Saint-Gilles in January 1208 by a man thought to be one of the count's retainers.

perekop.s: Perekop is a village on the narrow isthmus that joins the Crimean peninsula to the mainland, and the name of the isthmus itself. A fortress the Crimean Tatars called Or Qapı stood there behind an ancient ditch and rampart across the isthmus, guarding Crimea's only land approach.

pope-callixtus-iii.s: Callixtus III, born Alfons de Borja near Xàtiva in the Kingdom of Valencia, was pope from 1455 to 1458, the first of the Borgia popes. Formerly an adviser to Alfonso V of Aragon, he devoted his papacy to a crusade against the Ottomans after the fall of Constantinople and…

palma-cathedral.s: Palma Cathedral is the Gothic cathedral of Palma on Majorca, begun after James I of Aragon conquered the island in 1229 and built mainly between about 1300 and 1601 on the site of the city's main mosque. Rising above the sea wall, it has one of the tallest Gothic naves in…

petka.s: The Pětka, Czech for 'the Five', was the informal committee of the leaders of the five main Czech parties in the Czechoslovak First Republic from 1920: the Agrarians, Social Democrats, National Socialists, People's Party and National Democrats. Meeting outside parliament, it…

prague-spring.s: The Prague Spring was the period of reform in Czechoslovakia that began when Alexander Dubček became party leader in January 1968. Censorship was relaxed and the party's Action Programme promised wider freedoms and economic reform, socialism with a human face.

peter-tordenskjold.s: Peter Tordenskjold, born Peter Wessel in Trondheim, was a Norwegian-born naval officer in the service of Denmark-Norway during the Great Northern War. Ennobled in 1716, he won fame through bold actions such as the destruction of a Swedish transport fleet at Dynekilen in 1716…

p-v-glob.s: P. V. Glob was a Danish archaeologist, professor at Aarhus and from 1960 to 1981 national antiquary of Denmark. With Geoffrey Bibby he led the Danish expeditions to Bahrain from 1953, which identified the island as the centre of Dilmun.

parlement-of-paris.s: The Parlement of Paris was the highest court of justice of the Kingdom of France, developed from the king's court in the thirteenth century and housed in the royal palace on the Île de la Cité. Its jurisdiction covered much of northern and central France, and it heard appeals…

principality-of-aquitaine.s: The Principality of Aquitaine was the territory in south-western France that Edward III of England granted to his son Edward the Black Prince in 1362, after the Treaty of Brétigny had freed the English lands there from French overlordship. Governed from Bordeaux and Angoulême,…

palatinate-region.s: The Palatinate (Pfalz) is a historical region of south-western Germany on the middle Rhine. It took its name from the counts palatine of the Rhine, Wittelsbach princes from 1214, whose lands around Heidelberg, Mannheim and the left bank of the Rhine were called the Rhenish or…

philip-of-saint-pol.s: Philip of Saint-Pol was duke of Brabant and Limburg from 1427 until his death in 1430, the younger son of Duke Antoine. Count of Saint-Pol and Ligny before succeeding his brother John IV, he was made regent of Brabant by the estates in 1420 during their quarrel with John.

pieter-bruegel-the-elder.s: Pieter Bruegel the Elder was the leading Netherlandish painter of the sixteenth century, active in Antwerp and from 1563 in Brussels, where he died in 1569. He is famous for landscapes and scenes of peasant life such as The Hunters in the Snow and The Peasant Wedding, as well…

peter-i-duke-of-brittany.s: Peter Mauclerc was a French prince of the House of Dreux who ruled Brittany from 1213 to 1237 through his marriage to the heiress Alix of Thouars. He strengthened ducal power against the Breton barons and bishops, which earned him his nickname, and joined baronial revolts…

pierre-le-baud.s: Pierre Le Baud was a Breton priest and historian in the service of the dukes of Brittany and of Anne of Brittany. His chronicles of the kings, dukes and princes of Brittany, written in the late fifteenth century, gathered sources from Breton archives and presented Brittany as…

pinot-noir.s: Pinot noir is a red wine grape associated above all with Burgundy, where it has been grown since at least the fourteenth century. Duke Philip the Bold's ordinance of 1395 favoured it over Gamay, and it is the grape of the great red wines of the Côte d'Or.

portuguese-house-of-burgundy.s: The Portuguese House of Burgundy was the first royal dynasty of Portugal, ruling from 1139 to 1383. It descended from Henry of Burgundy, a grandson of Duke Robert I of Burgundy, who became count of Portugal, and his son Afonso Henriques, the first king.

place-stanislas.s: Place Stanislas is a large square in Nancy, laid out in 1752–1755 as the Place Royale by the architect Emmanuel Héré for Stanisław Leszczyński, duke of Lorraine, with a statue of Louis XV at its centre. It is framed by the town hall and other pavilions and by gilded iron gates…

protestantism.s: Protestantism is the branch of Christianity that arose from the Reformation of the sixteenth century, when Martin Luther, Huldrych Zwingli, John Calvin and others broke with the Roman Catholic Church. Its main traditions, Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican, rejected papal…

pietro-verri.s: Pietro Verri was a Milanese economist, historian and writer and a leader of the Italian Enlightenment. With his brother Alessandro he formed the Accademia dei Pugni and its journal Il Caffè (1764–1766), and he encouraged Cesare Beccaria's work on penal reform.

pays-d-auge.s: The Pays d'Auge is a region of Normandy in north-western France, lying between the valleys of the Touques and the Dives inland from the Channel coast, with Lisieux as its main town. Its green hills and pastures are famous for dairy farming and cider orchards, producing…

picquigny.s: Picquigny is a small town on the Somme in Picardy, northern France. In 942 William Longsword, ruler of Normandy, was murdered there by men of Arnulf I of Flanders during a meeting on an island in the river.

pope-clement-xiii.s: Clement XIII, born Carlo Rezzonico in Venice, was pope from 1758 to 1769. His pontificate was dominated by the defence of the Jesuits against the Catholic monarchies, which expelled them from Portugal, France, Spain, Naples and Parma.

palazzo-farnese.s: The Palazzo Farnese is a Renaissance palace in Rome, begun around 1514 for Cardinal Alessandro Farnese, later Pope Paul III, by Antonio da Sangallo the Younger and completed by Michelangelo and Giacomo della Porta. Its gallery was decorated with frescoes by Annibale Carracci.

parmigianino.s: Parmigianino, born Girolamo Francesco Maria Mazzola in Parma, was a painter and printmaker of the Mannerist style. After working in Rome and Bologna he returned to Parma, where he painted frescoes in the church of Santa Maria della Steccata.

philip-ii-duke-of-pomerania.s: Philip II was duke of Pomerania-Stettin from 1606 to 1618, of the Griffin dynasty. A learned collector and patron of the arts, he commissioned the Pomeranian Art Cabinet through the Augsburg agent Philipp Hainhofer and the great map of Pomerania by Eilhard Lubinus.

pyrzyce.s: Pyrzyce, German Pyritz, is a town in the West Pomeranian Voivodeship of north-western Poland, south-east of Szczecin. In 1124 Bishop Otto of Bamberg baptised several thousand Pomeranians there, beginning the region's conversion to Christianity.

palazzo-madama-turin.s: Palazzo Madama is a palace on Piazza Castello in Turin that grew from a Roman gate and a medieval castle of the Savoy-Achaea branch of the dynasty. It takes its name from two royal widows, Christine of France and Marie Jeanne Baptiste of Savoy-Nemours, who lived there as…

piedmontese-easter.s: The Piedmontese Easter was the massacre of Waldensian Protestants in the valleys west of Turin by troops of the Duchy of Savoy in April 1655. Sent to enforce restrictions on where the Waldensians could live, the soldiers killed many hundreds of villagers.

palazzina-di-caccia-of-stupinigi.s: The Palazzina di caccia of Stupinigi is a royal hunting lodge south-west of Turin, designed by Filippo Juvarra for King Victor Amadeus II and begun in 1729. Its star-shaped plan centres on an oval hall under a dome crowned by a bronze stag.

padri-war.s: The Padri War was a conflict in West Sumatra from 1803 to 1837. It began as a struggle between the Padri, Islamic reformers influenced by Wahhabism, and the Minangkabau nobility who upheld customary law; from 1821 the Dutch intervened on the side of the nobles.

piet-heyn.s: Piet Heyn was a Dutch naval officer and privateer in the service of the Dutch West India Company. In 1628 he trapped the Spanish treasure fleet in the Bay of Matanzas in Cuba and captured its silver; the booty financed the company's conquests in Brazil and paid its…

pepi-i.s: Pepi I Meryre was a pharaoh of the Sixth Dynasty of Egypt whose long reign was one of the most active of the Old Kingdom. He built widely across Egypt, sent military expeditions into the southern Levant under the official Weni and kept up trade with Byblos, where stone vessels…

palatinate-neuburg.s: Palatinate-Neuburg was a Wittelsbach principality of the Holy Roman Empire, created in 1505 after the Landshut War of Succession and centred on Neuburg an der Donau. Its ruler Wolfgang William became a Catholic in 1613 and gained Jülich and Berg in 1614, and in 1685 Philip…

pennsylvania-dutch.s: The Pennsylvania Dutch are descendants of German-speaking immigrants who settled in Pennsylvania in the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, many from the Palatinate, other south-western German lands and Switzerland; "Dutch" derives from "Deutsch". They include Lutheran…

pfalzgrafenstein-castle.s: Pfalzgrafenstein Castle is a toll castle on a small island in the Rhine near Kaub, Germany. Louis IV the Bavarian built its tower in 1326–1327 to collect river tolls, and a surrounding curtain wall was added soon after.

peace-of-passau.s: The Peace of Passau was an agreement of August 1552 between King Ferdinand I, acting for Emperor Charles V, and the Protestant princes led by Maurice of Saxony, who had risen against the emperor in the Princes' Revolt. It released the captive Landgrave Philip of Hesse and…

peace-of-prague-1635.s: The Peace of Prague was concluded on 30 May 1635 between Emperor Ferdinand II and Elector John George I of Saxony during the Thirty Years' War, and most Protestant princes of the Empire soon joined it. Saxony gained Upper and Lower Lusatia, the Edict of Restitution was…

peace-of-prague-1866.s: The Peace of Prague, signed on 23 August 1866, ended the Austro-Prussian War. Austria accepted the dissolution of the German Confederation and its own exclusion from German affairs, leaving Prussia free to annex Hanover, Hesse-Kassel, Nassau, Frankfurt and Schleswig-Holstein…

pirna.s: Pirna is a town on the Elbe in Saxony, Germany, upstream of Dresden at the entrance to Saxon Switzerland. In 1756, at the start of the Seven Years' War, the Saxon army was trapped in a fortified camp between Pirna and the fortress of Königstein and capitulated to Frederick the…

paul-alvarus.s: Paul Alvarus was a Christian scholar and poet of ninth-century Córdoba, a friend of Eulogius, whose biography he wrote. A defender of the Martyrs of Córdoba, he wrote the Indiculus luminosus (854), in which he lamented that young Christians preferred Arabic poetry and learning…

peter-of-castile.s: Peter of Castile, called the Cruel, was King of Castile and León from 1350 to 1369. His reign was marked by conflict with the nobility and a civil war against his half-brother Henry of Trastámara, backed by France, while Peter was aided by Edward the Black Prince, who won the…

perateia.s: The Perateia (lands beyond the sea) was the Byzantine name for the Crimean dependencies of the Empire of Trebizond, including Cherson and the Gothic lands of the southern coast. They paid tribute to Trebizond in the early thirteenth century but were soon lost to Seljuk, Mongol…

parrhasius.s: Parrhasius of Ephesus was one of the most celebrated Greek painters, active in Athens in the late fifth century BCE. Ancient writers praised his precise outlines and expressive faces; Pliny tells how he defeated his rival Zeuxis by painting a curtain so lifelike that Zeuxis…

pomorie.s: Anchialus, now Pomorie, is a town on the Black Sea coast of Bulgaria, founded in antiquity as a Greek colony of Apollonia. In the Middle Ages it was a Byzantine fortress on the frontier with Bulgaria and changed hands repeatedly.

peace-of-habenhausen.s: The Peace of Habenhausen was signed in November 1666 at Habenhausen, near Bremen, ending the second war between Sweden and the city of Bremen. Sweden, which ruled the surrounding duchies of Bremen-Verden, gave up its attempt to take the city.

philippeville-massacre.s: The Philippeville massacre took place on 20 August 1955 in and around Philippeville, now Skikda, in north-eastern Algeria. FLN fighters and armed villagers attacked Europeans and pro-French Muslims, killing over a hundred, including women and children at the mining village of…

phan-boi-chau.s: Phan Bội Châu was a Vietnamese nationalist and scholar who sought to free Vietnam from French rule. He founded the Modernisation Society in 1904 and the Đông Du movement, which sent young Vietnamese to study in Japan, and later formed a revolutionary league in China.

phan-chau-trinh.s: Phan Châu Trinh was a Vietnamese reformer who argued that Vietnam should modernise through education, commerce and legal reform within French rule rather than through armed revolt. He helped found the Đông Kinh Free School in Hanoi in 1907 and was imprisoned on Côn Sơn island…

pierre-boisson.s: Pierre Boisson was a French colonial administrator who, as governor-general of French West Africa from 1940, kept the federation loyal to the Vichy regime and repelled the British and Free French attack on Dakar in September 1940. After the Allied landings in North Africa in…

punctation-of-olmutz.s: The Punctation of Olmütz was an agreement signed on 29 November 1850 at Olmütz in Moravia between Prussia and Austria, with Russian backing for Austria. Prussia abandoned its plan for an Erfurt Union of German states under its leadership and accepted the restoration of the…

palais-thurn-und-taxis-frankfurt.s: The Palais Thurn und Taxis is a Baroque palace in Frankfurt am Main built in 1731–1739 for the princes of Thurn und Taxis, hereditary postmasters of the Holy Roman Empire. From 1816 to 1866 it was the seat of the Federal Assembly of the German Confederation, and in 1848–1849…

palgwanhoe.s: The Palgwanhoe was a state festival of the Korean kingdoms of Silla and Goryeo, named after the Buddhist eight precepts but combining Buddhist ritual with the worship of native spirits of heaven, mountains and rivers. In Goryeo it was held each winter in Kaegyong and…

princess-alice-of-the-united-kingdom.n: Princess Alice of the United Kingdom
princess-alice-of-the-united-kingdom.s: Princess Alice was the third child of Queen Victoria and Prince Albert. In 1862 she married Louis of Hesse, who became Grand Duke Louis IV in 1877, and in Darmstadt she promoted nursing and women's welfare.

prince-louis-of-battenberg.s: Prince Louis of Battenberg was a German-born British admiral of the Hessian Battenberg family. He joined the Royal Navy in 1868 and became First Sea Lord in 1912, but resigned in 1914 because of anti-German feeling.

peter-behrens.s: Peter Behrens was a German architect and designer. A member of the Darmstadt Artists' Colony, where he built his own house in 1901, he later became artistic adviser to the electrical firm AEG, designing its Turbine Factory in Berlin of 1909 as well as products and graphics.

perkunas.s: Perkūnas was the thunder god of the pagan Lithuanians and the most important deity of the Baltic religion, corresponding to the Latvian Pērkons. Associated with oak trees, rain and fertility, he was worshipped until Lithuania's conversion to Christianity from 1387.

podlachia.s: Podlasie is a historical region in north-eastern Poland, centred on Białystok and bordering Belarus. It formed part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania until the Union of Lublin in 1569 transferred it to the Crown of Poland.

polonisation.s: Polonisation is the adoption of the Polish language, culture and often Catholic religion by non-Polish groups. In the Grand Duchy of Lithuania it affected above all the Lithuanian and Ruthenian nobility after the unions with Poland, and in 1696 Polish replaced Ruthenian as the…

pripet-marshes.s: The Pripet Marshes are a vast area of forests, wetlands and rivers along the Pripyat River in southern Belarus and northern Ukraine, among the largest wetlands in Europe. Long a barrier to armies and a refuge for their inhabitants, they formed part of the Grand Duchy of…

province-of-luxembourg.s: The Province of Luxembourg is the largest and least populous province of Belgium, in the south-east of the country, with Arlon as its capital. It was created by the Treaty of London of 1839, which gave the French-speaking western part of the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg to Belgium.

princess-charlotte-of-wales.s: Princess Charlotte of Wales was the only child of the future George IV of the United Kingdom and second in line to the British throne. In 1816 she married Prince Leopold of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld, but she died in childbirth the following year, causing a succession crisis that…

pierre-werner.s: Pierre Werner was a Luxembourg Christian Social politician who served as prime minister from 1959 to 1974 and again from 1979 to 1984. In 1970 he chaired the group that produced the Werner Report, the first plan for economic and monetary union in the European Communities,…

peter-of-moscow.s: Peter of Moscow was Metropolitan of Kiev and All Rus' from 1308 until his death in 1326. Originally from Galicia-Volhynia, he clashed with the princes of Tver and spent increasing time in Moscow, where he settled around 1325 and began the first stone Dormition Cathedral in the…

philotheus-of-pskov.s: Philotheus of Pskov was a monk of the Eleazarov Monastery near Pskov, known for letters written in the early sixteenth century to Grand Prince Vasily III and to the official Misyur Munekhin. In them he set out the idea of Moscow as the 'Third Rome': since Rome had fallen into…

portoferraio.s: Portoferraio is the main town and port of the island of Elba, off the coast of Tuscany. Cosimo I de' Medici founded it in 1548 as a fortified port named Cosmopoli, with bastions designed to guard the Tuscan coast against pirates and the Ottomans.

pitti-palace.s: The Pitti Palace is a Renaissance palace in Florence south of the Arno, begun in the 1450s for the banker Luca Pitti and bought in 1550 by Eleonora of Toledo, wife of Cosimo I de' Medici. Enlarged over the following centuries, it became the main residence of the grand dukes of…

peace-of-zsitvatorok.s: The Peace of Zsitvatorok was signed on 11 November 1606 at the mouth of the Zsitva River in Hungary, ending the Long Turkish War between the Habsburg Monarchy and the Ottoman Empire. It confirmed the existing frontier, replaced the Habsburgs' annual tribute with a single…

pedro-calderon-de-la-barca.s: Pedro Calderón de la Barca was a Spanish dramatist and poet, the leading playwright of the later Golden Age. His plays include Life Is a Dream, a philosophical drama on free will and illusion, and The Mayor of Zalamea, as well as many sacramental plays performed for the feast…

paul-beneke.s: Paul Beneke was a Danzig sea captain and privateer during the Anglo-Hanseatic War of 1469–1474. In 1473, commanding the Peter von Danzig, he captured the galley San Matteo, which carried Hans Memling's Last Judgment, and the triptych was taken to Danzig.

pope-siricius.s: Siricius was bishop of Rome from 384 to 399. His letter of 385 to Bishop Himerius of Tarraco, answering questions on baptism, penance and clerical discipline, is the oldest surviving papal decretal, a ruling with the force of law.

peoples-consultative-assembly.s: The People's Consultative Assembly (MPR) is the highest legislative body of Indonesia. Under the 1945 constitution it was the supreme organ of state that elected the president and vice-president and set broad state policy, a role Suharto used to secure re-election unopposed…

permesta.s: Permesta was a regional rebellion in eastern Indonesia, named after the Universal Struggle Charter proclaimed by army officers in Makassar in March 1957. Based mainly in North Sulawesi, its leaders demanded greater regional autonomy and a fairer share of export revenue, and in…

pertamina.s: Pertamina is the Indonesian state oil and gas company, formed in 1968 from the merger of earlier state oil firms. Under its director Ibnu Sutowo it grew into a vast conglomerate that financed many of the New Order's projects, but in 1975 it was unable to repay debts of about…

prabowo-subianto.s: Prabowo Subianto is an Indonesian politician and former general who became president in October 2024. A commander of special forces and of the army strategic reserve, and a son-in-law of Suharto, he was discharged in 1998 over the abduction of pro-democracy activists.

prri-rebellion.s: The PRRI rebellion was a regional revolt against the central government of Indonesia, launched when dissident army officers and politicians proclaimed the Revolutionary Government of the Republic of Indonesia in West Sumatra in February 1958. Opposed to the growing power of…

payerne.s: Payerne is a town in the canton of Vaud in western Switzerland, known for its large Romanesque abbey church. The priory was founded in the tenth century by Queen Bertha of Burgundy, widow of Rudolf II, and her daughter the empress Adelaide, and was given to Cluny.

pennine-alps.s: The Pennine Alps are a range of the western Alps along the border between Switzerland and Italy, between the Great St Bernard Pass and the Simplon Pass. They include many of the highest peaks of the Alps, among them Monte Rosa and the Matterhorn.

pravia.s: Pravia is a town in western Asturias, near the mouth of the Nalón. It was the seat of the Asturian kings under Silo (774–783) and his successors, before Alfonso II made Oviedo the permanent capital.

paul-johann-anselm-von-feuerbach.s: Paul Johann Anselm von Feuerbach was a German jurist and a founder of modern criminal law. He drafted the Bavarian Criminal Code of 1813, which put into law his principle that there can be no crime or punishment without a prior law (nullum crimen, nulla poena sine lege) and…

paul-henri-spaak.s: Paul-Henri Spaak was a Belgian Socialist statesman, several times prime minister and foreign minister. He presided over the first General Assembly of the United Nations in 1946, chaired the committee whose Spaak Report of 1956 led to the Treaty of Rome, and served as Secretary…

plzen.s: Plzeň is a city in western Bohemia, Czech Republic, founded by King Wenceslaus II in 1295. It became an industrial centre in the nineteenth century, home to the Škoda Works and to the brewery founded in 1842 that created Pilsner lager.

prokop-the-great.s: Prokop the Great was a Hussite priest and military leader, the chief commander of the Taborites after Jan Žižka's death. He defeated crusading armies at Ústí nad Labem in 1426 and Domažlice in 1431 and led raids into Germany, Hungary and Silesia.

prague-slav-congress.s: The Prague Slav Congress met in June 1848, during the revolutions in the Austrian Empire, bringing together delegates of the Slav peoples of the monarchy and some from outside it. Presided over by František Palacký, it supported Austro-Slavism, a reformed federal Austria…

principia-mathematica-newton.s: Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica, usually called the Principia, is Isaac Newton's treatise on mechanics, published in Latin in London in 1687 with the support of Edmond Halley and the Royal Society. It set out the three laws of motion and the law of universal…

pierre-corneille.s: Pierre Corneille was a French dramatist, one of the three great playwrights of seventeenth-century France with Molière and Racine. His tragedy Le Cid of 1637 was a great success and set off a debate on the rules of drama in which the Académie française took part.

peace-of-vervins.s: The Peace of Vervins was signed on 2 May 1598 between Henry IV of France and Philip II of Spain, ending the war Spain had waged in support of the Catholic League. Spain returned Calais and other towns it had taken in northern France, restoring the frontiers of 1559.

poets-of-the-princes.s: The Poets of the Princes, in Welsh Gogynfeirdd, were the court poets of the native Welsh rulers from about 1100 to the Edwardian conquest of 1282 and shortly after. Writing in an elaborate, archaic style, they composed praise poems and elegies for princes such as Owain Gwynedd…

penmachno.s: Penmachno is a village in the Machno valley in Conwy county, north Wales. Early Christian gravestones found there include a sixth-century stone commemorating a man described as a citizen of Venedotis, one of the earliest written forms of the name Gwynedd, and another carved…

penmon-priory.s: Penmon Priory is a religious site at the eastern tip of Anglesey, traditionally founded in the sixth century by Saint Seiriol. It was one of the important early churches of Gwynedd, and in the thirteenth century it was reorganised as a house of Augustinian canons under the…

pannonhalma-archabbey.s: Pannonhalma Archabbey is a Benedictine monastery on a hill in western Hungary, founded in 996 under Grand Prince Géza and richly endowed by Stephen I. One of the oldest institutions in Hungary, it preserves the founding charter of the abbey of Tihany of 1055, which contains…

peter-orseolo.s: Peter Orseolo was king of Hungary from 1038 to 1041 and again from 1044 to 1046. The son of a Venetian doge and a sister of Stephen I, he was named Stephen's heir but was soon deposed in favour of Samuel Aba.

pharasmanes-ii-of-iberia.s: Pharasmanes II was a king of Iberia in eastern Georgia in the second century CE. According to Cassius Dio he was suspected of encouraging the Alan invasion of Armenia, Media and Cappadocia in the 130s, yet he later visited Rome with his family, probably under Antoninus Pius,…

pharnavazid-dynasty.s: The Pharnavazid dynasty was the first royal house of Iberia (Kartli) in eastern Georgia according to Georgian tradition, named after its founder Pharnavaz I, who is credited with uniting the kingdom around 300 BCE. Its kings ruled, with interruptions, into the early centuries…

peace-of-amasya.s: The Peace of Amasya was the treaty concluded on 29 May 1555 between Suleiman the Magnificent and Shah Tahmasp I, ending the Ottoman–Safavid war of 1532–1555. It divided the disputed lands between the two empires: Baghdad and most of Iraq went to the Ottomans, while western…

privy-council-of-ireland.s: The Privy Council of Ireland was the body of senior officials and nobles that advised the lord deputy or lord lieutenant in governing Ireland. Under Poynings' Law it shared with the English council control over which bills could be put before the Irish Parliament.

poynings-law.s: Poynings' Law was an act passed in 1494 by a parliament at Drogheda under Sir Edward Poynings, lord deputy for Henry VII. It provided that the Irish Parliament could meet only with royal licence and that its bills had to be approved in advance by the king and his council in…

parliament-of-great-britain.s: The Parliament of Great Britain was the legislature of the Kingdom of Great Britain, formed in 1707 by the union of the parliaments of England and Scotland and meeting at Westminster. By the Declaratory Act of 1720 it claimed the right to legislate for Ireland, a claim given…

pekah.s: Pekah was king of Israel from about 740 to 732 BCE, an army officer who seized the throne by killing Pekahiah. Allied with Rezin of Damascus, he tried to force Judah into an anti-Assyrian coalition, but Tiglath-pileser III invaded, annexed Galilee and Gilead and deported part…

pekahiah.s: Pekahiah was king of Israel for about two years around 742–740 BCE, succeeding his father Menahem. According to the Books of Kings he was assassinated in his palace at Samaria by his officer Pekah, who took the throne and then turned against Assyria in alliance with Damascus.

pact-of-steel.s: The Pact of Steel was a military and political alliance between Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany, signed in Berlin on 22 May 1939 by the foreign ministers Galeazzo Ciano and Joachim von Ribbentrop. It bound each country to support the other with all its forces in any war.

piave.s: The Piave is a river of north-eastern Italy that flows from the Carnic Alps through the Veneto to the Adriatic Sea north-east of Venice. After the defeat at Caporetto in late 1917 the Italian army made a stand on its banks, and in June 1918 it repulsed a major Austro-Hungarian…

pietro-badoglio.s: Pietro Badoglio was an Italian marshal and politician. He commanded the final phase of the conquest of Ethiopia in 1936, using chemical weapons, and was chief of the general staff until 1940.

pactum-warmundi.s: The Pactum Warmundi was a treaty of alliance concluded in 1123 between the Kingdom of Jerusalem and the Republic of Venice, named after Warmund, Patriarch of Jerusalem, who negotiated it while King Baldwin II was a captive. In return for naval help in the conquest of Tyre,…

pavapuri.s: Pavapuri is a village in the Nalanda district of Bihar, India, revered by Jains as the place where Mahavira, the 24th tirthankara, attained final liberation in the 6th or 5th century BCE. Its marble temple in the middle of a lotus pond, the Jal Mandir, marks the spot where he…

peterborough.s: Peterborough is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire, England, on the River Nene. It grew around the abbey of Medeshamstede, founded in the mid-7th century under Mercian royal patronage, destroyed by the Danes around 870 and refounded in the 10th century as Peterborough Abbey.

plegmund.s: Plegmund was Archbishop of Canterbury from 890 to 923, a Mercian scholar recruited by Alfred the Great to help revive learning in England. Alfred names him among those who helped him translate Pope Gregory the Great's Pastoral Care into English.

pybba-of-mercia.s: Pybba was an early king of the Mercians around 600, known only from later royal genealogies. These make him the son of Creoda and the father of Penda and Eowa, and trace the line back to the legendary Icel.

pope-clement-iv.s: Pope Clement IV (c. 1190–1268), born Guy Foulquois, was a French lawyer and adviser to Louis IX who became pope in 1265. Determined to remove the Hohenstaufen from southern Italy, he invested Charles of Anjou with the Kingdom of Sicily, leading to the defeat of Manfred in 1266…

pedro-alvarez-de-toledo-marquis-of-villa.n: Pedro Álvarez de Toledo, Marquis of Villafranca
pedro-alvarez-de-toledo-marquis-of-villa.s: Pedro Álvarez de Toledo, Marquis of Villafranca (1484–1553), was the Spanish viceroy of Naples from 1532 to 1553. He strengthened royal justice against the barons, fortified the coasts against Ottoman and Barbary raids and remodelled the capital, laying out the Via Toledo and…

pietro-giannone.s: Pietro Giannone (1676–1748) was a Neapolitan jurist and historian. His Civil History of the Kingdom of Naples (1723) traced the growth of church power in the kingdom and attacked the temporal claims of the papacy.

philip-iii-of-navarre.s: Philip III (1306–1343), count of Évreux, was king of Navarre from 1328 jointly with his wife Joan II, daughter of Louis X of France. Their accession restored a separate Navarrese monarchy after decades of union with France.

privilege-of-the-union.s: The Privilege of the Union was a charter issued by Charles III the Noble of Navarre on 8 September 1423 that united the three rival boroughs of Pamplona, the Navarrería, San Cernin and San Nicolás, into a single city. After centuries of conflict between them, it gave Pamplona…

puente-la-reina.s: Puente la Reina is a town in Navarre on the river Arga, where the main pilgrim routes to Santiago de Compostela from Roncesvalles and from Somport join. It takes its name from the six-arched Romanesque bridge built for pilgrims in the eleventh century, traditionally at the…

pope-adrian-iv.s: Pope Adrian IV (c. 1100–1159), born Nicholas Breakspear, was the only English pope, reigning from 1154 to 1159. As papal legate to Scandinavia in 1152–1154 he founded the archbishopric of Nidaros (Trondheim), giving Norway its own church province, and reorganised the Swedish…

phrygia.s: Phrygia was a region of west-central Anatolia, named after the Phrygians, who formed a kingdom there in the early first millennium BCE with its capital at Gordion and kings such as Midas. After the Cimmerian invasions it came under Lydian, Persian, Hellenistic and then Roman…

partitions-of-poland.s: The Partitions of Poland were three divisions of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth by Russia, Prussia and Austria in 1772, 1793 and 1795. The first took about a third of its territory; the second and third followed attempts at reform and the Kościuszko Uprising, and ended the…

prussian-war-academy.s: The Prussian War Academy (Kriegsakademie) in Berlin was founded in 1810 by Gerhard von Scharnhorst to train officers for the general staff. Carl von Clausewitz was its director from 1818 to 1830, and under Moltke the Elder its graduates formed the general staff that won the…

plombieres-agreement.s: The Plombières Agreement was a secret understanding reached on 21 July 1858 by Napoleon III and Cavour at the spa town of Plombières-les-Bains in France. France promised to help the Kingdom of Sardinia in a war against Austria provoked by Austria, in return for Savoy and Nice,…

pope-john-xxii.s: Pope John XXII, born Jacques Duèze in Cahors, was pope from 1316 to 1334, the second of the Avignon popes. He centralised papal finances and administration, fought a long conflict with the emperor Louis IV and condemned the Franciscan doctrine of absolute poverty.

parliament-of-scotland.s: The Parliament of Scotland was the national legislature of the Kingdom of Scotland from the thirteenth century until 1707. It met as a single chamber of three estates, clergy, nobility and burgh commissioners, much of whose business was prepared by the Lords of the Articles.

palermo-cathedral.s: Palermo Cathedral is the cathedral of the Sicilian capital, rebuilt from 1185 by Archbishop Walter Ophamil on the site of an earlier church that had served as a mosque under Muslim rule. Roger II was crowned in the earlier building on Christmas Day 1130, and the present…

peace-of-caltabellotta.s: The Peace of Caltabellotta, signed on 31 August 1302 at Caltabellotta in Sicily, ended the War of the Sicilian Vespers between the Angevins of Naples and the Aragonese. Frederick III kept the island for his lifetime with the title King of Trinacria, while the Angevin Charles…

pope-zachary.s: Pope Zachary was a Greek-speaking pope from Calabria who held office from 741 to 752. He negotiated with the Lombard kings to protect Rome and supported the church reforms of Boniface in Francia.

philips.s: Philips is a Dutch multinational company founded in Eindhoven in 1891 by Gerard Philips and his father Frederik to make incandescent light bulbs. It grew into one of the world's largest electronics firms, making radios, televisions, audio cassettes and compact discs, and…

piet-mondrian.s: Piet Mondrian was a Dutch painter and a pioneer of abstract art. With Theo van Doesburg he founded the De Stijl movement in 1917, and he developed Neo-Plasticism, painting grids of black lines with blocks of primary colours on white.

pim-fortuyn.s: Pim Fortuyn was a Dutch sociologist and politician whose criticism of immigration, Islam and the political establishment made him a leading figure in the election campaign of 2002. He was shot dead by an animal-rights activist on 6 May 2002, nine days before the election, in…

pastoral-care.s: Pastoral Care (Regula Pastoralis) is a treatise written by Pope Gregory the Great around 590 on the duties and conduct of bishops and clergy. Widely read in the Middle Ages, it was translated into Old English in the circle of Alfred the Great, with a preface in the king's name…

penrith.s: Penrith is a market town in Cumbria, north-west England, near the confluence of the rivers Eamont and Lowther. In the tenth century the area lay on the frontier of English, Scottish and Cumbrian power, and the northern rulers submitted to King Æthelstan at nearby Eamont Bridge…

punisa-racic.s: Puniša Račić was a Montenegrin Serb politician of the People's Radical Party. On 20 June 1928 he opened fire in the Yugoslav parliament, killing two Croatian Peasant Party deputies and mortally wounding its leader Stjepan Radić.
