pagan-min.s: Pagan Min was king of Burma from 1846 to 1853, the son of Tharrawaddy. His reign was marked by the execution of rivals and arbitrary rule, and a dispute over the treatment of British ship captains at Rangoon led to the Second Anglo-Burmese War in 1852, in which Britain annexed…

pharro.s: Pharro was a deity of the Kushan Empire personifying royal glory and fortune, the Bactrian form of the Iranian concept of khvarenah, or farr. He appears on the coins of Kanishka and Huvishka, usually holding fire or a purse, as the divine splendour that legitimated a king's rule.

psamtik-ii.s: Psamtik II was a pharaoh of the 26th Dynasty of Egypt, ruling from Sais. In 593 BCE he sent an army, including Greek and Carian mercenaries who left graffiti at Abu Simbel, deep into Nubia against the kingdom of Kush.

phra-mueang-kaeo.s: Phra Mueang Kaeo was a king of Lan Na from 1495 to 1525, the last strong ruler of its golden age. He built and restored many temples, fought wars against Ayutthaya, and patronised Pali scholarship; the chronicle Jinakalamali was completed during his reign.

phrae.s: Phrae is a town and province on the Yom River in northern Thailand. An old Tai principality, it was brought under the direct control of Chiang Mai by King Tilokarat in the mid-15th century and later passed with the rest of Lan Na under Burmese and then Siamese suzerainty.

ping-river.s: The Ping River is a river of northern Thailand that rises in the mountains of Chiang Mai Province and flows south past Chiang Mai to join the Nan at Nakhon Sawan, forming the Chao Phraya. Its valley was the heartland of the kingdom of Lan Na, whose capital Mangrai founded on…

photisarath.s: Photisarath was king of Lan Xang from 1520 to 1547, a devout Buddhist who in 1527 ordered the suppression of spirit cults in favour of Buddhist practice. He married a princess of Lan Na, which allowed his son Setthathirath to claim the Lan Na throne, and he died in an accident…

phra-that-si-song-rak.s: Phra That Si Song Rak is a stupa at Dan Sai in Loei Province, Thailand, built between 1560 and 1563 to commemorate the alliance between King Setthathirath of Lan Xang and King Maha Chakkraphat of Ayutthaya against Burma. Its name means "stupa of the love of two", and it marked…

pho-hien.s: Phố Hiến was a river port in Hưng Yên Province, south-east of Hanoi, that became the chief foreign trading town of northern Vietnam in the 17th century. Chinese, Japanese and European merchants, including the Dutch and English East India companies, traded there, and a saying…

parakramabahu-iii.s: Parakramabahu III was a king of Sri Lanka who reigned from 1287 to 1293, ruling from Polonnaruwa. After a Pandya army under Aryacakravarti had taken the fortress of Yapahuwa and carried off the Tooth Relic of the Buddha, he went to the Pandya court and recovered the relic by…

pagoda-of-fogong-temple.s: The Pagoda of Fogong Temple, or Sakyamuni Pagoda, at Yingxian in Shanxi, China, was built in 1056 under the Liao dynasty. About 67 metres high, it is the oldest and tallest fully wooden pagoda surviving in China, built without nails and standing through many earthquakes.

poppaea-sabina.s: Poppaea Sabina was a Roman noblewoman, wife of Otho and then, from 62 CE, of the emperor Nero. Nero sent Otho away to govern Lusitania in 58 to remove him as a rival, and ancient historians accuse Poppaea of encouraging the deaths of Nero's mother Agrippina and his first wife…

priscillianism.s: Priscillianism was an ascetic Christian movement founded in Hispania in the later 4th century by Priscillian, a layman who became bishop of Ávila. It stressed asceticism, the study of apocryphal writings and the role of lay teachers, and was attacked as heretical by bishops…

proserpina-dam.s: The Proserpina Dam is a Roman gravity dam near Mérida in Spain, built probably in the 1st or 2nd century CE to supply Emerita Augusta, capital of Lusitania. An earth embankment faced with a masonry wall some 425 metres long holds back a reservoir that fed the Aqueduct of Los…

prudentius.s: Prudentius (Aurelius Prudentius Clemens) was a Latin Christian poet from Hispania, probably born at Calagurris (Calahorra). After a career as a provincial governor and official at the court of Theodosius I, he turned to religious verse, writing the Cathemerinon, the…

publius-carisius.s: Publius Carisius was a Roman general under Augustus, legate in Hispania Ulterior during the Cantabrian Wars. He fought the Astures, capturing their stronghold of Lancia, and in 25 BCE founded Emerita Augusta (Mérida) on the Guadiana as a colony for discharged veterans.

philip-iii-arrhidaeus.s: Philip III Arrhidaeus was king of Macedon from 323 to 317 BCE, a son of Philip II and half-brother of Alexander the Great. Considered mentally impaired, he was proclaimed king after Alexander's death, jointly with Alexander's infant son Alexander IV, while real power lay with…

palapa-oath.s: The Palapa oath (Sumpah Palapa) is the vow attributed by the Javanese chronicle Pararaton to Gajah Mada, chief minister of Majapahit, on his appointment around 1336. He swore not to taste palapa, understood as a worldly pleasure, until the islands of the archipelago had been…

penataran.s: Penataran is the largest Hindu temple complex of East Java, near Blitar on the slopes of Mount Kelud in Indonesia. Built over some 250 years from the late 12th century under Kediri, Singhasari and Majapahit, it served as a state temple dedicated to Shiva, and Majapahit kings,…

petronas.s: Petronas (Petroliam Nasional Berhad) is Malaysia's state-owned oil and gas company, founded in 1974 and vested with ownership of the country's petroleum resources. Its revenues have been a major source of government income, and it operates internationally in exploration,…

petronas-twin-towers.s: The Petronas Twin Towers are a pair of 88-storey skyscrapers in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, designed by César Pelli and completed in 1998. At 452 metres they were the tallest buildings in the world until 2004 and remain the tallest twin towers.

proton.s: Proton is Malaysia's national car company, founded in 1983 on the initiative of Mahathir Mohamad in partnership with Mitsubishi. Its first model, the Proton Saga, went into production in 1985 and dominated the domestic market behind protective tariffs.

peace-of-basel-1795.s: The Peace of Basel was the set of treaties of 1795 by which Prussia, Spain and Hesse-Kassel made peace with revolutionary France. In the Prussian treaty of 5 April 1795, Prussia withdrew from the War of the First Coalition, accepted French occupation of the left bank of the…

potsdam.s: Potsdam is the capital of the German state of Brandenburg, on the Havel just south-west of Berlin. A residence of the Hohenzollerns from the Great Elector onwards, it became a garrison town under Frederick William I, and Frederick the Great built the palace of Sanssouci there.

province-of-brandenburg.s: The Province of Brandenburg was a province of Prussia from 1815 to 1947, formed from the old Margraviate of Brandenburg with some additions. Its capital was Potsdam, and Berlin, which lay within it, was separated as a distinct administrative unit in 1881.

peace-of-olomouc.s: The Peace of Olomouc of 1479 ended the war between Matthias Corvinus of Hungary and Vladislaus II of Bohemia over the Bohemian crown. Both kept the title King of Bohemia: Vladislaus held Bohemia proper, while Matthias kept Moravia, Silesia and Lusatia, which could be redeemed…

pribor.s: Příbor is a small town in north-eastern Moravia, in the Moravian-Silesian Region of the Czech Republic. Founded in the thirteenth century, it has a well-preserved historic centre and was long home to a Piarist college.

prokop-of-moravia.s: Prokop of Moravia was a margrave of Moravia of the Luxembourg dynasty, the younger son of John Henry and brother of Jobst. He shared Moravia with Jobst but fought him for years in a ruinous struggle, siding with his cousin King Wenceslaus IV of Bohemia against Jobst and…

panembahan-hanyakrawati.s: Panembahan Hanyakrawati was the second ruler of Mataram in Java, from 1601 to 1613, the son of Panembahan Senapati and father of Sultan Agung. He spent his reign putting down revolts by relatives and regional lords and fighting Surabaya.

pakubuwana-i.s: Pakubuwana I, earlier Pangeran Puger, was ruler of Mataram from 1704 to 1719. A son of Amangkurat I, he claimed the throne against his nephew Amangkurat III and won it with the help of the Dutch East India Company in the First Javanese War of Succession.

pakubuwono-ii.s: Pakubuwana II was ruler of Mataram from 1726 to 1749. During the Chinese War of 1740–1743 he first sided with the rebels against the Dutch East India Company and then changed sides; rebels sacked his capital Kartasura in 1742, and he regained it only with Company help and the…

pakubuwana-iii.s: Pakubuwana III was ruler of Mataram from 1749 and the first susuhunan of Surakarta, installed by the Dutch East India Company. His uncle Mangkubumi contested the throne, and the Treaty of Giyanti of 1755 divided the realm between them, leaving Pakubuwana III at Surakarta.

pasuruan.s: Pasuruan is a port city on the north coast of East Java, Indonesia, on the Madura Strait. In the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries it was a Muslim coastal state allied with Surabaya, and Sultan Agung of Mataram conquered it in 1617.

plan-of-agua-prieta.s: The Plan of Agua Prieta was the revolt proclaimed in April 1920 at Agua Prieta, Sonora, by supporters of Álvaro Obregón against President Venustiano Carranza. Most of the army joined it, and Carranza fled Mexico City and was killed in May 1920.

plutarco-elias-calles.s: Plutarco Elías Calles was a Mexican general and president from 1924 to 1928. His enforcement of the constitution's anticlerical laws provoked the Cristero War, and after Obregón's assassination he founded the National Revolutionary Party in 1929, dominating politics as the…

pancho-villa.s: Pancho Villa was a Mexican revolutionary general from northern Mexico who led the Division of the North in the Mexican Revolution. He helped overthrow Victoriano Huerta in 1914, but after breaking with Venustiano Carranza he was defeated by Álvaro Obregón at Celaya in 1915.

party-of-the-democratic-revolution.s: The Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) is a left-wing Mexican political party founded in 1989 by Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas and other dissidents from the ruling PRI, together with parties of the left, after the disputed election of 1988. It governed Mexico City from 1997 to…

pemex.s: Pemex (Petróleos Mexicanos) is Mexico's state oil company, created in 1938 after President Lázaro Cárdenas expropriated the foreign oil companies. It held a monopoly over oil production for most of its history, and its revenues long financed a large share of the federal budget.

plan-of-tuxtepec.s: The Plan of Tuxtepec was the revolt proclaimed by Porfirio Díaz in January 1876 against President Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada's bid for re-election, under the banner of no re-election. After his victory at Tecoac in November 1876 Díaz took Mexico City and became president,…

plaza-de-las-tres-culturas.s: The Plaza de las Tres Culturas is a square in the Tlatelolco district of Mexico City, named for the three cultures represented around it: the ruins of the Aztec city of Tlatelolco, the colonial church of Santiago and modern buildings. On 2 October 1968 soldiers fired on…

porfiriato.s: The Porfiriato was the period of Porfirio Díaz's rule in Mexico, from 1876 to 1911, with an interval from 1880 to 1884. It brought political stability, foreign investment, railways, mining and export agriculture, but also rigged elections, repression and the concentration of…

phrynichus-tragic-poet.s: Phrynichus was an Athenian tragic poet of the generation before Aeschylus, said to have been the first to put female characters on stage. His play The Capture of Miletus, on the Persian sack of 494 BCE, so distressed Athenian audiences that he was fined.

peoples-defence-force.s: The People's Defence Force is the armed wing of Myanmar's National Unity Government, formed in May 2021 after the military coup. Made up of many local units of volunteers, often trained by ethnic armed organisations, it fights the junta's forces across the country, especially…

pyidawtha.s: Pyidawtha, meaning 'happy, prosperous land', was the welfare-state programme of U Nu's government in Burma, launched in 1952. Drawn up with American economic consultants, it planned investment in industry, agriculture, health, education and housing, financed largely by rice…

peoples-court-germany.s: The People's Court was a special court set up in Nazi Germany in 1934 to try treason and other political offences outside the ordinary justice system. Under its president Roland Freisler from 1942 it held show trials, notably of the 20 July plotters and the White Rose…

puzrish-dagan.s: Puzrish-Dagan, the modern site of Drehem, was an administrative centre near Nippur in southern Iraq, founded by Shulgi of the Third Dynasty of Ur in the late 21st century BCE. It received, recorded and redistributed livestock delivered as taxes and offerings for the temples…

province-of-quebec-1763-1791.s: The Province of Quebec was the British colony created by the Royal Proclamation of 1763 from the conquered French colony of Canada. The Quebec Act of 1774 enlarged it to the Ohio valley and the Great Lakes and guaranteed French civil law and the Catholic faith.

pierre-gaultier-de-varennes-sieur-de-la-.n: Pierre Gaultier de Varennes, sieur de La Vérendrye
pierre-gaultier-de-varennes-sieur-de-la-.s: Pierre Gaultier de Varennes, sieur de La Vérendrye, was a French-Canadian officer, fur trader and explorer. From 1731, with his sons, he built a chain of trading posts west of Lake Superior to Lake Winnipeg and the Saskatchewan River in search of a route to the Western Sea,…

paul-de-chomedey-de-maisonneuve.s: Paul de Chomedey de Maisonneuve was a French officer who founded Ville-Marie, later Montreal, in May 1642 for the Société Notre-Dame de Montréal, a religious association that aimed to convert the Native peoples. He governed the settlement for more than twenty years, defending…

pierre-de-rigaud-marquis-de-vaudreuil-ca.n: Pierre de Rigaud, Marquis de Vaudreuil-Cavagnial
pierre-de-rigaud-marquis-de-vaudreuil-ca.s: Pierre de Rigaud, Marquis de Vaudreuil-Cavagnial, was the last governor general of New France, from 1755 to 1760, and the first born in Canada. A former governor of Louisiana, he quarrelled with the Marquis de Montcalm over strategy during the Seven Years' War.

peter-jackson.s: Peter Jackson is a New Zealand film director and producer best known for The Lord of the Rings trilogy (2001–2003), filmed in New Zealand, whose final part won eleven Academy Awards. He also directed Heavenly Creatures, King Kong and The Hobbit trilogy.

pechora-river.s: The Pechora is a river of northern European Russia, about 1,800 kilometres long, rising in the northern Urals and flowing north into the Barents Sea. Its basin was a source of furs for medieval Novgorod, which collected tribute from the region's peoples from the eleventh century.

publius-cornelius-scipio-consul-218-bce.s: Publius Cornelius Scipio was a Roman consul of 218 BCE and the father of Scipio Africanus. After failing to stop Hannibal in the Rhône valley, he was defeated and wounded at the Ticinus in Italy.

publius-sittius.s: Publius Sittius was a Roman adventurer from Nuceria who led a mercenary army in North Africa. During Caesar's African campaign in 46 BCE he invaded Numidia with King Bocchus II of Mauretania and took Cirta, forcing Juba I to divide his forces.

pact-of-brunnen.s: The Pact of Brunnen was an alliance concluded on 9 December 1315 at Brunnen, on Lake Lucerne, by Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden, weeks after their victory over the Habsburgs at Morgarten. Written in German, it renewed and extended their earlier league, forbidding any member to…

pfaffenbrief.s: The Pfaffenbrief, or Priests' Charter, was an agreement of 1370 between Zürich, Lucerne, Zug, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden. It required clergy and other residents to bring secular disputes before local courts rather than church or foreign courts, and it protected the safety of…

piet-cronje.s: Piet Cronjé was a Boer general of the South African Republic. He forced the surrender of the Jameson raiders in January 1896 and, in the Second Boer War, besieged Mafeking and defeated the British at Magersfontein in December 1899.

philippolis.s: Philippolis is a small town in the south of the Free State province of South Africa, founded in 1823 as a mission station of the London Missionary Society. It became the centre of the Griqua under Adam Kok II and Adam Kok III, who sold their lands to the Orange Free State in…

pyinbya.s: Pyinbya was an early king of Pagan who, according to the Burmese chronicles, reigned in the mid-ninth century and fortified the city in 849 on a bend of the Irrawaddy River. Little else is known of him, and modern historians treat the early chronicle dates with caution, but…

prajnaparamita.s: The Prajnaparamita, or Perfection of Wisdom, sutras are a group of Mahayana Buddhist scriptures on the emptiness of all phenomena and the wisdom of the bodhisattva, the earliest of which date from around the first century BCE. Copies of the Prajnaparamita in Eight Thousand…

pahlavas.s: Pahlavas is the name used in ancient Indian texts, such as the Manusmriti, the epics and the Puranas, for a people from the north-west usually identified with the Parthians, especially the Indo-Parthian rulers of the first century CE. They are often listed with the Shakas and…

parameshvaravarman-i.s: Parameshvaravarman I was king of the Pallava dynasty from about 670 to 695. His reign was dominated by renewed war with the Chalukya king Vikramaditya I, who invaded Pallava territory and occupied Kanchipuram, but Parameshvaravarman recovered and drove the Chalukyas back.

parameshvaravarman-ii.s: Parameshvaravarman II was the last king of the main line of the Pallava dynasty, reigning from about 728 to 731. The son of Narasimhavarman II Rajasimha, he was killed in war with the Western Gangas, and the leading men of the kingdom then chose the young Nandivarman II of a…

paranjothi.s: Paranjothi was a general of the Pallava king Narasimhavarman I who led the army that captured and sacked the Chalukya capital Vatapi in 642. He later renounced war and became a devotee of Shiva, revered as Siruthondar, one of the 63 Nayanar saints of Tamil Shaivism, whose…

prithvipati-i.s: Prithvipati I was a prince of the Western Ganga dynasty of southern Karnataka and an ally of the Pallavas in their wars with the Pandyas. He joined the Pallava king Aparajita at the Battle of Sripurambiyam around 885, where the Pandya king Varaguna II was defeated, but was…

pope-gregory-ii.s: Gregory II was pope from 715 to 731. He resisted the taxes and iconoclast policy of the Byzantine emperor Leo III, sent Boniface to convert the Germans, and in 728 received from the Lombard king Liutprand the town of Sutri, an act often seen as the first territorial grant to…

pope-gregory-xi.s: Gregory XI was pope from 1370 to 1378, the last French pope. Urged by Catherine of Siena among others, he moved the papal court from Avignon back to Rome in 1377 to restore papal authority in Italy and the Papal States.

pope-gregory-xiii.s: Gregory XIII was pope from 1572 to 1585. In 1582 he introduced the reformed Gregorian calendar, now used throughout the world, and he founded or endowed many colleges for the training of priests, notably the Jesuits' Roman College, later named the Pontifical Gregorian…

pope-innocent-xii.s: Innocent XII was pope from 1691 to 1700. Born into a Neapolitan noble family, he set out to reform the Curia, and in 1692 his bull Romanum decet Pontificem forbade popes to grant estates, offices or revenues to their relatives and limited to one the number of relatives who…

pope-leo-iv.s: Leo IV was pope from 847 to 855. Elected after Muslim raiders had sacked the basilica of Saint Peter in 846, he enclosed the Vatican hill with the Leonine Wall, creating the fortified Leonine City, and organised the alliance of southern Italian cities whose fleet defeated…

pope-paul-iv.s: Paul IV, born Gian Pietro Carafa, was pope from 1555 to 1559 and a leading figure of the Counter-Reformation. A co-founder of the Theatine order, he strengthened the Roman Inquisition and issued the first papal Index of Forbidden Books in 1559.

pontifical-swiss-guard.s: The Pontifical Swiss Guard is the small armed corps of Swiss soldiers that protects the pope and the Apostolic Palace, founded by Pope Julius II in 1506. During the Sack of Rome on 6 May 1527 most of the guard was killed covering the escape of Pope Clement VII to Castel…

porta-pia.s: Porta Pia is a gate in the Aurelian Walls of Rome, designed by Michelangelo for Pope Pius IV and built in the 1560s. On 20 September 1870 Italian troops entered Rome through a breach in the walls beside it, ending the temporal power of the popes, and the Capture of Rome is…

pope-sixtus-v.s: Sixtus V was pope from 1585 to 1590. In his short reign he suppressed banditry in the Papal States, built up the papal treasury, and in 1588 reorganised the Curia into fifteen permanent congregations of cardinals.

peoples-volunteer-army.s: The People's Volunteer Army was the force of the People's Republic of China that fought in the Korean War. Sent into Korea in October 1950 under Peng Dehuai, it drove United Nations forces back from the Yalu River and fought them to a stalemate before the armistice of July…

peng-dehuai.s: Peng Dehuai was a Chinese Communist general who commanded the Chinese People's Volunteers in the Korean War from 1950 and later served as minister of defence. After he criticised the Great Leap Forward at the Lushan Conference of 1959 he was dismissed by Mao Zedong; persecuted…

pingjin-campaign.s: The Pingjin campaign was the last of the three great campaigns of the Chinese Civil War, fought around Beiping (Beijing) and Tianjin from November 1948 to January 1949. Communist forces under Lin Biao and Nie Rongzhen stormed Tianjin, and the Nationalist commander Fu Zuoyi…

politburo.s: The Politburo (Political Bureau) is the executive committee of a communist party's Central Committee and the real centre of power in a communist state. First created by the Russian Bolsheviks in 1917 and made permanent in 1919, the model was copied by the Soviet Union, China,…

pierre-rousseau-journalist.s: Pierre Rousseau was a French writer and publisher from Toulouse who founded the Journal encyclopédique in Liège in 1756. The journal spread the ideas of the Encyclopédie and the Enlightenment; forced out of Liège, Rousseau moved it in 1760 to Bouillon, where he also ran a…

parliament-of-ravennika.s: The Parliament of Ravennika was an assembly held in May 1209 at Ravennika, in central Greece, by the Latin Emperor Henry of Flanders. The lords of Frankish Greece, among them Geoffrey I of Villehardouin of Achaea, recognised the emperor's suzerainty, and a second meeting in…

pedro-de-san-superano.s: Pedro de San Superano was a leader of the Navarrese Company, a band of mercenaries that seized much of the Principality of Achaea from the late 1370s. He ruled as vicar and from 1396 as prince of Achaea until his death in 1402, after which his widow Maria II Zaccaria succeeded.

peter-constable-of-portugal.s: Peter, Constable of Portugal, was a Portuguese prince and poet, son of the regent Peter, Duke of Coimbra. In 1463 the rebel Catalans, at war with John II of Aragon, chose him as their king; he died at Granollers in 1466 without winning the war.

prussian-academy-of-sciences.s: The Prussian Academy of Sciences was founded in Berlin in 1700 by Elector Frederick III of Brandenburg on the advice of Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, its first president. It became one of the leading learned societies of Europe; Dimitrie Cantemir of Moldavia was elected a member…

petru-i-of-moldavia.s: Petru I of Moldavia, known as Petru Mușat, was Prince of Moldavia from about 1375 until about 1391 and the first prince of the Mușatin dynasty. He issued the first Moldavian coins, did homage to King Władysław II Jagiełło of Poland at Lviv in 1387 to counter Hungarian…

paris-convention-of-1858.s: The Paris Convention of 1858 was an agreement of the great powers, signed on 19 August 1858, that reorganised the Danubian Principalities after the Crimean War. It created the United Principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia, each with its own prince and assembly but with a…

petru-aron.s: Petru Aron was Prince of Moldavia three times between 1451 and 1457, during the civil wars that followed the death of Alexander the Good. He seized power by killing Prince Bogdan II, father of Stephen the Great, and in 1456 became the first Moldavian ruler to agree to pay…

petru-rares.s: Petru Rareș was Prince of Moldavia from 1527 to 1538 and again from 1541 to 1546, an illegitimate son of Stephen the Great. He intervened in Transylvania and fought Poland over Pokuttya, but in 1538 Suleiman the Magnificent invaded, deposed him and annexed Tighina and the…

ptolemy-iv-philopator.s: Ptolemy IV Philopator was king of Ptolemaic Egypt from 221 to 204 BCE. In the Fourth Syrian War he defeated the Seleucid king Antiochus III at the Battle of Raphia in 217 BCE, with the help of native Egyptians trained as phalanx soldiers.

ptolemy-xii-auletes.s: Ptolemy XII Auletes was king of Ptolemaic Egypt from 80 to 58 BCE and again from 55 to 51 BCE, and father of Cleopatra VII. Dependent on Roman goodwill, he paid huge sums to Roman politicians for recognition, was driven out by the Alexandrians in 58 BCE, and was restored in 55…

paul-julius-reuter.s: Paul Julius Reuter was a German-born British businessman who founded the Reuters news agency in London in 1851, using the telegraph to sell news to newspapers and financial houses. In 1872 he obtained from Naser al-Din Shah of Iran a sweeping concession for railways, mines and…

persian-cossack-brigade.s: The Persian Cossack Brigade was a cavalry force formed in Qajar Iran in 1879 on the model of the Russian Cossacks and commanded by Russian officers. It became the shah's most effective military unit and bombarded the Majlis in 1908 for Mohammad Ali Shah.

ponna.s: Ponna was a Jain poet of the tenth century at the court of the Rashtrakuta emperor Krishna III, who gave him the title Ubhayakavichakravarti, 'emperor among poets in two languages', for his writing in Kannada and Sanskrit. His best-known work is the Shantipurana, on the life…

phra-aphai-mani.s: Phra Aphai Mani is an epic verse romance by the Thai poet Sunthorn Phu, composed in instalments over some two decades in the early nineteenth century. It tells of a prince who prefers the magic flute to swordsmanship and his adventures with giants, mermaids and Western…

phraya-phahon-phonphayuhasena.s: Phraya Phahon Phonphayuhasena was a Thai army officer, the senior leader of the People's Party that carried out the revolution of 24 June 1932, ending absolute monarchy in Siam. In June 1933 he overthrew the conservative government of Phraya Manopakorn in a coup and served as…

phuket.s: Phuket is the largest island of Thailand, in the Andaman Sea off the west coast of the Malay Peninsula. Long known for tin mining, which drew many Chinese settlers, it was attacked by Burmese forces in 1785, when its chief town, Thalang, was successfully defended under the…

pierre-deval.s: Pierre Deval was the French consul in Algiers in the 1820s. During an audience in April 1827, in a dispute over unpaid French debts for grain supplied by the Bacri and Busnach trading houses, Hussein Dey struck him with a fly-whisk.

pablo-zarate-willka.s: Pablo Zárate Willka was an Aymara leader who raised indigenous forces in support of the Liberals of La Paz during Bolivia's Federal War of 1898–1899. His fighters helped defeat the Conservatives of Sucre, but the movement also pursued its own aims of land restitution and…

pedro-antonio-olaneta.s: Pedro Antonio Olañeta was a Spanish royalist general who commanded in Upper Peru, present-day Bolivia, during the wars of independence. In 1824 he rebelled against Viceroy La Serna, weakening the royalist cause before the Battle of Ayacucho.

patricio-aylwin.s: Patricio Aylwin was a Chilean Christian Democrat politician and the first president after the military regime of Augusto Pinochet. Elected at the head of the Concertación coalition, he governed from 1990 to 1994.

pablo-neruda.s: Pablo Neruda was a Chilean poet and diplomat, born Ricardo Eliécer Neftalí Reyes Basoalto. His works, including Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair and Canto General, made him one of the most widely read poets of the twentieth century.

pacts-of-may.s: The Pacts of May were agreements signed by Chile and Argentina on 28 May 1902 that ended a period of tension over their long Andean border. They committed both countries to arbitration of disputes and halted their naval arms race by limiting warship construction, one of the…

panama-canal.s: The Panama Canal is an 82-kilometre waterway across the Isthmus of Panama linking the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. After a failed French attempt, it was built by the United States between 1904 and 1914 and opened on 15 August 1914, using locks to lift ships over the isthmus.

parliamentary-republic-chile.s: The Parliamentary Republic was the period of Chilean history from the civil war of 1891 to the Constitution of 1925, during which Congress dominated weak presidents and cabinets changed frequently. Financed by nitrate exports, the oligarchic governments of the time did little…

pachamama.s: Pachamama is the earth and fertility goddess of the Andean peoples, revered by Quechua and Aymara communities since before the Inca Empire. She is honoured with offerings, especially at planting and harvest, and her cult survived Spanish rule alongside Catholicism.

paquisha-war.s: The Paquisha War was a brief armed conflict between Ecuador and Peru in January and February 1981 in the Cordillera del Cóndor, in a border area left undemarcated by the Rio de Janeiro Protocol. Peruvian forces expelled Ecuadorian troops from outposts that Ecuador had named…

party-of-national-conciliation.s: The Party of National Conciliation (PCN) was the official party of El Salvador's military governments, founded in 1961. Its candidates, mostly army officers, held the presidency until the coup of 1979, winning elections that were often managed or, as in 1972 and 1977, openly…

pio-romero-bosque.s: Pío Romero Bosque was president of El Salvador from 1927 to 1931. Chosen as successor by the Meléndez–Quiñónez family, he broke with it and allowed freer political activity.

parliament-of-finland.s: The Parliament of Finland, or Eduskunta, is the country's single-chamber legislature of 200 members. Created by the reform of 1906, which replaced the Diet of four estates while Finland was a grand duchy of the Russian Empire, it was elected by universal suffrage.

petsamo.s: Petsamo is a region on the Arctic coast near the Norwegian border, now the Pechengsky district of Russia's Murmansk Oblast. Ceded to Finland by the Treaty of Tartu of 1920, it gave the country an ice-free outlet to the Arctic Ocean, and its nickel mines became strategically…

porkkala.s: Porkkala is a peninsula on the Gulf of Finland about 30 kilometres west of Helsinki. Under the armistice of September 1944 Finland had to lease it to the Soviet Union for fifty years as a naval base, an arrangement that placed Soviet artillery within range of the capital.

pope-clement-vii.s: Pope Clement VII (1478–1534), born Giulio de' Medici, was pope from 1523 to 1534. The illegitimate son of Giuliano de' Medici, he governed Florence for his cousin Pope Leo X before his election.

palazzo-vecchio.s: The Palazzo Vecchio is the town hall of Florence, built from 1299 as the seat of the Signoria, probably to designs by Arnolfo di Cambio. Its fortress-like mass and tall tower dominate the Piazza della Signoria.

paolo-uccello.s: Paolo Uccello (1397–1475) was a Florentine painter known for his fascination with linear perspective. His works include the painted equestrian monument to John Hawkwood in Florence Cathedral of 1436 and the three panels of the Battle of San Romano, now divided between London,…

piero-di-lorenzo-de-medici.s: Piero di Lorenzo de' Medici (1472–1503), known as Piero the Unfortunate, was the eldest son of Lorenzo de' Medici and ruler of Florence from 1492 to 1494. When Charles VIII of France invaded Italy in 1494, he surrendered key fortresses without the city's consent and was…

primo-popolo.s: The Primo Popolo was the first popular regime of Florence, established in 1250 when the guilds and the armed neighbourhood companies of the popolo took power under a Captain of the People alongside the commune's older institutions. It began the Palazzo del Popolo, now the…

pietro-doria.s: Pietro Doria (died 1380) was a Genoese admiral during the War of Chioggia against Venice. In August 1379 his fleet captured Chioggia at the southern edge of the Venetian lagoon, threatening Venice itself, but the Venetians under Vettor Pisani and Carlo Zeno blockaded the…

philippe-guerrier.s: Philippe Guerrier (1757–1845) was a Haitian general who served as president from May 1844 until his death in April 1845. A veteran of the Haitian Revolution who had been made a duke under King Henri Christophe, he was installed in old age by the mixed-race elite as the first…

puerto-cortes.s: Puerto Cortés is a city on the Caribbean coast of north-western Honduras and the country's main seaport. Its deep natural harbour developed from the late nineteenth century as the terminus of the national railway and an outlet for banana exports, and it is linked to the…

p-v-narasimha-rao.s: P. V. Narasimha Rao was an Indian National Congress politician who served as prime minister of India from 1991 to 1996. Taking office during a severe balance-of-payments crisis, he and his finance minister Manmohan Singh dismantled the licence system, devalued the rupee and…

pokhran.s: Pokhran is a town in the Thar Desert of Rajasthan, in western India, near which lies the Indian Army's test range. India carried out its first nuclear test there on 18 May 1974, code-named Smiling Buddha, and five further tests in May 1998, after which it declared itself a…

pavel-bermondt-avalov.s: Pavel Bermondt-Avalov was a Russian officer and adventurer who in 1919 commanded the West Russian Volunteer Army, a force of anti-Bolshevik Russians and German Freikorps soldiers in Latvia and Lithuania backed by German commanders. In October 1919 he attacked Riga but was…

parex-bank.s: Parex Bank was a Latvian commercial bank founded in Riga in 1992 that grew into the country's second-largest bank, with many deposits from non-resident customers. During the financial crisis of 2008 it suffered a run and was taken over by the state in November 2008, and the…

perkonkrusts.s: Pērkonkrusts (Thunder Cross) was a Latvian ultranationalist, antisemitic and anti-German organisation founded in 1933 by Gustavs Celmiņš. It was banned in 1934, after Kārlis Ulmanis's coup, and its leaders were imprisoned.

popular-front-of-latvia.s: The Popular Front of Latvia was a mass movement founded in October 1988 to campaign for Latvian sovereignty and, soon, full independence from the Soviet Union. It won a majority in the Supreme Council elections of March 1990, after which the council declared the restoration of…

pedro-joaquin-chamorro-cardenal.s: Pedro Joaquín Chamorro Cardenal was a Nicaraguan journalist, editor of the newspaper La Prensa and a leading opponent of the Somoza dictatorship, who was repeatedly jailed and exiled. His assassination in Managua on 10 January 1978 provoked strikes, riots and a national…

panama-canal-zone.s: The Panama Canal Zone was a strip of territory about ten miles wide along the Panama Canal, administered by the United States from 1903 to 1979 under the Hay–Bunau-Varilla Treaty. It had its own government, courts, police and schools, and its American residents, the Zonians,…

philippe-bunau-varilla.s: Philippe Bunau-Varilla was a French engineer who worked on Ferdinand de Lesseps's failed Panama canal and later lobbied the United States to buy the French company's assets and build the canal in Panama rather than Nicaragua. After helping to organise Panama's secession from…

panama-canal-neutrality-treaty.n: Treaty Concerning the Permanent Neutrality and Operation of the Panama Canal
panama-canal-neutrality-treaty.s: The Treaty Concerning the Permanent Neutrality and Operation of the Panama Canal, usually called the Neutrality Treaty, was one of the two Torrijos–Carter Treaties signed by Panama and the United States in 1977. It declared the canal permanently neutral and open to ships of…

panama-canal-authority.s: The Panama Canal Authority is the autonomous Panamanian government agency that has operated the Panama Canal since 31 December 1999, when it took over from the US-run Panama Canal Commission. Created under a constitutional amendment and a law of 1997, it is run on commercial…

panamanian-defense-forces.s: The Panamanian Defense Forces were Panama's armed forces from 1983 to 1989, formed when the National Guard was reorganised into a combined army, navy, air force and police under the command of Manuel Noriega. They were the real centre of power, controlling the state and much…

panama-papers.s: The Panama Papers were 11.5 million leaked documents from the Panamanian law firm Mossack Fonseca, published from April 2016 by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists and partner newspapers. They revealed how politicians, officials and wealthy individuals…

panama-railroad.s: The Panama Railroad is a railway across the isthmus of Panama between the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, built by an American company between 1850 and 1855 and the first railway to cross the Americas from ocean to ocean. It carried large numbers of travellers to and from…

pedro-castillo.s: Pedro Castillo is a Peruvian rural schoolteacher and trade unionist who was president of Peru from July 2021 to December 2022. Elected as the candidate of the left-wing Free Peru party in a narrow run-off against Keiko Fujimori, he faced repeated impeachment attempts.

pan-africanist-congress-of-azania.s: The Pan Africanist Congress (PAC) is a South African political party founded in 1959 by Robert Sobukwe and others who broke from the ANC to pursue an Africanist programme. Its campaign against the pass laws led to the Sharpeville massacre of March 1960, after which it was banned.

pactum-lotharii.s: The Pactum Lotharii was an agreement of 23 February 840 between the Frankish emperor Lothair I and the Venetian doge Pietro Tradonico. It regulated borders, trade, justice and the return of fugitives between Venice and the Carolingian kingdom of Italy, and is the oldest…

paolo-veronese.s: Paolo Veronese was a painter from Verona who worked mainly in Venice, known for his huge, brightly coloured feasts and allegories. His works include The Wedding at Cana and the ceilings of the Doge's Palace.

peace-of-aachen-812.s: The Peace of Aachen of 812 was the settlement between Charlemagne and the Byzantine emperor Michael I, whose envoys at Aachen acknowledged Charlemagne as emperor. In return Charlemagne gave up his claims to Venice and the coastal cities of Dalmatia, which stayed under nominal…

peace-of-turin-1381.s: The Peace of Turin was concluded in August 1381 through the mediation of Amadeus VI of Savoy and ended the War of Chioggia between Venice and Genoa and their allies. Venice gave up Treviso, recognised Hungarian rule in Dalmatia and agreed that the disputed island of Tenedos…

pellestrina.s: Pellestrina is a long, narrow barrier island between the Venetian lagoon and the Adriatic Sea, south of the Lido and north of Chioggia. Its fishing villages were among the old lagoon settlements, and in 810 it was overrun by the Frankish king Pepin of Italy.

pindale-min.s: Pindale Min was king of the Restored Toungoo dynasty of Burma from 1648 to 1661, succeeding his father Thalun. His reign was troubled by the arrival of the fugitive Ming Yongli Emperor and by Ming loyalist armies that raided Upper Burma.

pye-min.s: Pye Min was king of the Restored Toungoo dynasty of Burma from 1661 to 1672. He seized the throne by overthrowing his brother Pindale, drove back the Ming loyalist forces, and in 1662 handed the fugitive Yongli Emperor to the Qing army, ending the threat on the northern frontier.

posidonius.s: Posidonius was a Greek Stoic philosopher, historian and scientist from Apamea in Syria who settled on Rhodes, where he ran a famous school and held public office. He wrote on philosophy, history, geography, astronomy and the tides, and estimated the circumference of the Earth.

palmyra.s: Palmyra was an ancient oasis city in the Syrian desert that grew rich on the caravan trade between the Roman Empire, Mesopotamia and the East. In the third century its rulers Odaenathus and then Queen Zenobia built a short-lived Palmyrene Empire, which seized Egypt and much of…

pachomius-the-great.s: Pachomius was an Egyptian Christian monk who founded the first communal monasteries, beginning at Tabennisi in Upper Egypt in the 320s. Unlike the hermits, his monks lived together under a written rule, sharing work, prayer and meals.

plotinus.s: Plotinus was a Greek-speaking philosopher, born in Egypt, who studied in Alexandria under Ammonius Saccas and from 244 taught in Rome. His treatises, edited by his pupil Porphyry as the Enneads, describe all reality as flowing from a single source, the One.

philo-of-alexandria.s: Philo of Alexandria was a Jewish philosopher who lived in Alexandria and wrote in Greek. He interpreted the Hebrew scriptures allegorically in the light of Greek, especially Platonic, philosophy, and his works influenced early Christian theologians.

plautus.s: Plautus, in full Titus Maccius Plautus, was a Roman comic playwright. His comedies, adapted from Greek New Comedy and set in Greek cities, are lively plays of scheming slaves, young lovers and misers, and twenty of them survive.

perpetual-edict.s: The Perpetual Edict (Edictum perpetuum) was the fixed, final version of the edict of the Roman praetors, which set out the legal remedies they would grant. Around 130 CE the emperor Hadrian had the jurist Salvius Julianus revise and consolidate it, after which only the emperor…

prefect-of-egypt.s: The prefect of Egypt (praefectus Aegypti) was the governor of the Roman province of Egypt from its annexation in 30 BCE. Because of Egypt's wealth and grain, Augustus gave the post to equestrians rather than senators, and senators could not enter Egypt without the emperor's…

petrograd-military-revolutionary-committ.s: The Military Revolutionary Committee of the Petrograd Soviet was formed in October 1917, nominally to defend the capital, and came under Bolshevik control with Leon Trotsky as its leading figure. On 25 October (7 November) 1917 its forces seized key points of Petrograd and…

peoples-commissar.s: A people's commissar was a minister of the Soviet government between 1917 and 1946, a member of the Council of People's Commissars in charge of a branch of administration such as war, foreign affairs or nationalities. The title was chosen to break with the ministers of the…

peace-of-riga.s: The Peace of Riga was signed on 18 March 1921 between Poland on one side and Soviet Russia and Soviet Ukraine on the other, ending the Polish–Soviet War. It fixed a border that left western Belarus and western Ukraine to Poland, and it remained in force until the Soviet…

provincial-reform-of-catherine-ii.s: The provincial reform of Catherine II, set out in the Statute for the Administration of the Provinces of 1775, reorganised local government in the Russian Empire after Pugachev's Rebellion. It divided the empire into some fifty governorates of 300,000 to 400,000 inhabitants,…

pamir-mountains.s: The Pamir Mountains are a high mountain system of Central Asia, lying mainly in Tajikistan and reaching into Afghanistan, China and Kyrgyzstan, with peaks above 7,000 metres. Known as the 'Roof of the World', they were crossed by branches of the Silk Road linking the Tarim…

pozzuoli.s: Pozzuoli is a city on the Bay of Naples in Campania, Italy. Founded around 530 BCE by exiles from Samos as Dicaearchia, it became the Roman colony of Puteoli in 194 BCE and Rome's main port for trade with Egypt and the eastern Mediterranean until Ostia was enlarged.

pissuthnes.s: Pissuthnes was the Persian satrap of Sardis from about 440 BCE. He supported the Samian oligarchs in their revolt against Athens in 440 BCE, helping them recover their hostages, and later intervened in other Ionian cities.

polycrates.s: Polycrates was tyrant of Samos from about 538 to 522 BCE. With a fleet of a hundred penteconters and a thousand archers he made Samos the leading naval power of the Aegean, raiding widely and allying first with Amasis of Egypt and then with Cambyses II of Persia.

pythagoreio.s: Pythagoreio is a small town on the south-eastern coast of Samos, Greece, on the site of the island's ancient capital. Renamed in 1955 after the philosopher Pythagoras, a native of Samos, it preserves remains of the ancient city walls, the harbour mole and the Tunnel of Eupalinos.

polyaenus.s: Polyaenus was a Macedonian rhetorician and writer of the second century CE who lived at Rome. Around 163 he dedicated to the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus his Stratagems, a collection of some 900 ruses of war drawn from Greek, Roman and barbarian history, meant to…

prokhorovka-culture.s: The Prokhorovka culture is the early Sarmatian archaeological culture of the steppes of the southern Urals and lower Volga, dated to about the fourth to second centuries BCE. Named after kurgans excavated near Prokhorovka in Orenburg region, it is known from burials with long…

paisius-of-hilendar.s: Paisius of Hilendar was a Bulgarian monk of the Hilendar Monastery on Mount Athos and a founder of the Bulgarian National Revival. In 1762 he completed the Slavonic-Bulgarian History, which celebrated medieval Bulgarian tsars and saints and urged Bulgarians to take pride in…

panlongcheng.s: Panlongcheng is an archaeological site of the Erligang period near Wuhan in Hubei, China, close to the Yangtze River. Excavated from the 1950s, it has a walled enclosure, palace foundations and rich burials with bronzes in the same style as those of Zhengzhou.

perpetual-maritime-truce.s: The Perpetual Maritime Truce was an agreement of 1853 between Britain and the rulers of the coast now forming the United Arab Emirates, forbidding all hostilities at sea between them. It made permanent a series of seasonal truces begun in 1835 and gave Britain the role of…

palace-of-the-shirvanshahs.s: The Palace of the Shirvanshahs is a fifteenth-century palace complex in the old city of Baku, Azerbaijan, built when the Shirvanshahs moved their capital there from Shamakhi. Besides the palace, it includes a divankhana, a burial vault of 1435, a mosque of 1441 with its…

protectorate-general-to-pacify-the-east.n: Protectorate General to Pacify the East
protectorate-general-to-pacify-the-east.s: The Protectorate General to Pacify the East was set up by Tang China at Pyongyang in 668, after the fall of Goguryeo, to rule the conquered lands of Goguryeo and Baekje. Its existence led to the Silla–Tang War, and in 676 the Tang moved it to Liaodong in Manchuria.

paracel-islands.s: The Paracel Islands are a group of small islands and reefs in the northern South China Sea, east of Vietnam and south of Hainan. China took the western part of the group from South Vietnam in a naval battle in January 1974 and has controlled all of them since.

paris-peace-agreements.s: The Paris Peace Agreements were signed on 23 October 1991 by Cambodia's Supreme National Council, representing the rival factions, and eighteen other states to end the war in Cambodia that followed Vietnam's invasion of 1978. They provided for a ceasefire, the disarming of the…

peoples-army-of-vietnam.s: The People's Army of Vietnam is the armed force of Vietnam, founded in December 1944 as a small propaganda unit under Vo Nguyen Giap. It fought the French in the First Indochina War, winning at Dien Bien Phu in 1954, and defeated South Vietnam and its American allies by 1975.

pham-van-dong.s: Pham Van Dong was a Vietnamese communist leader and close associate of Ho Chi Minh. He led the Viet Minh delegation at the Geneva Conference of 1954 and was prime minister of North Vietnam from 1955 and of reunified Vietnam until 1987, one of the longest-serving heads of…

pretoria-convention.s: The Pretoria Convention was the peace settlement signed on 3 August 1881 that ended the First Boer War. Britain restored self-government to the Transvaal, which it called the Transvaal State, but retained suzerainty, control of its foreign relations and a resident in Pretoria.

parnon.s: Parnon is a mountain range in the eastern Peloponnese of Greece, running from Arcadia south-east through Laconia and rising to about 1,935 metres. It closes the Eurotas valley to the east, opposite the Taygetus range, and separated ancient Sparta from the borderlands of…

peace-of-nicias.s: The Peace of Nicias was a treaty between Athens and Sparta concluded in the spring of 421 BCE, ending the first phase of the Peloponnesian War, known as the Archidamian War. Named after the Athenian general Nicias who negotiated it, it was meant to last fifty years and…

pang-juan.s: Pang Juan was a general of the State of Wei in the Warring States period. According to the Shiji he had studied strategy alongside Sun Bin and, out of jealousy, had him mutilated.

polish-teutonic-war-1519-1521.s: The Polish–Teutonic War of 1519–1521 was fought between the Kingdom of Poland and the Teutonic Order under Grand Master Albert of Brandenburg-Ansbach, who refused homage to the Polish king. Polish forces devastated much of Prussia, and the Order received little help from the…

pha-mueang.s: Pha Mueang, or Pho Khun Pha Mueang, was a Tai chief of Mueang Rat in north-central Thailand in the thirteenth century. According to a Sukhothai inscription, he joined forces with Bang Klang Hao to expel the Khmer governor of Sukhothai, around the conventional date of 1238,…

phra-phuttha-chinnarat.s: Phra Phuttha Chinnarat is a gilded bronze seated Buddha image in Wat Phra Si Rattana Mahathat in Phitsanulok, Thailand, cast in the late Sukhothai style, probably in the fourteenth century. With its flame-shaped halo it is regarded as one of the most beautiful Buddha images in…

piriya-krairiksh.s: Piriya Krairiksh is a Thai art historian and former professor at Thammasat University. In the late 1980s he argued, on stylistic and linguistic grounds, that the Ram Khamhaeng inscription was not a thirteenth-century document but a later composition, possibly of the nineteenth…

palawan.s: Palawan is a long island in the western Philippines between the South China Sea and the Sulu Sea, now a province. Its southern coasts were long linked to the sultanates of Brunei and Sulu, which drew tribute from local chiefs, before Spain extended its control in the…

pararaton.s: The Pararaton, or Book of Kings, is a Javanese chronicle in Kawi prose telling the history of the kingdoms of Singhasari and Majapahit, beginning with the founder Ken Arok. Its oldest surviving manuscripts date from the early seventeenth century, though it draws on older…

portuguese-malacca.s: Portuguese Malacca was the Portuguese colony at Malacca on the Malay Peninsula, founded when Afonso de Albuquerque captured the city from its sultan in 1511. Its fortress, A Famosa, controlled traffic through the Strait of Malacca and served as a base for Portuguese trade and…

prabu-siliwangi.s: Prabu Siliwangi is the legendary ideal king of Pajajaran, the Sunda Kingdom of western Java, and the central royal figure of Sundanese oral tradition and the bardic pantun. Popular belief often identifies him with Sri Baduga Maharaja, who reigned from 1482 to 1521, but the…

purnavarman.s: Purnavarman was a king of Tarumanagara, the earliest known Hindu kingdom of western Java, who ruled in the fifth century CE. He is known from several Sanskrit inscriptions in a south Indian script, among them the Ciaruteun stone near Bogor, which bears his footprints, and the…

progressive-reform-party-suriname.s: The Progressive Reform Party (VHP) is a Surinamese political party founded in 1949 as the United Hindustani Party under Jagernath Lachmon, and renamed in 1973. It has drawn its support chiefly from the Indo-Surinamese community and has taken part in many coalition governments.

paramaribo.s: Paramaribo is the capital and largest city of Suriname, on the Suriname River near the Atlantic coast. It grew around Fort Zeelandia as the administrative and commercial centre of the English and then Dutch plantation colony.

pyramid-of-the-moon.s: The Pyramid of the Moon is the second-largest pyramid of Teotihuacan, standing at the northern end of the Avenue of the Dead with Cerro Gordo behind it. Excavations have shown that it was enlarged in seven stages between about 100 and 450 CE, and burials of sacrificed humans…

pyramid-of-the-sun.s: The Pyramid of the Sun is the largest building at Teotihuacan and one of the largest pyramids of Mesoamerica, about 65 metres high, raised on the east side of the Avenue of the Dead and probably completed by about 200 CE. A man-made cave runs beneath it.

princess-jincheng.s: Princess Jincheng was a Tang princess, an adopted daughter of the emperor Zhongzong, who was sent to Tibet in 710 to marry the young emperor Me Agtsom as part of a peace settlement. The Tang ceded the Jiuqu district on the upper Yellow River as part of the arrangement.

padmasambhava.s: Padmasambhava was an Indian tantric master who, according to Tibetan tradition, was invited to Tibet by the emperor Trisong Detsen in the eighth century, subdued the local spirits hostile to Buddhism and helped found Samye monastery. Revered as Guru Rinpoche, the "precious…

princess-wencheng.s: Princess Wencheng was a member of the Tang imperial clan who was sent to Tibet in 641 as a bride for the royal house of Songtsen Gampo, sealing peace with the emperor Taizong after a Tibetan attack on the Tang frontier. Tibetan tradition credits her with bringing the Jowo…

patriarch-nikon.s: Nikon was Patriarch of Moscow from 1652 to 1666. A close adviser of Tsar Alexis, he reformed Russian liturgical books and rituals to bring them into line with contemporary Greek practice, ordering for example the sign of the cross with three fingers rather than two.

patta-chundawat.s: Patta, also known as Fatta, was a Sisodia Rajput chief of Kelwa in Mewar who with Jaimal Rathore led the defence of Chittor against Akbar's siege of 1567–1568. He was killed in the final assault in February 1568.

padmavat.s: Padmavat is an epic poem in Awadhi by the Sufi poet Malik Muhammad Jayasi, completed in 1540. It tells how Ratansen, king of Chittor, won the Sinhalese princess Padmavati and how Alauddin Khalji besieged Chittor to possess her, ending with the king's death and the queen's…

padmini.s: Padmini, or Padmavati, is a legendary queen of Chittor, wife of King Ratnasimha, said to have committed jauhar with the women of the fort when Alauddin Khalji captured it in 1303. Her story first appears in Malik Muhammad Jayasi's poem Padmavat of 1540, more than two centuries…

population-registration-act-1950.s: The Population Registration Act of 1950 required every South African to be classified and registered by race, as white, coloured or native, later black, with Indians added as a subgroup. Classification, decided by appearance, descent and social acceptance, determined where…

promotion-of-bantu-self-government-act-1.s: The Promotion of Bantu Self-Government Act of 1959 was a South African law of Hendrik Verwoerd's government that divided the African population into ethnic 'national units', each to be given self-government in a homeland, or bantustan. It abolished the representation of…

port-rashid.s: Port Rashid is a port in Dubai, named after the ruler Rashid bin Saeed Al Maktoum and opened in 1972. Built to expand the emirate's traditional role as a regional entrepot, it was soon overtaken in scale by the deep-water port of Jebel Ali, opened in 1979, and was later turned…

parliament-acts-1911-and-1949.s: The Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 are two acts of the UK Parliament that limit the power of the House of Lords. The 1911 Act, passed after the Lords rejected the People's Budget, removed their veto over money bills and replaced their veto over other bills with a delay of two…

premier-league.s: The Premier League is the top division of English men's football, founded in 1992 when the leading clubs broke away from the Football League. Backed by large television contracts, it became the most watched and richest football league in the world, and its global audience has…

petroleos-de-venezuela.s: Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. (PDVSA) is Venezuela's state oil company, created on 1 January 1976 when the government nationalised the oil industry. For years it ranked among the world's largest oil companies.

petrocaribe.s: Petrocaribe is an oil alliance between Venezuela and Caribbean and Central American states, launched in June 2005 under Hugo Chávez. Members could buy Venezuelan oil on preferential terms, paying part of the cost over long periods at low interest or in goods.

purandara-dasa.s: Purandara Dasa was a Kannada poet-saint and composer of the Haridasa devotional movement who lived in the Vijayanagara Empire. A wealthy merchant before he gave away his property, he composed thousands of devotional songs to Vishnu.

pietro-i-candiano.s: Pietro I Candiano was Doge of Venice for a few months in 887, the first of the Candiano family to hold the office, which his descendants would dominate in the 10th century. He led a naval expedition against the Narentine pirates of the eastern Adriatic and was killed in battle…

pietro-ii-orseolo.s: Pietro II Orseolo was Doge of Venice from 991 to 1009. He secured trading privileges from the Byzantine emperor and the Holy Roman Emperor, and in 1000 led a fleet along the Dalmatian coast that broke the power of the Narentine pirates and brought the coastal towns under…

pagaruyung.s: Pagaruyung is a village in the Tanah Datar regency of West Sumatra, Indonesia, the seat of the Minangkabau royal house from the time of Adityawarman in the 14th century. The royal family was largely killed during the Padri War around 1815.

paku-alam-i.s: Paku Alam I, born Prince Natakusuma, was a son of Sultan Hamengkubuwono I of Yogyakarta. During the British occupation of Java he sided with the British, who stormed the Yogyakarta court in 1812, and in 1813 Stamford Raffles rewarded him with an apanage and the title Paku…

pura-pakualaman.s: The Pura Pakualaman is the palace of the Paku Alam princes in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, built in the 19th century after the founding of the house in 1813. Smaller than the sultan's kraton, it has a pendopo pavilion, a library of Javanese manuscripts and a museum, and it is still…

potnia.s: Potnia, meaning 'Mistress' or 'Lady', is a title of a goddess or goddesses recorded in the Linear B tablets of Mycenaean Greece and Crete, from Knossos, Pylos and other palaces, often with an epithet such as 'Potnia of the labyrinth' or 'Potnia of the horses'. She received…

protopalatial-period.s: The Protopalatial or Old Palace period is the phase of Minoan Crete, roughly 1900 to 1700 BCE, in which the first palaces were built at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia. It saw the rise of writing in Cretan hieroglyphic and Linear A and of fine Kamares ware pottery, and it ended…

phaistos-disc.s: The Phaistos Disc is a clay disc found by the Italian archaeologist Luigi Pernier in the Minoan palace of Phaistos on Crete in 1908. Both sides bear a spiral of 241 signs, of 45 different types, pressed into the clay with stamps, an early example of printing with movable type.

phalsbourg.s: Phalsbourg (German Pfalzburg) is a town in Lorraine, France, on the road across the northern Vosges. It was founded in 1570 by George John I, Count Palatine of Veldenz, and named after the Palatinate, but was sold to the Duke of Lorraine in 1583.

palatinate-kleeburg.s: Palatinate-Kleeburg was a cadet line of the Palatinate-Zweibrücken branch of the Wittelsbachs, named after Kleeburg (Cleebourg) in northern Alsace. Its founder John Casimir married Catherine, a half-sister of Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden, and their son became king of Sweden as…

palvancha.s: Palvancha is an industrial town in Bhadradri Kothagudem district of Telangana, India, near the Kinnerasani river. It was the seat of the Paloncha samasthan, a hereditary estate in the forested Godavari valley.

painted-grey-ware-culture.s: The Painted Grey Ware culture is an Iron Age archaeological culture of the western Ganges plain and the Ghaggar-Hakra valley in northern India, dated to roughly 1200–600 BCE. It is named after its fine grey pottery painted with black geometric patterns.

panna-national-park.s: Panna National Park is a national park of about 540 square kilometres in Panna and Chhatarpur districts of Madhya Pradesh, India, on the Ken river. Declared in 1981 and made a tiger reserve in 1994, it lost all its tigers to poaching by 2009 and then became known for a…

paracas-candelabra.s: The Paracas Candelabra is a large geoglyph cut into a sandy hillside on the north side of the Paracas peninsula in Peru, facing Pisco Bay. About 180 metres tall, it shows a branched figure like a candlestick or trident and is best seen from the sea.

pisco-river.s: The Pisco River rises in the Andes of Huancavelica and flows west to the Pacific near the port of Pisco in southern Peru. Its irrigated valley supported the Paracas culture and later held the Inca administrative centre of Tambo Colorado.

pierre-joseph-proudhon.s: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon was a French socialist thinker and the first person to call himself an anarchist. His book What Is Property? of 1840 answered that 'property is theft', and he advocated mutualism, a society of independent producers exchanging through free credit and…

petuaria.s: Petuaria was a Roman town at Brough on the Humber in the East Riding of Yorkshire, England, listed by Ptolemy as the town of the Parisi. A 2nd-century inscription set up by an aedile of the vicus of Petuaria records the gift of a new theatre stage.

parion.s: Parion was an ancient Greek city on the Asian shore of the Hellespont, near the village of Kemer in Çanakkale province of Turkey. Founded in the 8th or 7th century BCE by colonists from Paros, Miletus and Erythrae, it prospered from trade through the straits and later became a…

parvagupta.s: Parvagupta was a scribe and minister who seized the throne of Kashmir in 949, ending the Utpala dynasty by killing the young king Sangramadeva. According to Kalhana's Rajatarangini he ruled for little more than a year before dying in 950.

paser-regency.s: Paser Regency is a regency in the south of East Kalimantan province, Indonesia, on the island of Borneo, with its seat at Tana Paser. It covers much of the territory of the former Paser Sultanate, whose old palace at Paser Belengkong is now a museum.

parga.s: Parga is a coastal town in Epirus in north-western Greece, on the Ionian Sea opposite Paxos. Held by Venice from 1401 as an outpost on the mainland, it passed after 1797 through French, Russian and Ottoman hands and came under British protection in 1814.

pate-chronicle.s: The Pate Chronicle is a Swahili history of the town and sultanate of Pate in the Lamu archipelago of Kenya, written down in the 19th century from older traditions. It traces the Nabhani rulers to Oman and describes Pate's wars with Lamu, the Portuguese and Oman and its…

parliament-of-friuli.s: The Parliament of Friuli was the representative assembly of the Patria del Friuli, the state of the patriarchs of Aquileia, documented from the 13th century. It brought together representatives of the clergy, the nobility and the towns, voted taxes and troops and shared in…

phaya-tu-nakpa.s: Phaya Tu Nakpa was the ruler of Pattani on the east coast of the Malay Peninsula who, according to the Hikayat Patani, converted to Islam after a Muslim from Pasai cured him of an illness, taking the name Sultan Ismail Shah. His conversion, dated by scholars between the…

paulicians.s: The Paulicians were a Christian sect of Armenia and eastern Anatolia, recorded from the 7th century, who rejected the church hierarchy and the veneration of icons and were described by their opponents as dualists. Persecuted by Byzantium, they set up a militarised state at…

porus.s: Porus was an Indian king who ruled the land between the Jhelum and Chenab rivers in the Punjab. In 326 BCE he fought Alexander the Great at the Battle of the Hydaspes with a large army including war elephants, and was defeated.

peoples-court-bulgaria.s: The People's Court was a special tribunal set up in Bulgaria after the communist-led Fatherland Front took power in September 1944. In trials from December 1944 to 1945 it judged former regents, ministers, members of parliament, officers and others for collaboration and war…

pangkor-treaty-of-1874.s: The Pangkor Treaty of 1874 was signed in January 1874 off the island of Pangkor between the British governor of the Straits Settlements, Sir Andrew Clarke, and Malay chiefs of Perak. It recognised Raja Abdullah as sultan and obliged him to accept a British Resident, whose…

perak-river.s: The Perak River is the second-longest river of Peninsular Malaysia, flowing about 400 kilometres south from the mountains near the Thai border through the state of Perak to the Strait of Malacca. Its valley was the heartland of the Perak Sultanate, whose royal towns, including…

perak-war.s: The Perak War was a conflict of 1875–1876 between Britain and Malay chiefs of Perak. It began after the first British Resident, J. W. W. Birch, was killed at Pasir Salak in November 1875 in resentment at his interference in local affairs.

pamphylia.s: Pamphylia was the coastal plain of southern Anatolia between Lycia and Cilicia, around the modern city of Antalya in Turkey. Its Greek cities, including Perge, Aspendos and Side, spoke a distinctive Greek dialect and passed under Persian, Macedonian, Ptolemaic, Seleucid and…

perusine-war.s: The Perusine War was a Roman civil conflict of 41–40 BCE between Octavian and the consul Lucius Antonius, backed by Fulvia, wife of Mark Antony. It arose from the confiscation of Italian land for veterans after Philippi.

perigueux.s: Périgueux is a city of south-western France on the Isle river, capital of the Dordogne department. It grew from Vesunna, the Roman capital of the Gallic Petrocorii, whose remains include the Tour de Vésone and a museum built over a Roman house.

peucetius.s: Peucetius is a figure of Greek legend, a son of the Arcadian king Lycaon, said to have led Arcadian settlers to Italy with his brother Oenotrus. Ancient writers such as Dionysius of Halicarnassus used him to explain the name of the Peucetians of central Apulia, although that…

phthia.s: Phthia was a region of southern Thessaly in ancient Greece, celebrated in Homer as the homeland of Achilles and his Myrmidons. Its exact extent is uncertain, but ancient writers placed it around the Spercheios valley and the plain of Pharsalus.

polydamas-of-pharsalus.s: Polydamas of Pharsalus was a leading citizen of Pharsalus in Thessaly in the 370s BCE, trusted by the city's factions to hold its citadel and revenues. According to Xenophon he sought Spartan help against Jason of Pherae in 375 BCE, and when none came he agreed to bring…

publius-servilius-vatia-isauricus.s: Publius Servilius Vatia Isauricus was a Roman general and statesman, consul in 79 BCE. As proconsul of Cilicia from 78 to 74 BCE he fought the pirates of the southern Anatolian coast, captured their strongholds in Lycia, including Phaselis and Olympus, and subdued the…

people-power-revolution.s: The People Power Revolution was a peaceful popular uprising in the Philippines on 22–25 February 1986 that ended the rule of Ferdinand Marcos. After a disputed presidential election, military rebels and huge crowds gathered on Epifanio de los Santos Avenue (EDSA) in Manila,…

phimai.s: Phimai is a town on the Mun river in Nakhon Ratchasima province, north-eastern Thailand. It grew around Prasat Phimai, a large Khmer Buddhist temple built in the late 11th and early 12th centuries and linked by a road to Angkor.

phichit.s: Phichit is a town in the lower north of Thailand, on the Nan river, and the capital of Phichit province. The ruins of the old city of Phichit lie a short distance away, and it was a provincial centre of the Sukhothai and Ayutthaya kingdoms.

phitsanulok.s: Phitsanulok is a city on the Nan river in the lower north of Thailand. Under the later Sukhothai kings it became their main seat, and King Borommatrailokkanat of Ayutthaya ruled from it from 1463 to 1488 to direct the wars with Lan Na.

pratinas.s: Pratinas of Phlius was a Greek dramatist and lyric poet active in Athens around 500 BCE, when he competed against Aeschylus. Ancient writers credited him with introducing the satyr play, the comic drama with a chorus of satyrs that followed each set of tragedies.

phocis.s: Phocis is a region of central Greece around Mount Parnassus and the valley of the Cephissus, between Boeotia and the Locrian lands. Its towns formed the Phocian League, and its territory included the sanctuary of Delphi, which the Phocians seized in the Third Sacred War of…

phalaecus.s: Phalaecus was the last general of the Phocians in the Third Sacred War, a son of Onomarchus, who took command in the late 350s BCE. Running short of Delphi's treasure, he surrendered to Philip II of Macedon in 346 BCE in return for safe passage with his mercenaries.

philomelus.s: Philomelus was a Phocian general who began the Third Sacred War. In 356 BCE, after the Amphictyonic Council fined the Phocians, he seized Delphi and used its treasures to hire mercenaries.

picenum.s: Picenum was the ancient name of the region of Italy between the Apennines and the Adriatic, roughly the southern Marche and northern Abruzzo, home of the Picentes. Rome conquered it in 268 BCE, and Augustus made it the fifth region of Italy.

poitiers.s: Poitiers is a city of west-central France on the Clain river, the historic capital of Poitou. As Lemonum it was the chief town of the Gallic Pictones, and it became a Roman city and early bishopric associated with Saint Hilary.

pitkern.s: Pitkern is a creole language based on 18th-century English and Tahitian, spoken by the inhabitants of Pitcairn Island. It developed among the Bounty mutineers and their Tahitian companions after 1790.

polans-western.s: The Polans were a West Slavic tribe of Greater Poland, in the basin of the Warta river around Gniezno and Poznań. In the 10th century their Piast rulers, beginning with Mieszko I, united the neighbouring tribes into the Polish state, which took its name from them.

pythodoris.s: Pythodoris was queen of Pontus, a granddaughter of Mark Antony and the wife of Polemon I. After Polemon's death in 8 BCE she ruled the kingdom in her own name for many decades and later married Archelaus of Cappadocia.

parakrama-samudra.s: The Parakrama Samudra is a large reservoir beside Polonnaruwa in Sri Lanka, built by King Parakramabahu I in the 12th century by joining several older tanks behind a long embankment. Covering about 22 square kilometres, it supplied the city and irrigated wide rice lands.

parakramabahu-i.s: Parakramabahu I was king of Sri Lanka from 1153 to 1186, ruling from Polonnaruwa. After a long civil war he reunited the island, reformed and unified the Buddhist sangha, and built great irrigation works, including the Parakrama Samudra, and monuments such as the Gal Vihara.

phalasarna.s: Phalasarna was an ancient Greek harbour city at the western tip of Crete, known for its enclosed artificial harbour, protected by walls and towers. It was a rival of Polyrrhenia and is thought to have served pirates in the Hellenistic period.

paigc.n: African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde
paigc.s: The African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC) was founded in 1956 by Amílcar Cabral and others to free both Portuguese colonies. From 1963 it waged a guerrilla war in Portuguese Guinea that won control of much of the countryside and declared…

praia.s: Praia is the capital and largest city of Cape Verde, on the south coast of Santiago island. It grew from a sheltered harbour near the older capital of Ribeira Grande, which suffered from pirate raids, and became the colony's capital in 1770.

piri-reis.s: Piri Reis was an Ottoman admiral and cartographer, best known for his world map of 1513, which preserves part of an early map of the Americas, and for his book of navigation, the Kitab-ı Bahriye. As admiral of the Indian Ocean fleet he took Muscat from the Portuguese in 1552…

paestum.s: Paestum is an ancient city in Campania in southern Italy, founded as the Greek colony of Poseidonia around 600 BCE. Taken by the Lucanians around 410 BCE and refounded as a Latin colony in 273 BCE, it is renowned for three well-preserved Doric temples and the painted Tomb of…

potchefstroom.s: Potchefstroom is a city in North West province, South Africa, on the Mooi River. Founded by Voortrekkers under Andries Hendrik Potgieter in 1838, it was the first European town north of the Vaal River and the first capital of the South African Republic until Pretoria replaced…

pallene.s: Pallene, now Kassandra, is the westernmost of the three peninsulas of Chalcidice in northern Greece. Potidaea, a Corinthian colony, stood on its narrow isthmus and controlled access to its cities, among them Mende, Scione and Aphytis.

pamunkey.s: The Pamunkey are a Native American people of Virginia, the most powerful member of the Powhatan Confederacy, living along the Pamunkey River. Their leaders Opechancanough and Cockacoeske dealt with the English colony in the 17th century, and the Treaty of Middle Plantation of…

pocahontas.s: Pocahontas was a daughter of Wahunsenacah, paramount chief of the Powhatan, in Virginia. Captured by the English in 1613, she converted to Christianity, took the name Rebecca and married John Rolfe in 1614, a match that brought a brief peace.

powis-castle.s: Powis Castle is a medieval castle near Welshpool in mid Wales, built in the 13th century by the princes of Powys Wenwynwyn as their seat. It passed to the Charlton lords of Powis and was bought in 1587 by Sir Edward Herbert, whose family remodelled it.

pope-clement-ii.s: Pope Clement II, born Suidger, was bishop of Bamberg when Emperor Henry III had him made pope in 1046, after the Synod of Sutri removed three rival claimants. He crowned Henry emperor and began the reform of the papacy, but died in 1047 after less than a year.

porrentruy.s: Porrentruy is a town in the canton of Jura in north-western Switzerland, near the French border. After the Reformation reached Basel, the prince-bishops of Basel made its castle their residence until the French Revolution.

puster-valley.s: The Puster Valley is a long east–west Alpine valley in South Tyrol, Italy, and East Tyrol, Austria, drained by the Rienz and the Drava. It was granted to the bishops of Brixen in 1091 and later came under the counts of Gorizia and of Tyrol.

pierre-de-la-baume.s: Pierre de La Baume was bishop of Geneva from 1522 and the last bishop to reside in the city. Caught between the Duke of Savoy and the citizens, who allied with Fribourg and Bern, he left Geneva in 1533, and the city adopted the Reformation in 1536.

peace-of-fexhe.s: The Peace of Fexhe was a charter agreed on 18 June 1316 between the prince-bishop of Liège, Adolph de la Marck, and the estates of the principality, ending a period of civil strife. It declared that laws could be changed only with the consent of the 'sense of the country', the…

petershagen.s: Petershagen is a town on the Weser north of Minden in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. Its castle, built in the early 14th century, was the favoured residence of the prince-bishops of Minden, who often avoided the city of Minden because of friction with its citizens.

petar-i-petrovic-njegos.s: Petar I Petrović-Njegoš was prince-bishop of Montenegro from 1782 to 1830. He defeated Kara Mahmud Pasha Bushati of Scutari at Martinići and Krusi in 1796, securing Montenegro's de facto independence, and issued its first law code.

petar-ii-petrovic-njegos.s: Petar II Petrović-Njegoš was prince-bishop of Montenegro from 1830 to 1851 and one of the great poets of the South Slavs. He created a senate, introduced taxes and strengthened central rule over the clans, and he wrote the verse drama The Mountain Wreath.

pope-john-xix.s: Pope John XIX, born Romanus, was pope from 1024 to 1032, a member of the family of the counts of Tusculum. A layman, he succeeded his brother Benedict VIII and received all holy orders in a single day.

polabian-slavs.s: The Polabian Slavs were the West Slavic peoples who lived between the Elbe and the Oder, among them the Obotrites, the Lutici and the Sorbs. Conquered and converted by German rulers between the 10th and 12th centuries, culminating in the Wendish Crusade of 1147 and the…

philippsburg.s: Philippsburg is a town on the right bank of the Rhine in Baden-Württemberg, Germany. Originally called Udenheim, it was a residence of the bishops of Speyer, and Bishop Philipp Christoph von Sötern fortified it in the early 17th century and named it after himself.

province-wellesley.s: Province Wellesley, now Seberang Perai, is the mainland part of the Malaysian state of Penang, a strip of coast facing Penang island. The Sultan of Kedah ceded it to the British East India Company in 1800, and it was named after Richard Wellesley, governor-general of India.

philanthropinum.s: The Philanthropinum was a progressive school founded at Dessau in 1774 by the educator Johann Bernhard Basedow with the support of Prince Leopold III Friedrich Franz of Anhalt-Dessau. Inspired by Enlightenment ideas, it taught through play, practical work, physical exercise…

plotzkau.s: Plötzkau is a village on the Saale in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany, dominated by a Renaissance castle. In the 1603 partition of Anhalt it became the seat of the small principality of Anhalt-Plötzkau, held by a younger son of Prince Joachim Ernest.

port-of-saint-symeon.s: The Port of Saint Symeon was the harbour of Antioch at the mouth of the Orontes, near the ancient port of Seleucia Pieria and present-day Samandağ in Turkey. It took its name from the monastery of Saint Symeon the Stylite the Younger on a nearby mountain.

place-des-vosges.s: The Place des Vosges is a square in the Marais district of Paris, built between 1605 and 1612 on the orders of Henry IV and originally called the Place Royale. Surrounded by uniform houses of brick and stone above arcades, it is the oldest planned square in Paris and a model…

place-ducale.s: The Place Ducale is the central square of Charleville, now Charleville-Mézières in the Ardennes, France. It was built between 1606 and about 1628 for Charles of Gonzaga, Duke of Nevers, as the heart of his new capital, with uniform arcaded houses of brick and stone on the…
