panj-river.s: The Panj is the upper course of the Amu Darya in Central Asia, formed by the junction of the Pamir and Wakhan rivers. For much of its length of about 920 kilometres it forms the border between Afghanistan and Tajikistan, a line fixed by Russian and British agreements of the…

plassenburg.s: The Plassenburg is a castle on a hill above the town of Kulmbach in Upper Franconia, Bavaria. From the 14th century it was the main fortress of the Hohenzollern burgraves of Nuremberg and their Franconian lands.

psekups.s: The Psekups is a river of the North-West Caucasus in Russia, a left tributary of the Kuban, flowing north from the Caucasus foothills through Krasnodar Krai and Adygea. The spa town of Goryachy Klyuch stands on its banks.

petersberg-citadel.s: The Petersberg Citadel is a fortress on a hill in the centre of Erfurt, Germany, built from 1665 after the Elector of Mainz had brought the city under his control. It is one of the largest surviving baroque fortresses in central Europe.

przemysl.s: Przemyśl is a city on the San river in south-eastern Poland, near the Ukrainian border. One of the Cherven towns, it was ruled by Rus' princes from the 11th century and was the seat of Volodar Rostyslavych, then part of the principalities of Galicia and Galicia-Volhynia before…

pshavi.s: Pshavi is a historic mountain region of north-eastern Georgia, in the valley of the Pshavi Aragvi river. Its people, the Pshavs, lived in clan communities with their own shrines and customs, and with the neighbouring highlanders of Tusheti and Khevsureti they supplied warriors…

putna-monastery.s: Putna Monastery is a Romanian Orthodox monastery in Bukovina, north-eastern Romania, founded by Stephen the Great in 1466 and consecrated in 1470. It became the burial place of Stephen and his family and a centre of manuscript copying and embroidery.

podgorica.s: Podgorica is the capital and largest city of Montenegro, at the confluence of the Ribnica and Morača rivers. Near the Roman town of Doclea, it grew as an Ottoman market town and was gained by Montenegro at the Congress of Berlin in 1878.

peter-and-fevronia-of-murom.s: Peter and Fevronia are Russian Orthodox saints, a prince of Murom and the peasant healer who cured him and became his wife, traditionally identified with Prince David of Murom, who died in 1228, and his wife. Their 16th-century tale by Yermolai-Erazm became a classic of Old…

peter-paul-rubens.s: Peter Paul Rubens was the leading painter of the Flemish Baroque, born at Siegen in Nassau, where his parents lived in exile. Trained in Antwerp and Italy, he ran a large workshop in Antwerp producing altarpieces, portraits and mythological scenes for the courts of Europe, and…

panjikent.s: Panjikent is a town in north-western Tajikistan on the Zarafshan river, east of Samarkand. Beside it lie the ruins of ancient Panjikent, a Sogdian town of the 5th to 8th centuries whose excavated houses and temples have yielded extensive wall paintings of epics, gods and…

pereslavl-zalessky.s: Pereslavl-Zalessky is a town in Yaroslavl Oblast, Russia, on Lake Pleshcheyevo. Founded by Yuri Dolgoruky in 1152 and named after Pereyaslavl in the south, it was the seat of an appanage principality and the birthplace of Alexander Nevsky.

pereiaslav.s: Pereiaslav is a town in Kyiv Oblast, Ukraine, south-east of Kyiv near the Dnieper. As Pereyaslavl it was one of the chief towns of Kievan Rus' and the seat of a principality guarding the steppe frontier, until the Mongols sacked it in 1239.

pirot.s: Pirot is a town in south-eastern Serbia on the Nišava river, near the Bulgarian border, on the old road from Belgrade to Sofia and Constantinople. Ottoman for over four centuries, it was taken by Serbia in the war of 1877 to 1878 and confirmed to it by the Congress of Berlin.

pribislav-henry.s: Pribislav-Henry was the last prince of the Slavic Hevelli, ruling from Brandenburg. A Christian who took the baptismal name Henry, he allied himself with the German margrave Albert the Bear and made him his heir.

partium.s: The Partium was the group of eastern counties of the Kingdom of Hungary, around Nagyvárad (Oradea) and Szatmár, that were ruled by the princes of Transylvania from the 16th century, as confirmed by the Treaty of Speyer in 1570. The name means 'parts' of Hungary.

pinsk.s: Pinsk is a city in the Brest region of southern Belarus, where the Pina joins the Pripyat, in the heart of the Pinsk Marshes. First recorded in 1097, it was a town of the Turov lands and later a Lithuanian appanage duchy.

pennal-letter.s: The Pennal Letter was written by Owain Glyndŵr at Pennal on 31 March 1406 to Charles VI of France. In it Glyndŵr offered to transfer the allegiance of the Welsh Church from the pope in Rome to the pope in Avignon in return for French support, and set out plans for an…

percy-family.s: The Percy family were a powerful English noble house in Northumberland, Earls of Northumberland from 1377. Henry Percy, Earl of Northumberland, and his son Harry Hotspur helped Henry IV to the throne, then rebelled against him, joining Owain Glyndŵr and Edmund Mortimer;…

phung-hung.s: Phùng Hưng was a local leader in Tang-ruled Annan, in northern Vietnam, who led a revolt against heavy taxation in the late 8th century. His forces took the protectorate's seat at Tống Bình, and he ruled briefly until his death, after which Tang authority was restored.

providence-island-company.s: The Providence Island Company was an English joint-stock company chartered in 1630 by Puritan nobles and gentry, including the Earl of Warwick, Lord Saye and Sele and John Pym. It founded a Puritan colony on Providence Island off the coast of Central America, which also became…

piscataqua-river.s: The Piscataqua River is a short tidal river forming part of the border between New Hampshire and Maine, flowing into the Atlantic at Portsmouth. English fishing settlements were founded along it from 1623, among the earliest in northern New England.

portsmouth-new-hampshire.s: Portsmouth is a port city in New Hampshire, United States, at the mouth of the Piscataqua River. Settled around 1630 as Strawbery Banke, it took its present name in 1653 and was the colonial capital of New Hampshire.

portsmouth-rhode-island.s: Portsmouth is a town on the northern part of Aquidneck Island in Rhode Island, United States. It was founded in 1638 by Anne Hutchinson, William Coddington and other religious dissenters exiled from Massachusetts, who signed the Portsmouth Compact.

princeton-university.s: Princeton University is a private university in Princeton, New Jersey, chartered in 1746 as the College of New Jersey, the fourth college founded in British North America. It moved to Princeton in 1756, where its Nassau Hall briefly housed the Congress of the Confederation in…

panagiotis-danglis.s: Panagiotis Danglis was a Greek army general and politician, known for designing the Schneider-Danglis mountain gun, who served as chief of staff to Crown Prince Constantine in the Balkan Wars. In 1916 he formed, with Eleftherios Venizelos and Admiral Pavlos Kountouriotis, the…

pskov-krom.s: The Pskov Krom is the medieval citadel of Pskov in north-western Russia, standing on a rocky promontory where the Pskova River flows into the Velikaya. Its stone walls enclosed the Trinity Cathedral and the square where the veche assembly of the Pskov Republic met.

ptolemy-vi-philometor.s: Ptolemy VI Philometor was king of Ptolemaic Egypt from 180 to 145 BCE, at times jointly with his brother Ptolemy VIII and his sister-wife Cleopatra II. He survived the invasion of Antiochus IV, which Rome halted in 168 BCE, and through Roman arbitration his brother received…

pedro-albizu-campos.s: Pedro Albizu Campos was a Puerto Rican lawyer who became president of the Nationalist Party in 1930 and led the movement for independence from the United States. A Harvard law graduate, he was imprisoned for seditious conspiracy in 1936 and again after the Nationalist…

puerto-rican-nationalist-party.s: The Puerto Rican Nationalist Party was founded in 1922 to seek independence from the United States and, under Pedro Albizu Campos from 1930, turned to militant action. Police killed its marchers in the Ponce massacre of 1937, and its members led the uprisings of 1950 and the…

ponce-puerto-rico.s: Ponce is the largest city on the southern coast of Puerto Rico, named after Juan Ponce de León y Loayza, great-grandson of the island's first governor. It grew rich from sugar and trade in the 19th century.

puno.s: Puno is a city in south-eastern Peru on the western shore of Lake Titicaca, at about 3,800 metres above sea level. Founded by the Spanish in 1668 near rich silver mines, it is the capital of the Puno Region.

puno-region.s: Puno Region is a region of south-eastern Peru on the border with Bolivia, covering the northern and western shores of Lake Titicaca and the high Altiplano. It was home to Pukará and later to the Colla and Lupaca kingdoms, and as the department of Puno it joined the South…

patzcuaro.s: Pátzcuaro is a town in Michoacán, Mexico, near the southern shore of Lake Pátzcuaro. It was one of the early capitals of the Purépecha and a sacred site, and after the Spanish conquest Bishop Vasco de Quiroga made it the seat of the diocese of Michoacán in 1538 and promoted…

prabhakaravardhana.s: Prabhakaravardhana was a king of the Pushyabhuti dynasty of Thanesar in northern India in the late 6th century, and the father of Rajyavardhana and Harsha. The first of his line to take the imperial title maharajadhiraja, he fought the Hunas and neighbouring kingdoms and…

persian-constitutional-revolution.s: The Persian Constitutional Revolution (1905–1911) was a movement of merchants, clergy and reformers that forced the Qajar ruler Mozaffar ad-Din Shah to grant a constitution and an elected parliament, the Majlis, in 1906. Mohammad Ali Shah's bombardment of the Majlis in 1908…

prester-john.s: Prester John was a legendary Christian priest-king believed in medieval Europe to rule a powerful realm in the East. The story spread after Bishop Hugh of Jabala told the papal court in 1145 that he had defeated the Muslims of Persia, a garbled echo of the Qara Khitai victory…

palk-strait.s: The Palk Strait is a shallow strait between Tamil Nadu in India and the Jaffna peninsula of northern Sri Lanka, linking the Bay of Bengal with Palk Bay. To its south the chain of shoals called Adam's Bridge or Rama Setu runs from Rameswaram island to Mannar.

policarpo-toro.s: Policarpo Toro was a Chilean naval officer who annexed Easter Island (Rapa Nui) for Chile. After visiting the island in 1870 and urging its acquisition, he bought land there from foreign owners and on 9 September 1888 signed an agreement of cession with the ariki Atamu Tekena…

polynesia.s: Polynesia is the region of the central and southern Pacific Ocean within a triangle formed by Hawaii, New Zealand and Rapa Nui (Easter Island), with over a thousand islands. Its peoples descend from seafarers of the Lapita culture who reached Tonga and Samoa nearly 3,000 years…

prajadhipok.s: Prajadhipok, King Rama VII of Siam, reigned from 1925 to 1935. Facing the Great Depression and demands for reform, he became the last absolute monarch of Siam when the Khana Ratsadon's revolution of 24 June 1932 imposed a constitutional monarchy.

portobelo.s: Portobelo is a port on the Caribbean coast of Panama, founded in 1597 to replace Nombre de Dios as the Atlantic end of the treasure route across the isthmus. Its fairs, held when the Spanish galleons arrived, exchanged Peruvian silver for European goods, and its forts were…

penon-of-algiers.s: The Peñón of Algiers was a small rocky islet facing the port of Algiers on which Spain built a fortress around 1510 to dominate the city. Its guns hampered the corsairs until Hayreddin Barbarossa captured it in 1529 and joined the islets to the mainland with a mole.

ponary-massacre.s: The Ponary massacre was the mass murder of about 100,000 people, some 70,000 of them Jews, by German SS units and Lithuanian collaborators at Ponary (Paneriai) near Vilnius between 1941 and 1944. Victims were shot in pits in the forest, and Poles and Soviet prisoners were also…

porte-de-mars.s: The Porte de Mars is a Roman triumphal arch in Reims, France, built in the 3rd century CE. About 32 metres wide, it was among the largest arches of the Roman world, and its vaults bear reliefs of the months of the year, Romulus and Remus with the she-wolf, and Leda and the swan.

parcham.s: Parcham ('Banner') was one of the two factions of the People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan, led by Babrak Karmal. Drawn mainly from urban, Persian-speaking intellectuals, it backed Mohammad Daoud Khan's coup of 1973, while its rival faction, Khalq, was more radical.

peoples-democratic-party-of-afghanistan.s: The People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan was a Marxist-Leninist party founded in Kabul in 1965 by Nur Muhammad Taraki, Babrak Karmal and others. Split into the Khalq and Parcham factions, it seized power in the Saur Revolution of April 1978 and ruled the Democratic…

pact-of-biak-na-bato.s: The Pact of Biak-na-Bato was a truce agreed in December 1897 between the Spanish governor-general Fernando Primo de Rivera and Emilio Aguinaldo's revolutionaries, mediated by Pedro Paterno. Aguinaldo and other leaders accepted exile in Hong Kong in return for payments and…

pedro-paterno.s: Pedro Paterno was a Filipino lawyer, writer and politician from a wealthy Manila family. He mediated the Pact of Biak-na-Bato between Spain and the revolutionaries in 1897, then presided over the Malolos Congress and served as prime minister of the First Philippine Republic in…

pepoli-family.s: The Pepoli were a family of bankers who dominated Bologna in the early 14th century. Romeo Pepoli, reputed the richest man in the city, led the commune until his expulsion in 1321, and his son Taddeo Pepoli became lord of Bologna in 1337.

pablo-escobar.s: Pablo Escobar was a Colombian drug lord who led the Medellín Cartel, which supplied most of the cocaine smuggled into the United States in the 1980s. He won popularity in Medellín through housing projects and briefly sat in Congress, but waged a war of bombings and murders…

pope-eugene-iv.s: Eugene IV, born Gabriele Condulmer in Venice, was pope from 1431 to 1447. His reign was dominated by conflict with the Council of Basel, which deposed him and elected the antipope Felix V.

puerto-limon.s: Puerto Limón, often called simply Limón, is the main Caribbean port of Costa Rica and capital of Limón Province. It grew from the 1870s as the terminus of the railway from the Central Valley, built by Minor C. Keith with many workers from Jamaica, and became the export hub of…

puntarenas.s: Puntarenas is a port city on the Gulf of Nicoya on the Pacific coast of Costa Rica and capital of Puntarenas Province. In the 19th century it was the country's main port, shipping coffee from the Central Valley to Europe, until the railway to Limón shifted trade to the Caribbean.

pact-of-zanjon.s: The Pact of Zanjón was the agreement of 10 February 1878 that ended most of the fighting in the Ten Years' War between Cuban rebels and Spain. Negotiated with General Arsenio Martínez Campos, it granted an amnesty and freed slaves and Chinese indentured workers who had fought…

pentapolis-cyrenaica.s: The Pentapolis was the group of five leading Greek cities of Cyrenaica in eastern Libya: Cyrene, its port Apollonia, Taucheira, Barca or its successor Ptolemais, and Euesperides, later refounded as Berenice. The name was used in Hellenistic and Roman times, and the region as a…

pentapolis-italy.s: The Pentapolis was a group of five cities on the Adriatic coast of Italy, Rimini, Pesaro, Fano, Senigallia and Ancona, governed by the Byzantine Exarchate of Ravenna. After the Lombards took Ravenna in 751, the Frankish king Pepin gave the area to the papacy in 756, and it…

pan-arabism.s: Pan-Arabism is the ideology that the Arabs form a single nation and should be united politically. It grew from the Arab cultural revival and anti-Ottoman nationalism of the late 19th and early 20th centuries and was championed by the Ba'ath Party and above all by Gamal Abdel…

peruzzi-family.s: The Peruzzi were a Florentine family of merchant-bankers whose company was one of the great trading and banking firms of the early 14th century, dealing in grain, wool and cloth and handling papal revenues. Large loans to Edward III of England and other rulers, together with…

platonic-academy.s: The Academy was the school founded by Plato in Athens around 387 BCE, in a grove sacred to the hero Akademos outside the city walls. Aristotle studied there for twenty years, and under later heads it turned towards scepticism.

pittsburg-new-hampshire.s: Pittsburg is a town in Coös County in the far north of New Hampshire, the largest town in the state by area, bordering the Canadian province of Quebec. Its territory was claimed by both the United States and British Canada because the Treaty of Paris of 1783 left the boundary…

peoples-council-of-latvia.s: The People's Council of Latvia was the provisional parliament formed by Latvian political parties in Riga, which proclaimed the independence of Latvia on 18 November 1918. Chaired by Jānis Čakste, it appointed Kārlis Ulmanis to head the Provisional Government.

pope-gregory-ix.s: Gregory IX was pope from 1227 to 1241, a relative of Innocent III. He repeatedly excommunicated Emperor Frederick II and fought him for control of Italy, and from 1231 he appointed papal inquisitors to pursue heresy.

pechina.s: Pechina, called Bajjana in Arabic, is a town in the province of Almería in Andalusia, Spain, in the lower Andarax valley. From the late 9th century it was the base of a self-governing community of Andalusi seafarers trading with North Africa, and it became one of the main…

paraiba.s: Paraíba is a state in north-eastern Brazil on the Atlantic coast, between Rio Grande do Norte and Pernambuco, with its capital at João Pessoa. Founded as a Portuguese captaincy in 1585 to grow sugar, it was occupied by the Dutch between 1634 and 1654.

poljica.s: Poljica is a hilly district in central Dalmatia, Croatia, between the Cetina river, the Mosor mountains and the Adriatic coast south-east of Split. From the Middle Ages its villages governed themselves as an autonomous community under an elected grand knez, recognising in turn…

poljica-statute.s: The Poljica Statute is the legal code of the self-governing community of Poljica in Dalmatia, written in Croatian in the Bosnian Cyrillic script. Its oldest part is traditionally dated to 1440, with additions up to the 17th century.

prekmurje.s: Prekmurje is the north-easternmost region of Slovenia, lying beyond the Mura river on the borders of Austria, Hungary and Croatia, with its centre at Murska Sobota. It belonged to the Kingdom of Hungary for most of its history and had a Slovene-speaking majority, a Hungarian…

palazzo-pubblico-siena.s: The Palazzo Pubblico is the town hall of Siena, built from 1297 to about 1310 on the Piazza del Campo as the seat of the republic's government of the Nine. Its tall bell tower, the Torre del Mangia, was completed in 1348.

piero-strozzi.s: Piero Strozzi was a Florentine exile and soldier, the son of Filippo Strozzi, who fought against the Medici and became a marshal of France. He commanded French and Sienese forces in the war for Siena but was defeated by the imperial and Florentine army at Marciano…

pomaks.s: The Pomaks are Bulgarian-speaking Muslims living mainly in the Rhodope Mountains of Bulgaria and in neighbouring parts of Greece and Turkey. They are descended from Slavic Christians who converted to Islam under Ottoman rule, mostly between the 16th and 18th centuries.

paolo-lucio-anafesto.s: Paolo Lucio Anafesto is, according to Venetian tradition, the first Doge of Venice, elected in 697 by the lagoon communities under Byzantine overlordship. Later chronicles credit him with an agreement with the Lombard king Liutprand fixing the borders of the Venetian territory.

perdido-river.s: The Perdido River is a river on the Gulf Coast of the United States that forms most of the boundary between Florida and Alabama. Under French and Spanish rule it marked the border between Louisiana and West Florida, and in the early 19th century the United States claimed the…

podhale.s: Podhale is a highland region of southern Poland at the foot of the Tatra Mountains, centred on Nowy Targ and Zakopane. Its Górale highlanders are known for their distinctive dialect, costume, music and wooden architecture.

praxedes-mateo-sagasta.s: Práxedes Mateo Sagasta was a Spanish politician and leader of the Liberal Party during the Bourbon Restoration. He served as prime minister seven times between 1870 and 1902, alternating in power with Antonio Cánovas del Castillo's Conservatives under the turno pacífico.

penyengat.s: Penyengat is a small island off Tanjung Pinang in the Riau Islands of Indonesia. It was the seat of the Bugis viceroys, the Yang Dipertuan Muda, of the Riau-Lingga Sultanate and in the 19th century a centre of Malay learning, where Raja Ali Haji wrote.

piratini.s: Piratini is a town in the south of Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. It was the first capital of the Riograndense Republic, proclaimed during the Ragamuffin War in 1836, and the rebel government sat there until 1839, when it moved to Caçapava.

pashto.s: Pashto is an Eastern Iranian language spoken by the Pashtuns of Afghanistan and north-western Pakistan, written in a modified Arabic script. It is one of the two official languages of Afghanistan.

pope-pius-vi.s: Pius VI, born Giovanni Angelo Braschi, was pope from 1775 to 1799. He condemned the French Revolution's Civil Constitution of the Clergy, and in 1797 Napoleon forced him to cede the Legations by the Treaty of Tolentino.

pope-pius-vii.s: Pius VII, born Barnaba Chiaramonti, was pope from 1800 to 1823. He concluded the Concordat of 1801 with Napoleon and attended his coronation in 1804, but after Napoleon annexed the Papal States in 1809 he was held captive in France until 1814.

pellegrino-rossi.s: Pellegrino Rossi was an Italian-born economist, jurist and politician who taught in Geneva and Paris and served as French ambassador to Rome. Appointed chief minister of the Papal States by Pius IX in 1848, he was stabbed to death in November 1848 on the steps of the…

parmehutu.s: Parmehutu (Party of the Hutu Emancipation Movement) was a Rwandan political party founded by Grégoire Kayibanda in 1959 from his earlier Hutu social movement. It led the Hutu revolution against Tutsi dominance, won the elections before independence and ruled Rwanda as a…

palancia.s: The Palancia is a river of eastern Spain that rises in the Sierra de El Toro and flows south-east to the Mediterranean near Sagunto, north of Valencia. The ancient Iberian and Roman town of Saguntum stood on a long hill above its lower course.

pawon.s: Pawon is a small 9th-century Buddhist temple in Central Java, Indonesia, standing between Mendut and Borobudur on a straight line with both. Built under the Sailendra dynasty, it is decorated with reliefs of wish-granting trees and celestial beings.

port-au-prince.s: Port-au-Prince is the capital and largest city of Haiti, on a bay at the eastern end of the Gulf of Gonâve. Founded by the French in 1749, it became the seat of government of Saint-Domingue in 1770 and has been Haiti's capital for most of the time since independence in 1804.

philip-j-pierre.s: Philip J. Pierre is a Saint Lucian politician who became prime minister in July 2021. Long the member of parliament for Castries East, he was elected leader of the Saint Lucia Labour Party in 2016 and led it to a large victory over the United Workers Party in the general…

pitons-saint-lucia.s: The Pitons are two volcanic plugs, Gros Piton and Petit Piton, that rise steeply from the sea near Soufrière on the south-west coast of Saint Lucia. Together with the surrounding area of hot springs and coral reefs they were inscribed as the Pitons Management Area, a UNESCO…

pazyryk-burials.s: The Pazyryk burials are a group of kurgans of the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE in the Pazyryk valley of the Altai mountains in southern Siberia, Russia, excavated in 1929 and, by Sergei Rudenko, in 1947–1949. Ice formed in the tombs preserved tattooed bodies, felt hangings,…

pentri.s: The Pentri were the largest and most powerful of the four Samnite peoples of ancient Italy, living in the mountains of modern Molise around their chief town, Bovianum. The great sanctuary of Pietrabbondante lay in their territory.

pietrabbondante.s: Pietrabbondante is a village in Molise, Italy, beside the remains of the largest sanctuary of the ancient Samnites. Built mainly in the 2nd century BCE, the complex includes temples and a theatre, and it served as a religious and political centre for the Samnite peoples.

pythagoras.s: Pythagoras was a Greek philosopher from Samos who, by tradition to escape the tyranny of Polycrates, settled at Croton in southern Italy around 530 BCE. There he founded a religious and philosophical community whose members taught the immortality and transmigration of the soul…

patwardhan.s: The Patwardhan were a Chitpavan Brahmin family from the Konkan whose members rose as cavalry commanders under the Peshwas in the 18th century. Rewarded with jagirs in the southern Maratha country, they fought in the wars against Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan.

pedro-de-peralta.s: Pedro de Peralta was a Spanish colonial official who served as governor of New Mexico from 1610 to 1614. On royal orders he moved the capital of the colony from San Gabriel to a new site and founded the town of Santa Fe around 1610.

pope.s: Popé was a Tewa religious leader from Ohkay Owingeh in New Mexico who organised the Pueblo Revolt of 1680. Flogged by the Spanish in 1675 for practising traditional religion, he later coordinated the rising from Taos, using knotted cords to fix the day of the attack.

pueblo-peoples.s: The Pueblo peoples are Native American communities of the south-western United States, chiefly in New Mexico and Arizona, who live in compact villages of stone and adobe called pueblos. Descended from the Ancestral Puebloans, they speak several unrelated languages, including…

pueblo-revolt.s: The Pueblo Revolt was a coordinated uprising of the Pueblo peoples of New Mexico against Spanish rule that began on 10 August 1680. Led by Popé, the rebels killed about 400 colonists and 21 Franciscan friars, besieged Santa Fe and forced the survivors to retreat south to El Paso.

pohnpei.s: Pohnpei is a volcanic island in the eastern Caroline Islands of the western Pacific, the largest island of the Federated States of Micronesia and home to its capital, Palikir. Under the Saudeleur dynasty, from roughly the 12th to the 17th century, it was ruled from Nan Madol,…

philippine-executive-commission.s: The Philippine Executive Commission was the civil administration set up by the Japanese army in January 1942, after the occupation of Manila, to govern the Philippines under military control. Chaired by Jorge B. Vargas and composed of prewar Filipino politicians, it handled…

popular-front-spain.s: The Popular Front was an electoral coalition of Spanish left-wing parties, including Republicans, Socialists and Communists, formed in January 1936. It narrowly won the general election of February 1936, and Manuel Azaña became prime minister and then president of the Republic.

popular-front-of-estonia.s: The Popular Front of Estonia was a mass political movement founded in 1988 to support Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms and win greater self-government for Estonia within the Soviet Union, later moving towards full independence. It joined in organising the Baltic Way human chain of…

popular-front-chile.s: The Popular Front was a coalition of Chilean centre and left parties, led by the Radical Party with the Socialists and Communists, formed in 1936. Its candidate Pedro Aguirre Cerda narrowly won the presidential election of 1938, and his government founded the development…

putrajaya.s: Putrajaya is the planned administrative capital of Malaysia, built south of Kuala Lumpur from the mid-1990s. Government ministries and the prime minister's office began moving there in 1999, and in 2001 Selangor ceded the area to become a federal territory.

paynes-prairie.s: Paynes Prairie is a large savanna and wetland basin south of Gainesville in north-central Florida, known in the 18th century as the Alachua prairie. Around 1750 the chief Cowkeeper led settlers there, and his town of Cuscowilla became a centre of the emerging Seminole people.

paxos.s: Paxos is a small island of the Ionian Sea, south of Corfu, in Greece. Under Venetian rule for centuries, it became part of the Septinsular Republic in 1800 and later of the British protectorate of the Ionian Islands.

peace-of-szeged.s: The Peace of Szeged was a ten-year truce agreed in 1444 between the Ottoman sultan Murad II and the Kingdom of Hungary. It restored Đurađ Branković to his Serbian Despotate and returned Smederevo to him.

pec.s: Peć, known in Albanian as Peja, is a city in western Kosovo below the Rugova gorge. From 1346 it was the seat of the Serbian Patriarchate, whose monastery complex there is a World Heritage Site.

pecs.s: Pécs is a city of southern Hungary, the centre of Baranya county, at the foot of the Mecsek hills. Founded as the Roman town of Sopianae, it has an early Christian necropolis now on the World Heritage list.

polans-eastern.s: The Polans were an East Slavic tribe of the middle Dnieper, living around Kyiv in the 8th to 10th centuries. The Primary Chronicle describes them as a peaceful people who paid tribute to the Khazars before falling under the rule of the Rus' princes.

phad-painting.s: Phad painting is a folk tradition of Rajasthan in which long cloth scrolls are painted with the stories of local hero-deities such as Pabuji and Devnarayan. The scrolls serve as portable shrines for travelling priest-singers called bhopas, who perform the epics before them at…

parashurameshvara-temple.s: The Parashurameshvara Temple is a Hindu temple dedicated to Shiva in Bhubaneswar, Odisha, generally dated to the 7th century. It is one of the oldest and best-preserved temples of the Kalinga style, with a curved tower and richly carved walls.

palace-of-the-shaki-khans.s: The Palace of the Shaki Khans is a summer residence of the khans of Shaki, in northern Azerbaijan, completed in the late 18th century. It is famous for its painted interiors and its shebeke windows, wooden lattices fitted with coloured glass without nails or glue.

piprahwa.s: Piprahwa is a village in Siddharthnagar district of Uttar Pradesh, India, near the border with Nepal. In 1898 excavation of its stupa revealed a relic casket inscribed in Brahmi naming the relics of the Buddha and the Shakyas.

pan-geng.s: Pan Geng was a king of the Shang dynasty of China, traditionally credited with moving the capital to Yin, near modern Anyang, around 1300 BCE. The move ended a series of earlier relocations and Yin remained the capital until the fall of the dynasty.

pushyamitra-shunga.s: Pushyamitra Shunga was the founder of the Shunga dynasty of northern India. Commander of the Maurya army, he assassinated the last Maurya emperor, Brihadratha, around 185 BCE and took the throne at Pataliputra.

palici.s: The Palici were twin deities of the native Sicels of Sicily, worshipped at bubbling volcanic pools near modern Palagonia. Their sanctuary was a place for swearing solemn oaths, where perjurers were believed to be punished, and a refuge for runaway slaves.

princess-juliana-international-airport.s: Princess Juliana International Airport is the main airport of the Caribbean island of Saint Martin, on the Dutch side, Sint Maarten. Opened in 1943 as a military airstrip and named after the Dutch Crown Princess Juliana, it is one of the busiest airports of the eastern…

philipsburg.s: Philipsburg is the capital of Sint Maarten, a constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands on the southern part of the Caribbean island of Saint Martin. Founded in 1763 by the Scottish-born commander John Philips, it lies on a narrow strip of land between Great Bay…

policoro.s: Policoro is a town in the province of Matera in Basilicata, southern Italy, near the Gulf of Taranto between the Sinni and Agri rivers. It stands on the site of the ancient Greek city of Heraclea, founded in 433 BCE, and some scholars link its hill with the earlier Ionian…

presov.s: Prešov is the third-largest city of Slovakia, in the north-east of the country on the Torysa river. A royal free town of the Kingdom of Hungary from the 14th century, it became a centre of Lutheranism, with a Protestant college founded in 1667, and later of Greek Catholic and…

presian-i.s: Presian I was ruler (khan) of the First Bulgarian Empire from 836 to 852. During his reign Bulgaria expanded into Macedonia, taking the lands of Slavic tribes such as the Smolyani after their revolt against Byzantium in 837, and fought a war against the Serbs of Prince…

presbyterian-church-of-wales.s: The Presbyterian Church of Wales, long known as the Calvinistic Methodist Church, grew out of the Welsh Methodist revival of the 18th century led by Howell Harris and Daniel Rowland, and became a separate denomination in 1811. It shaped Welsh-language religious life and from…

perpignan.s: Perpignan is a city in southern France near the Mediterranean, the historic capital of Roussillon and of French Catalonia. It became the seat of the counts of Roussillon in the 12th century and from 1276 to 1344 the mainland capital of the Kingdom of Majorca, whose Palace of…

paul-kruger.s: Paul Kruger (1825–1904) was president of the South African Republic (Transvaal) from 1883 to 1902. A veteran of the Great Trek and leader of the resistance to British annexation in the First Boer War, he dominated Afrikaner politics, refused political rights to the Uitlanders…

parliament-of-southern-ireland.s: The Parliament of Southern Ireland was the home-rule legislature created for the 26 counties of Southern Ireland by the Government of Ireland Act 1920. Sinn Féin won 124 of the 128 seats in its House of Commons unopposed in May 1921 but sat instead as the Second Dáil, so only…

palau.s: Palau is an island country in the western Pacific, at the western end of the Caroline Islands, made up of about 340 islands. Ruled in turn by Spain, by Germany from 1899 and by Japan from 1914, whose South Seas Government sat at Koror, it saw hard fighting at Peleliu in 1944…

peleliu.s: Peleliu is a small coral island in southern Palau in the western Pacific. In the Battle of Peleliu, from September to November 1944, US Marines and soldiers fought for over two months to take its Japanese airfield from defenders dug into limestone caves, with heavy losses on…

polisario-front.s: The Polisario Front is a Sahrawi nationalist movement founded in May 1973 to end Spanish rule in Western Sahara. After Spain handed the territory to Morocco and Mauritania, it proclaimed the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic in February 1976 and fought both countries, forcing…

pyu-ancient-cities.s: The Pyu Ancient Cities are three walled cities of the Pyu people in the Irrawaddy basin of Myanmar, Halin, Beikthano and Sri Ksetra, inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2014. Flourishing from about 200 BCE to 900 CE, they contain brick walls, palaces, Buddhist stupas, burial…

pact-of-san-jose-de-flores.n: Pact of San José de Flores
pact-of-san-jose-de-flores.s: The Pact of San José de Flores, signed on 11 November 1859 after Urquiza's victory at the Battle of Cepeda, ended the separation of the State of Buenos Aires from the Argentine Confederation. Buenos Aires agreed to rejoin the nation and accept the Constitution of 1853, subject…

peoples-front-for-democracy-and-justice.n: People's Front for Democracy and Justice
peoples-front-for-democracy-and-justice.s: The People's Front for Democracy and Justice is the ruling and only legal party of Eritrea, formed in February 1994 from the Eritrean People's Liberation Front, which had won the war of independence against Ethiopia. Led by President Isaias Afwerki, it has governed without…

pedro-teixeira.s: Pedro Teixeira (c. 1587–1641) was a Portuguese explorer and soldier in Brazil. In 1637–1639 he led an expedition of some 2,000 people in canoes up the Amazon from Belém to Quito and back, the first European journey up the whole river.

piaui.s: Piauí is a state in north-eastern Brazil, with its capital at Teresina, and the only north-eastern state whose capital lies inland. It was settled from the late seventeenth century by cattle ranchers moving from Bahia and Pernambuco, and became a captaincy dependent on Maranhão.

panton-leslie-and-company.s: Panton, Leslie and Company was a trading firm founded by Scottish Loyalist merchants, among them William Panton and John Leslie, that dominated the deerskin trade with the Creek, Seminole and other peoples of the south-east after 1783. Spain, unable to supply the trade itself,…

porto-santo-stefano.s: Porto Santo Stefano is a port town on the north side of Monte Argentario in southern Tuscany. From 1557 it was one of the fortified harbours of the Spanish State of the Presidi, guarded by a Spanish fortress built in the early 17th century.

puyang.s: Puyang is a city in north-eastern Henan, near the Yellow River. In the Spring and Autumn period it was Diqiu, capital of the State of Wey from 629 BCE, and the remnant of Wey survived around it until 209 BCE.

phra-ruang-dynasty.s: The Phra Ruang dynasty was the ruling house of the Sukhothai Kingdom in Thailand from about 1238 to 1438. Founded by Si Inthrathit, it included Ram Khamhaeng and Li Thai, and its later kings became vassals of Ayutthaya from 1378 until Sukhothai was absorbed.

prabu-geusan-ulun.s: Prabu Geusan Ulun was a ruler of Sumedang Larang in the Priangan highlands of western Java in the late 16th century. After the Banten Sultanate destroyed Pakuan Pajajaran in 1579, he received the Sundanese royal regalia, including the Binokasih crown, and claimed to rule as…

prabu-geusan-ulun-museum.s: The Prabu Geusan Ulun Museum is a museum in the former regents' palace of Sumedang in West Java, Indonesia, named after the 16th-century ruler of Sumedang Larang. It holds the heirlooms of the Sumedang ruling family, including the Binokasih crown traditionally said to have…

pakuan-pajajaran.s: Pakuan Pajajaran was the capital of the Sunda Kingdom in western Java, on the site of modern Bogor. Sri Baduga Maharaja ruled from it after uniting Sunda and Galuh in 1482 and strengthened it with a moat, as the Batutulis inscription records.

purana-qila.s: The Purana Qila, the Old Fort, is a fortress in Delhi built on a site traditionally identified with Indraprastha. Humayun began a city called Dinpanah there in the 1530s, and Sher Shah Suri rebuilt and completed the fort, adding the Qila-i-Kuhna mosque.

paxton-boys.s: The Paxton Boys were frontier settlers from around Paxton in central Pennsylvania who, during Pontiac's War, attacked the peaceful Conestoga Indians, survivors of the Susquehannock, in December 1763, killing all of them, including those sheltered in the Lancaster workhouse. In…

potomac-river.s: The Potomac River flows about 650 kilometres from the Appalachian Mountains to Chesapeake Bay, forming much of the border between Maryland and Virginia. Its lower course was home to Algonquian peoples within the Powhatan Confederacy and beyond, and it became a key route for…

pongola-river.s: The Pongola is a river of southern Africa that rises in Mpumalanga, South Africa, and flows east along the northern edge of KwaZulu-Natal to join the Usutu River on the Mozambique border. In the 18th century the Dlamini ancestors of the Swazi settled on its lower course, and…

poel.s: Poel is an island in the Baltic Sea at the entrance to Wismar Bay, in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Germany. With Wismar and the district of Neukloster it was granted to Sweden by the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.

pisa.s: Pisa is a city in Tuscany, Italy, on the Arno near the Ligurian coast. From the 11th to the 13th century it was a leading maritime republic, fighting Muslim powers in Sardinia and the Balearics, trading across the Mediterranean and competing with Genoa.

pamiris.s: The Pamiris are a group of peoples of the Pamir Mountains, living mainly in Gorno-Badakhshan in Tajikistan and in neighbouring Afghanistan, China and Pakistan. They speak several Eastern Iranian languages, such as Shughni and Wakhi, distinct from Tajik, and most follow Ismaili…

phoenicia.s: Phoenicia was the ancient coastal region of the Levant, roughly modern Lebanon with parts of Syria and northern Israel, home of city-states such as Tyre, Sidon, Byblos and Arwad. From about 1200 BCE its merchants and sailors traded across the Mediterranean, founded colonies…

partheniai.s: The Partheniai ('sons of maidens') were, according to Greek tradition, Spartans of inferior status born during the First Messenian War. Denied full citizenship, they plotted against Sparta and were sent away under their leader Phalanthus to found Taras (Tarentum) in southern…

phalanthus.s: Phalanthus was the legendary leader of the Partheniai who, according to Greek tradition, founded the Spartan colony of Taras (Tarentum) in southern Italy in 706 BCE. Ancient writers said the Delphic oracle guided him to the site, and the people of Taras honoured him as their…

prophetstown.s: Prophetstown was a Native American town founded in 1808 by Tenskwatawa and Tecumseh near the junction of the Tippecanoe and Wabash rivers, in present-day Indiana. It became the centre of their pan-tribal movement, drawing followers from many nations.

pangu-party.s: The Pangu Party is a political party of Papua New Guinea, founded in 1967 as the country's first organised party. Led by Michael Somare, it campaigned for self-government and independence, which came in 1973 and 1975, and Somare became the first prime minister.

panguna-mine.s: The Panguna mine is a large open-pit copper and gold mine on Bougainville Island, Papua New Guinea, opened in 1972 by Bougainville Copper, a subsidiary of the Rio Tinto group. It was among the world's largest copper mines and a major source of the country's export income.

paul-hasluck.s: Paul Hasluck was an Australian politician, historian and diplomat. As minister for territories from 1951 to 1963 he directed policy in Papua and New Guinea, stressing gradual, uniform development through schools, health services and patrol posts.

peraea.s: Peraea was a region east of the Jordan River, between the Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea, in what is now Jordan. Settled by Jews in the Hasmonean period, it was ruled together with Galilee by Herod Antipas after 4 BCE and later by Herod Agrippa I before passing to direct…

pridi-banomyong.s: Pridi Banomyong was a Thai lawyer and statesman, a leader of the civilian wing of the People's Party that ended absolute monarchy in 1932. He drafted early constitutions, founded Thammasat University and led the Free Thai movement against Japan in the Second World War.

polygnotus.s: Polygnotus was a Greek painter from Thasos, active in Athens in the mid-5th century BCE. He painted large murals of mythical and historical scenes, among them the Sack of Troy and the Underworld in the Lesche of the Knidians at Delphi, and works in the Stoa Poikile at Athens.

pinedjem-i.s: Pinedjem I was High Priest of Amun at Thebes from about 1070 to 1032 BCE, during the Twenty-first Dynasty. Ruling Upper Egypt in practice, he took royal titles and married Duathathor-Henuttawy, probably a daughter of Ramesses XI, and his sons became kings and high priests.

parsley-massacre.s: The Parsley Massacre was the killing of thousands of Haitians and Dominicans of Haitian descent in the Dominican borderlands in October 1937, on the orders of the dictator Rafael Trujillo. Soldiers reportedly identified victims by asking them to pronounce perejil, the Spanish…

pharnabazus-ii.s: Pharnabazus II was the Persian satrap of Hellespontine Phrygia under the Achaemenid Empire. He supported Sparta against Athens late in the Peloponnesian War, then joined the Athenian admiral Conon in destroying the Spartan fleet at Cnidus in 394 BCE.

philae.s: Philae is an island in the Nile near Aswan, at the southern frontier of ancient Egypt, famed for its temple of Isis, begun under Nectanebo I and built mainly under the Ptolemies and Romans. The sanctuary drew worshippers from Nubia, including the Blemmyes, until its closure…

peten.s: Petén is the northern lowland region of Guatemala, largely covered by tropical forest and now forming the country's largest department. In the Classic period it was the heartland of Maya civilisation, with cities such as Tikal, Naranjo, Waka' and Uaxactun.

pachuca.s: Pachuca is the capital of the state of Hidalgo in central Mexico, north-east of Mexico City. The nearby Sierra de las Navajas was a major source of green obsidian, worked by Teotihuacan and the Toltecs, and from the 16th century the district became one of the great…

panfilo-de-narvaez.s: Pánfilo de Narváez was a Spanish conquistador who took part in the conquest of Cuba. In 1520 the governor of Cuba sent him to Mexico with a large force to arrest Hernán Cortés, but Cortés surprised him at Cempoala, captured him and won over most of his men.

peuce.s: Peuce was an island in the Danube delta known to Greek and Roman writers, named after its pine trees and lying between the river's arms in modern Romania. In 335 BCE the Triballian king Syrmus took refuge there when Alexander the Great campaigned on the Danube, and a branch of…

pittheus.s: Pittheus was a legendary king of Troezen in Greek mythology, a son of Pelops and renowned for his wisdom. He arranged for his daughter Aethra to lie with the Athenian king Aegeus, and their son Theseus was born and raised at Troezen in his grandfather's house.

providenciales.s: Providenciales is an island in the Caicos group of the Turks and Caicos Islands, a British overseas territory. Thinly settled until the late 20th century, it grew rapidly after a resort opened on its long Grace Bay beach in 1984 and an international airport was built.

pisuerga.s: The Pisuerga is a river of northern Spain, a major tributary of the Duero. It rises in the Cantabrian Mountains in the north of Palencia province, flows south across the plateau of Old Castile and through the city of Valladolid, and joins the Duero below it.

pierre-montet.s: Pierre Montet was a French Egyptologist. In the 1920s he excavated at Byblos in Lebanon, uncovering royal tombs of the Middle Bronze Age, and from 1929 he directed excavations at Tanis in the Nile Delta.

pi-ramesses.s: Pi-Ramesses was the capital built by Ramesses II in the eastern Nile Delta, at modern Qantir, on the site of the older city of Avaris. It held palaces, temples, chariot workshops and barracks for campaigns into Asia.

psusennes-i.s: Psusennes I was a king of the Twenty-first Dynasty of Egypt who ruled from Tanis in the late 11th century BCE for about 46 years. He built the great enclosure wall of the temple of Amun at Tanis, within which he was buried.

psusennes-ii.s: Psusennes II was the last king of the Twenty-first Dynasty of Egypt, reigning in the mid-10th century BCE. He may also have held the office of High Priest of Amun at Thebes, uniting the northern kingship and the Theban priesthood.

psammuthes.s: Psammuthes was a king of the Twenty-ninth Dynasty of Egypt who ruled for about a year in the 390s BCE, after the death of Nepherites I. His brief reign reflected rivalry between branches of the royal family, and he was soon displaced by Hakor.

pelusium.s: Pelusium was a city at the easternmost mouth of the Nile, near modern Port Said, guarding the route into Egypt from Sinai and Palestine. Invading armies often fought there: the Persian king Cambyses II defeated Psamtik III nearby in 525 BCE, and Artaxerxes III defeated…

pedubast-i.s: Pedubast I was a king of Egypt in the late 9th century BCE, usually counted as the founder of the Twenty-third Dynasty. Around 837 BCE, amid conflict within the Twenty-second Dynasty, he proclaimed himself king and was recognised at Thebes, rivalling Takelot II and his son,…

pagasae.s: Pagasae was an ancient port town in Thessaly at the head of the Gulf of Pagasae, near modern Volos in Greece. It served as the harbour of Pherae, whose tyrants drew strength from its trade and shipping, and myth made it the place where the Argo was built.

peoples-secretariat.s: The People's Secretariat was the government of the Bolshevik-led Ukrainian People's Republic of Soviets, formed in Kharkiv in December 1917 as a rival to the Central Rada in Kyiv. Its members included Yevhenia Bosh, Mykola Skrypnyk and Volodymyr Zatonsky.

pavlo-skoropadsky.s: Pavlo Skoropadsky was a Ukrainian aristocrat and former Russian imperial general who ruled Ukraine as Hetman from April to December 1918. Brought to power by a German-backed coup against the Central Rada, his Ukrainian State built an administration, schools and an Academy of…

portuguese-constituent-cortes.s: The Portuguese Constituent Cortes was the elected assembly that met in Lisbon from January 1821 to November 1822 after the liberal revolution of 1820 in Porto. It drew up Portugal's first constitution, adopted in 1822, and called King John VI back from Brazil.

patria-boba.s: Patria Boba, the 'Foolish Fatherland', is the name given to the first period of independence in New Granada, present-day Colombia, from 1810 to 1816. Federalists of the United Provinces and centralists of Cundinamarca fought each other in civil wars instead of uniting against…

primera-junta.s: The Primera Junta was the first autonomous government of the Río de la Plata, formed in Buenos Aires on 25 May 1810 after the May Revolution deposed the Spanish viceroy Baltasar Hidalgo de Cisneros. Presided over by Cornelio Saavedra, with Mariano Moreno and Manuel Belgrano…

puabi.s: Puabi was a queen or noblewoman of Ur around 2600 BCE, known from her richly furnished tomb in the Royal Cemetery, excavated by Leonard Woolley in 1927–1928. A cylinder seal names her with the title nin, 'lady' or 'queen'.

pyramid-of-the-magician.s: The Pyramid of the Magician is the tallest structure at the Maya city of Uxmal in Yucatán, Mexico, about 35 metres high, with an unusual oval plan. It was built in several phases from about the 6th to the 10th century, each enclosing earlier temples.

palencia.s: Palencia is a city on the Carrión river in Castile and León, northern Spain, capital of the province of the same name. It succeeded the Vaccaean and Roman town of Pallantia and was restored as a bishopric in the 11th century.

pallantia.s: Pallantia was the chief town of the Vaccaei, a Celtiberian people of the Douro basin, on the site of modern Palencia in Spain. It resisted Roman attacks several times in the 2nd century BCE, including a siege by Lucullus in 151 BCE and another by Marcus Aemilius Lepidus in the…

pintia.s: Pintia is an archaeological site of the Vaccaei near Padilla de Duero in the province of Valladolid, Spain, occupied from about the 4th century BCE into Roman times. It comprises a fortified town, a craftsmen's quarter and the necropolis of Las Ruedas, where grave goods,…

prabhavatigupta.s: Prabhavatigupta was a Gupta princess, daughter of Emperor Chandragupta II, who married the Vakataka king Rudrasena II. After her husband's early death she ruled the Vakataka kingdom as regent for her young sons for about twenty years, from around 390, bringing it under strong…

pravarapura.s: Pravarapura was a capital of the main branch of the Vakataka dynasty in central India, founded by King Pravarasena II in the 5th century. It is identified with Pavnar near Wardha in Maharashtra, where excavations and sculptures of the Vakataka period, including scenes from the…

pravarasena-i.s: Pravarasena I was the son of Vindhyashakti and the second ruler of the Vakataka dynasty of the Deccan. He was the only Vakataka king to take the imperial title samrat, and inscriptions credit him with four horse sacrifices and other great Vedic rites.

phong-chau.s: Phong Chau is the area of Phu Tho province in northern Vietnam, near the meeting of the Red, Lo and Da rivers, that Vietnamese tradition names as the capital of Van Lang under the Hung kings. Archaeological sites of the Phung Nguyen and Dong Son periods there show long…

phu-tho-province.s: Phu Tho is a province of northern Vietnam, north-west of Hanoi, where the Red River leaves the mountains. Vietnamese tradition places here the homeland and capital of the Hung kings of Van Lang, and its temple on Nghia Linh mountain is the centre of their national cult, with…

pietro-gasparri.s: Pietro Gasparri was an Italian cardinal, canon lawyer and diplomat of the Holy See. He directed the codification of canon law published in 1917, and served as Cardinal Secretary of State under Benedict XV and Pius XI from 1914 to 1930.

pope-leo-xiv.s: Pope Leo XIV, born Robert Francis Prevost in Chicago in 1955, was elected pope on 8 May 2025 after the death of Pope Francis, becoming the first pope from the United States. An Augustinian friar, he spent many years as a missionary and bishop in Peru, of which he is also a…

pope-pius-xi.s: Pope Pius XI, born Achille Ratti, was pope from 1922 to 1939. A scholar and former librarian, he signed the Lateran Treaty with Mussolini's Italy in 1929, creating Vatican City, and concordats with many states, including Germany in 1933.

paillon.s: The Paillon is a short Alpine river in south-eastern France that flows down from the hills behind Nice into the Mediterranean. In ancient times it separated the Greek port of Nikaia from the Ligurian hill country behind it.

portonaccio-temple.s: The Portonaccio Temple was an Etruscan sanctuary outside the walls of Veii, dedicated to the goddess Minerva (Menrva), whose temple was built in the late 6th century BCE. Its roof ridge carried a group of life-size terracotta statues, including the famous Apollo of Veii,…

punto-fijo-pact.s: The Punto Fijo Pact was an agreement signed on 31 October 1958 by Venezuela's main democratic parties, Democratic Action, COPEI and the Democratic Republican Union, after the fall of the dictator Marcos Pérez Jiménez. Named after the house of COPEI leader Rafael Caldera, it…

peltuinum.s: Peltuinum was an ancient town of the Vestini on a high plateau near Prata d'Ansidonia in the province of L'Aquila, Abruzzo, Italy. It grew as a stopping place on the drove road used by flocks moving between the mountains and Apulia, and became a Roman municipium on the Via…

penne-abruzzo.s: Penne is a hill town in the province of Pescara, Abruzzo, Italy, between the Gran Sasso and the Adriatic. As Pinna it was the chief town of the Vestini, which sided with the Italian allies in the Social War of 91–88 BCE, and later a Roman municipium.

pietrera-tumulus.s: The Pietrera Tumulus is a monumental Etruscan burial mound at Vetulonia in Tuscany, built in the 7th century BCE. More than 60 metres across, it covers a stone chamber with a central pillar and a corbelled dome.

panehesy.s: Panehesy was viceroy of Kush under Ramesses XI, the last king of Egypt's Twentieth Dynasty. Around 1080 BCE he intervened in Thebes with Nubian troops and came into conflict with the High Priest of Amun, Amenhotep.

pedro-de-la-gasca.s: Pedro de la Gasca was a Spanish priest and royal official sent to Peru in 1546 to end the rebellion of Gonzalo Pizarro. Offering pardons and the repeal of the harshest New Laws, he won over most rebels, defeated Pizarro at Jaquijahuana in 1548 and had him executed, then…

penukonda.s: Penukonda is a town in Andhra Pradesh, India, below a hill fortress. A provincial stronghold of the Vijayanagara Empire, it became the capital of the Aravidu kings after the sack of Hampi in 1565, until they moved to Chandragiri towards the end of the 16th century.

polo-forest.s: Polo Forest is a forested area near Vijaynagar in the Sabarkantha district of Gujarat, India, at the foot of the Aravalli hills on the Harnav river. It contains ruins of Hindu and Jain temples dating from about the 10th to the 15th centuries and remains of an old fortified…

pau.s: Pau is a city on the Gave de Pau facing the Pyrenees, in south-western France, and the historic capital of Béarn. The viscounts moved their seat there in 1464, and its castle was the birthplace in 1553 of Henry III of Navarre, later Henry IV of France.

pompeius-trogus.s: Gnaeus Pompeius Trogus was a Roman historian of the Augustan age from the Vocontii of Gallia Narbonensis, whose grandfather had received Roman citizenship from Pompey. His Philippic Histories, a universal history in 44 books centred on Macedon and the Hellenistic kingdoms, is…

persius.s: Aulus Persius Flaccus was a Roman satirical poet born at Volaterrae (Volterra) in Etruria to a wealthy equestrian family. A pupil of the Stoic philosopher Cornutus in Rome, he died at the age of 27, leaving six satires, published after his death, that attack moral corruption…

porta-allarco.s: The Porta all'Arco is an arched gate in the walls of Volterra, Tuscany, built of large stone blocks when the Etruscan city of Velathri was fortified in the 4th century BCE, with its arch rebuilt in the 1st century BCE. Three weathered stone heads set in its outer face are…

pont-du-gard.s: The Pont du Gard is a three-tiered Roman aqueduct bridge over the Gardon river in southern France, built in the 1st century CE to carry water some 50 km to Nemausus (Nîmes). About 49 metres high, it is the tallest of all Roman aqueduct bridges and one of the best preserved,…

privernum.s: Privernum was a Volscian town in southern Lazio, near modern Priverno, in the hills above the Pontine plain. After repeated wars with Rome it was captured in 329 BCE, and its people later received Roman citizenship.

passamaquoddy.s: The Passamaquoddy are an Algonquian-speaking Indigenous people of the Passamaquoddy Bay and St Croix river region on the border of Maine and New Brunswick. Members of the Wabanaki Confederacy, they lived by fishing and hunting along the coast.

penobscot.s: The Penobscot are an Algonquian-speaking Indigenous people of the Penobscot river valley in Maine, members of the Wabanaki Confederacy. Under leaders such as Madockawando they traded with and fought both the French and the English in the colonial wars.

pierre-chanel.s: Pierre Chanel (1803–1841) was a French Catholic priest of the Marist order who landed on Futuna in 1837 as one of the first missionaries in the western Pacific. After a son of the island's king Niuliki sought baptism, men from the king's household killed him on 28 April 1841.

pikillacta.s: Pikillacta is a large Wari archaeological site in the Lucre basin about 30 kilometres south-east of Cusco, Peru. Built from around 600 CE as a provincial centre of the Wari Empire, it consists of hundreds of rectangular enclosures laid out on a rigid grid and covering about 2…

pasleka.s: The Pasłęka, in German the Passarge, is a river of about 170 kilometres in the Warmian-Masurian region of northern Poland that flows north-west into the Vistula Lagoon near Braniewo. In the Middle Ages it marked the boundary between the Baltic Prussian lands of Pogesania and…

potawatomi.s: The Potawatomi are an Anishinaabe people of the western Great Lakes, closely related to the Odawa and Ojibwe, who in the 18th century lived around the southern shores of Lake Michigan. Allies of the French, they later joined the Western Confederacy and Tecumseh's Confederacy…

pingyang-shanxi.s: Pingyang was an ancient city in the Fen valley of southern Shanxi, China, on the site of present-day Linfen. Tradition places there the capital of the legendary sage-king Yao.

phalo.s: Phalo (c. 1702–1775) was a paramount chief of the Xhosa in what is now the Eastern Cape of South Africa. Under him the Xhosa moved west towards the Fish River and absorbed Khoikhoi groups.

pemba-island.s: Pemba Island is an island of the Zanzibar Archipelago off the coast of Tanzania, north of Unguja (Zanzibar Island). Long part of the Swahili coast, it came under Omani influence from the late 17th century and under the Sultanate of Zanzibar in the 19th, when it became the…

prince-shotoku.s: Prince Shōtoku (574–622) was a regent and statesman of the Yamato court in Japan under Empress Suiko. Tradition credits him with the Seventeen-Article Constitution of 604, the adoption of Chinese-style court ranks, embassies to Sui China and the founding of temples such as…

pope-leo-xiii.s: Pope Leo XIII (1810–1903), born Vincenzo Gioacchino Pecci, was head of the Catholic Church from 1878 to 1903. His encyclical Rerum novarum of 1891 laid the foundations of modern Catholic social teaching on labour and capital.

phaung-daw-oo-pagoda.s: The Phaung Daw Oo Pagoda is a Buddhist shrine on Inle Lake in Shan State, Myanmar, and one of the most venerated sites in the country. It houses five small Buddha images, so thickly covered with gold leaf by devotees that their shapes are obscured.

peljesac.s: Pelješac is a peninsula in southern Dalmatia, Croatia, joined to the mainland at the narrow isthmus of Ston. Bought by the Republic of Ragusa in 1333, it was protected by the long defensive walls of Ston and valued for its salt pans and wine.

punakha.s: Punakha is a town in western Bhutan where the Pho Chhu and Mo Chhu rivers meet. Ngawang Namgyal built its great fortress-monastery, Punakha Dzong, in 1637 to 1638, and the town was the capital of Bhutan until the 1950s.

pingshan-county.s: Pingshan County is a county of Shijiazhuang in western Hebei, China, on the edge of the Taihang Mountains. It contains the remains of Lingshou, capital of the ancient state of Zhongshan, and the royal tombs excavated there in the 1970s.

patriotic-front-zimbabwe.s: The Patriotic Front was the alliance formed in 1976 by Robert Mugabe's ZANU and Joshua Nkomo's ZAPU, the two main nationalist movements fighting white minority rule in Rhodesia. It rejected the internal settlement and the state of Zimbabwe Rhodesia, took part in the Lancaster…

polish-muscovite-war-1605-1618.s: The Polish–Muscovite War of 1605–1618 was a series of conflicts in which the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth intervened in Russia's Time of Troubles, first through the pretenders known as False Dmitry and from 1609 openly under Sigismund III. After the victory at Klushino…

portuguese-mamluk-naval-war.s: The Portuguese–Mamluk naval war was fought from 1505 to 1517 in the Arabian Sea and western Indian Ocean between Portugal and the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt, allied with the Sultanate of Gujarat and the Zamorin of Calicut. A Mamluk fleet won at Chaul in 1508, but the Portuguese…

polish-swedish-war-1600-1611.s: The Polish–Swedish War of 1600–1611 was fought between the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and Sweden, mainly over Livonia, and grew out of the dynastic quarrel between Sigismund III Vasa and his uncle Charles IX of Sweden. Sweden invaded Livonia in 1600, but the Commonwealth…

portuguese-restoration-war.s: The Portuguese Restoration War was fought from 1640 to 1668 after Portugal rebelled against Spanish rule and proclaimed John IV of the House of Braganza king, ending the Iberian Union. After long border warfare, Portuguese victories at Ameixial (1663), Castelo Rodrigo (1664)…

polish-lithuanian-war.s: The Polish–Lithuanian War was an undeclared conflict of 1920 between Poland and Lithuania over the Vilnius region. After the Suwałki Agreement, the Polish general Lucjan Żeligowski seized Vilnius in October 1920 in a staged mutiny; Lithuanian forces then halted his advance at…

polish-lithuanian-teutonic-war.s: The Polish–Lithuanian–Teutonic War was fought from 1409 to 1411 between the Teutonic Knights and the allied Kingdom of Poland and Grand Duchy of Lithuania. Its decisive event, the Battle of Grunwald in 1410, broke the order's military power, though its castle of Marienburg…

polish-soviet-war.s: The Polish–Soviet War was fought from 1919 to 1921 between the Second Polish Republic and Soviet Russia and Soviet Ukraine over the lands between them. After Polish forces took Kyiv in 1920, the Red Army advanced to Warsaw, where Józef Piłsudski's counter-offensive won the…

polish-ottoman-war-1620-1621.s: The Polish–Ottoman War of 1620–1621 was fought between the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and the Ottoman Empire over Moldavia and Cossack raids on Ottoman lands. A Polish army was destroyed at Cecora in 1620, where Hetman Stanisław Żółkiewski was killed, but in 1621 Polish…

pequot-war.s: The Pequot War was fought from 1636 to 1638 in southern New England between the Pequot people and the colonies of Massachusetts Bay, Plymouth and Connecticut, with their Narragansett and Mohegan allies. Its central event was the Mystic massacre of May 1637, in which colonists…

polish-swedish-war-1626-1629.s: The Polish–Swedish War of 1626–1629 was fought between Sweden under Gustavus Adolphus and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, chiefly in Royal and Ducal Prussia. Despite a Polish naval victory at Oliwa (1627) and Koniecpolski's win at Trzciana (1629), the Truce of Altmark…

portuguese-conquest-of-the-banda-orienta.n: Portuguese conquest of the Banda Oriental
portuguese-conquest-of-the-banda-orienta.s: The Portuguese conquest of the Banda Oriental was the war of 1816–1820 in which the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves invaded the territory east of the Uruguay River, held by José Gervasio Artigas and his federalists. After Artigas was defeated at Tacuarembó…

platine-war.s: The Platine War was fought in 1851–1852 between the Argentine Confederation under Juan Manuel de Rosas and an alliance of the Empire of Brazil, Uruguay and the Argentine provinces of Entre Ríos and Corrientes under Justo José de Urquiza. The allies ended the siege of…

pemmican-war.s: The Pemmican War was a conflict between the North West Company and the Hudson's Bay Company's Red River Colony in present-day Manitoba. It began when the colony's governor banned the export of pemmican, the Métis and fur traders' staple food, in 1814.

polish-teutonic-war-1326-1332.s: The Polish–Teutonic War of 1326–1332 was fought between the Kingdom of Poland under Władysław I the Elbow-high and the Teutonic Order, over Pomerelia, which the knights had seized in 1308. The Order, allied with John of Bohemia, invaded Kuyavia and Greater Poland, and the…

pyrrhic-war.s: The Pyrrhic War was fought from 280 to 275 BCE between Rome and Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, who came to Italy to help the Greek city of Tarentum. Pyrrhus defeated the Romans at Heraclea and Asculum but with heavy losses, giving rise to the phrase Pyrrhic victory.

peruvian-war-of-independence.s: The Peruvian War of Independence ended Spanish rule in Peru, the stronghold of royalist power in South America. José de San Martín's expedition landed in 1820 and proclaimed independence in Lima in July 1821, but royalist armies held the highlands.

prussian-crusade.s: The Prussian Crusade was the series of thirteenth-century campaigns by Polish dukes and above all the Teutonic Order to conquer and Christianise the pagan Old Prussians on the south-eastern Baltic coast. The Teutonic Knights arrived in the 1230s and built castles such as Thorn…

priest-king.s: The Priest-King is a small steatite sculpture of a bearded man, found at Mohenjo-daro in Sindh, Pakistan, in the 1920s and dated to about 2000–1900 BCE, in the city's Late Period. Broken off at the bottom and perhaps unfinished, it is 17.5 centimetres high, with a fillet round…

phaistos.s: Phaistos is a Bronze Age archaeological site in south-central Crete, Greece, with the remains of a Minoan palace and the town around it, one of the largest cities of Minoan Crete. First settled about 3600 BCE, it had a palace from about 2000 BCE, which was destroyed and…

palace-of-malia.s: The Palace of Malia is a Minoan palace and settlement site 3 kilometres east of the town of Malia in Crete, Greece. Dating from the Middle Bronze Age, the palace was destroyed by an earthquake and rebuilt, and most of the visible ruins belong to the rebuilding.

palace-of-nestor.s: The Palace of Nestor is a Mycenaean palace site on the hill of Epano Englianos in Messenia, Greece, about 17 kilometres north of Pylos, traditionally identified with the palace of Homer's King Nestor at "sandy Pylos". A two-storey building with storerooms, workshops, baths and…

pueblo-bonito.s: Pueblo Bonito is the largest great house of Chaco Canyon in northern New Mexico, built in stages by the Ancestral Puebloans and occupied between 828 and 1126. It had some 800 rooms, rising four and five storeys in places, two great kivas and more than thirty other kivas.

pyrgi-tablets.s: The Pyrgi Tablets are three gold plates of about 500 BCE, two inscribed in Etruscan and one in Phoenician, found in 1964 at ancient Pyrgi, on the Tyrrhenian coast of Lazio. They record the dedication of a temple by Thefarie Velianas, ruler of nearby Caere, to the goddess…

phoenician-alphabet.s: The Phoenician alphabet is a script of 22 consonant letters, written from right to left, used in Phoenicia and across the Mediterranean for most of the 1st millennium BCE. Conventionally dated from about 1050 BCE, it developed from the Proto-Sinaitic script, itself derived…

philip-melanchthon.s: Philip Melanchthon was a German Lutheran reformer, Martin Luther's collaborator and the first systematic theologian of the Protestant Reformation. A scholar of Greek and a Christian humanist, he became professor of Greek at Wittenberg in 1518, and his Loci communes of 1521 was…

peterloo-massacre.s: The Peterloo Massacre took place at St Peter's Field in Manchester, England, on 16 August 1819, when cavalry charged into a crowd of tens of thousands gathered to demand parliamentary reform. An estimated eighteen people were killed and 400–700 injured.

prince-gong.s: Yixin, Prince Gong, was a Qing imperial prince and statesman, the sixth son of the Daoguang Emperor and a leader of China's Self-Strengthening Movement. Left behind with full powers when the Xianfeng Emperor fled Beijing in 1860, he signed the Convention of Peking with the…

pottery.s: Pottery is the craft and products of forming vessels and other objects from clay fired at high temperatures; the earliest known pottery vessels, from Xianren Cave in Jiangxi, China, date to 20,000–19,000 years ago. Ceramic figurines are older: the Venus of Dolní Věstonice in…

potters-wheel.s: The potter's wheel is a machine for shaping, or throwing, clay into round ceramic ware; the oldest found, from the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture in western Ukraine, dates to the middle of the 5th millennium BCE. Slow wheels (tournettes) were in use in the Near East around 3500…

plough.s: A plough is a farm tool for loosening or turning soil before sowing; ploughs were at first powered by people, and the larger ox-drawn ard, or scratch plough, followed the domestication of oxen in Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley, perhaps as early as the 6th millennium BCE. A…

pound-lock.s: A pound lock is a chamber with gates at both ends in which the water level is raised or lowered to move boats between levels of a waterway, first built in Song dynasty China by Qiao Weiyue in 984. He placed two sluice gates 250 feet apart under a roof, replacing double…

proto-sinaitic-script.s: The Proto-Sinaitic script is the earliest known trace of alphabetic writing, found in about 30–40 inscriptions at Serabit el-Khadim in Sinai and in two at Wadi el-Hol in Middle Egypt dated to between 1900 and 1800 BCE. By the common theory, speakers of a Canaanite language…

pendulum-clock.s: A pendulum clock is a clock that uses a swinging weight, the pendulum, as its timekeeping element; it was invented on 25 December 1656 by the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens, inspired by Galileo Galilei's investigations of pendulums, and patented the following year. The…

periodic-table.s: The periodic table is an ordered arrangement of the chemical elements into rows (periods) and columns (groups), in which elements of the same group tend to show similar chemical properties; the first to become generally accepted was that of the Russian chemist Dmitri…

pasteurisation.s: Pasteurisation is the preservation of foods such as milk and fruit juice by mild heat, usually below 100 °C, to kill pathogens and extend shelf life; it is named after the French chemist Louis Pasteur, who found in 1864, at Arbois, that briefly heating young wine to about…

penicillin.s: Penicillin is a β-lactam antibiotic first obtained from Penicillium moulds; it was discovered in 1928 by the Scottish physician Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital in London, who saw that mould contaminating a bacterial culture appeared to kill the bacteria. A team led by…

polio-vaccine.s: Polio vaccines prevent poliomyelitis and come in two types, an inactivated virus given by injection and a weakened virus given by mouth; Hilary Koprowski first tested a live, attenuated oral vaccine successfully in New York in 1950. Jonas Salk's injected vaccine was announced…

photography.s: Photography, whose name means 'drawing of light', is the capture of camera images on light-sensitive materials; the first such image to be fixed was made by the French scientist Nicéphore Niépce in 1826 or 1827, after an exposure of hours or days. His partner Louis Daguerre…

perioeci.s: The perioeci, "those dwelling around", were the second-tier citizens of Sparta until about 200 BCE, free people living in several dozen dependent cities, mostly in Laconia and Messenia. These cities ran their own domestic affairs but followed Sparta's foreign policy and sent…

pronoia.s: Pronoia, Greek for "care" or "forethought", was a grant of state revenue in the late Byzantine Empire, from the 11th century to the 15th. It transferred imperial fiscal rights, chiefly the taxes of cultivated land, usually for the holder's lifetime; the emperor could revoke it…

pipiltin.s: The pipiltin (singular pilli) were the hereditary nobles of the Mexica, or Aztec, Empire. Some sources describe them as the children of rulers and lords (tlatoque and teteuctin); in a narrower sense the word named the lowest rank of the hereditary nobility, above commoners…

peninsulares.s: Peninsulares were Spaniards born in Spain who lived in the empire's possessions overseas, in the Americas, the Spanish East Indies or Spanish Guinea. Higher offices in Spanish America and the Philippines were held by peninsulares, who were distinguished from the criollos,…
